#1463. The nine major strategic blunders Ineos have made at Man United that prove they cannot be trusted to choose Michael Carrick's replacement

Published: 21:00 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 13:20 EST, 11 November 2026

Michael Carrick looks set to pay for Manchester United’s miserable start to the season with his job this week – but removing him won't fix the club's deep-seated problems.

Carrick took more points than any other Premier League manager between his arrival as Ruben Amorim's interim replacement in January and the end of last season.

He was rewarded with the job on a permanent basis but the Carrick era has quickly unravelled and United entered the November international break 18th in the Premier League, out of the Carabao Cup at the first hurdle and middling at best in the Champions League.

Carrick's dismissal is the latest shameful episode for Ineos, who took control of football decisions in February 2024 when Sir Jim Ratcliffe came on board as a minority owner.

Daily Mail Sport understands CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox still retain Ratcliffe's backing despite being the subject of fan chants calling for their dismissal at recent matches.

Berrada and Wilcox have failed time and time again and yet seem to escape accountability. Here are nine Ineos mistakes that have dragged Manchester United into the unlikeliest of relegation battles – and raise the question of whether they should be trusted to get the next managerial appointment right.

Michael Carrick's dismissal is the latest shameful episode for Ineos, who took control of football decisions in February 2024 when Sir Jim Ratcliffe came on board as a minority owner

Carrick looks set to pay for Manchester United’s miserable start to the season with his job this week – but removing him won't fix the club's deep-seated problems

Erik ten Hag looked to be on thin ice from the moment Ineos walked through the doors at Carrington.

One of his first conversations with the new hierarchy saw the Dutchman offer to put together a plan to overhaul United’s failing data department. The offer was rejected.

‘I offered my knowledge and abilities to Ineos to help them to construct, but they were of the opinion that they already knew everything,’ Ten Hag told The Athletic recently. ‘They were convinced of, say, the philosophy, the strategy, the work methods. But they came from petrochemicals, from Formula 1, from cycling. Top football demands something totally different.’

That summer, Ineos were caught on the hop by the groundswell of support to keep Ten Hag after United beat rivals City in the FA Cup final, when all indications were they had been ready to sack him. Ineos were put in an awkward spot. That said, they still openly flirted with other managers just days after United’s Wembley victory.

Future England boss Thomas Tuchel met with Ratcliffe in Monaco before he dropped out of the race. Gareth Southgate, Mauricio Pochettino, Thomas Frank and Roberto De Zerbi were considered as Ten Hag remained in limbo, all while United navigated the situation without a sporting director or a CEO.

In the end, with tail between legs, an Ineos delegation flew to Ibiza to interrupt Ten Hag’s holiday and agreed to extend his contract by a year, make changes to his coaching staff, as well as make promises for the upcoming transfer market.

Ineos were caught on the hop and kept on Erik ten Hag (right) after United beat rivals City in the FA Cup final, when all indications were they had been ready to sack him

‘They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned,’ Ten Hag explained. ‘We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep.’

According to Ten Hag, Ineos went back on their word having said they would not sell Scott McTominay, who joined Napoli that summer for £27.5million, and the manager was sacked 116 days after his deal was extended with another £200m splurged in the transfer window.

By the time Ten Hag was finally dismissed, with a compensation package of £10.4m for him and his coaching staff, Ineos had wasted close to a quarter of a billion through indecision.

Ratcliffe relentlessly pursued Dan Ashworth as he sought an elite sporting director to lead the new sporting structure. He believed the Englishman to be ‘clearly one of the top sporting directors in the world’ and ‘a very capable person’.

Ashworth spent five months on gardening leave after United eventually agreed a near-£3m compensation package with Newcastle United to get him, only to be gone after five months in the North West.

Ratcliffe would go on to blame Ashworth for the decision to stick with Ten Hag and there was a sense that Ashworth was not on board with the move to bring Ruben Amorim in. It all culminated in his shock exit after a 3-2 home defeat by Nottingham Forest in which he was escorted through the press room at Old Trafford with his head bowed en route to a meeting where he was sacked.

Ashworth was paraded as a move that showed Ineos could deliver on their ‘best in class’ mantra, only for them to ditch him embarrassingly quickly.

Dan Ashworth (second right) was paraded as a move that showed Ineos could deliver on their ‘best in class’ mantra, only to embarrassingly ditch him less than six months later

Sir Dave Brailsford, one of Ratcliffe’s most trusted lieutenants, was also an unmitigated disaster. He started off as a crucial figure behind the scenes and his ‘marginal gains’ mantra became a key focus for everyone as he led the renovation of the Carrington training base.

Brailsford drove the appointments of Omar Berrada and Dan Ashworth, and was one of the key men behind ‘Mission 21’, United's bid to win a 21st Premier League title, and ‘Mission 1’, to win a first Women’s Super League title. Both fell under the ‘Project 150’ umbrella he was particularly proud of, to win titles in the club’s 150th anniversary in 2028.

Sixteen months after coming in, Brailsford was removed from day-to-day operations and earlier this year he fully separated from the club by coming off the board.

Brailsford ran football operations at a time of mass redundancies, fans being alienated by ownership, a failing team that produced its worst Premier League finish of 15th, and millions wasted in the transfer market on players that quickly depreciated in value.

Ruthless job cuts, something key Ineos figures have long insisted were essential for the health of the football club, totally destroyed morale and have, according to some remaining staff, completely changed the club for the worse.

In July 2024, staff were told of the need to cut 250 jobs, as company credit cards were cancelled, and staff were asked to contribute towards expenses. In February 2025, Ineos announced a further 150-200 jobs would need to be cut all while austerity measures – the scrapping of free lunches among them – escalated.

All of this against the backdrop of the senior executives continuing to be paid handsomely for gross levels of under-performance.

Having arrived as a technical director working under Ashworth, Wilcox soon found himself thrust into the biggest executive job in the Premier League, as director of football at United.

Omar Berrada (right) is a close friend and supporter of Jason Wilcox (left) and trusts him implicitly, as does Ratcliffe, who believes he has the ‘best eyes’ at the club

He pitched up at United having navigated close to nine months in the same role at Championship side Southampton. Prior to that his expertise had been across at Manchester City in youth development.

Berrada is a close friend and supporter of Wilcox and trusts him implicitly, as does Ratcliffe, who believes he has the ‘best eyes’ at the club. Wilcox was one of the driving forces behind the appointment of Amorim and it was he who would go on to clash with the Portuguese at the end, leading to his eventual sacking.

Wilcox is very hands-on, routinely seen close to training sessions, and has travelled with the team on numerous occasions.

‘When I listen to Jason speak, I get what he’s saying,’ Ratcliffe told The Times in March 2025. ‘He’s a warm character, he’s got a sense of humour, he knows what he’s talking about.’

Wilcox has been accused of interfering too much while not establishing the game model Ineos long promised to implement, regardless of who the head coach is. The director of football was called out in a post-match interview by Lisandro Martinez this season and Wilcox has inexplicably remained in the shadows while players and Carrick face up to the club’s failings.

A patchy recruitment record, all while preparing to search for a third permanent manager in less than 12 months, Wilcox has had next to no positive impact on United’s first team since assuming Ashworth’s job.

Hurting from the way they totally miscalculated and mishandled the Ten Hag situation, Berrada and Wilcox pushed to convince Amorim to abandon Sporting Lisbon mid-season – something he did not want to do – and bring his philosophy to Old Trafford.

It was explained that his 3-4-2-1 system would take a long time to embed onto a squad that had been playing 4-2-3-1 but United's decision-makers were undeterred and forked out £11m to get Amorim and his staff in.

It was explained that Ruben Amorim's 3-4-2-1 system would take a long time to embed but United chiefs were undeterred and forked out £11m to get Amorim and his staff in

A further £250m was spent on the squad the next summer but Amorim's standing took another pounding following a League Cup giantkilling at Grimsby Town

Hiring Amorim in isolation wasn’t an error. He represented a bright young manager that had a clear philosophy – something Ineos haven’t shown in two and a half years – but he had been overlooked by West Ham and Liverpool.

One well-placed source told Daily Mail Sport that Liverpool compiled a dossier on all the reasons Amorim would not be able to succeed at Anfield, largely down to how many players would need to be recruited to make his vision a successful reality.

Amorim was ‘rewarded’ with just two arrivals in January 2025 in the shape of Patrick Dorgu and Ayden Heaven, while the following summer saw a clash of ideas in terms of transfer targets. Senne Lammens arrived despite Amorim seeking a veteran goalkeeper to replace the hapless Andre Onana.

Amorim guided United to their lowest Premier League finish and lost the Europa League final in Bilbao to Ange Postecoglou’s Tottenham Hotspur. A further £250m was spent on the squad with the attack overhauled but his standing took another pounding following a League Cup giantkilling at Grimsby Town.

Relations between Amorim and Wilcox deteriorated severely and they clashed in a meeting on the eve of the trip to Leeds United, which would prove his final game. Amorim unleashed a fierce rant which intimated that figures such as Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell were overstepping the mark with their input and that they needed to allow him to be the ‘manager’ of the club.

Having come under pressure to change formation and the style of play, Amorim was sacked the morning after drawing at Leeds.

Rather than actually devise a plan to deliver Amorim’s vision, Ineos instead tried to get clever and turned to Harry Marra, a renowned track and field coach, to come in as a consultant.

He was given the remit of assessing individual player running mechanics, acceleration and deceleration. Mason Mount was one of those who Marra identified and he attempted to adjust the 36-cap England midfielder’s running gait.

Ratcliffe imparted advice on stretching techniques he had learned from running the London Marathon to figures in the Carrington physio room

Add from the episode in which Ratcliffe imparted advice on stretching techniques he had learned from running the London Marathon to figures in the Carrington physio room, you got the picture of an ownership that didn’t seem to understand that top-level football isn’t track, field, or cycling.

Performance on the pitch only got worse after this, not better.

8. Prioritising new stadium over a new left back

Speaking to reporters in Dublin this summer shortly after being given the United job full-time, Carrick used the word ‘push’ almost a dozen times when referencing what the club still had to do in the transfer market.

But Ineos, again believing they are the smartest people in the room, ignored those pleas and stuck to their plan to ‘fix’ one part of the team per summer. It was the attack in 2025, and in 2026 it would be the midfield, with the defence to come next year.

So, despite knowing full well that expecting another injury-free campaign from Luke Shaw was an enormous gamble, they did it anyway and made no defensive reinforcements. It hasn’t taken long for that move to backfire spectacularly.

Instead, the decision was made to purchase land to the tune of £60m so they can plough on with plans for a swanky new 100,000-seat 'Wembley of the North' stadium that many fans believe will never be built.

Rather than fixing the team's defence, United chiefs spent £60m on a slither of land to progress with their plans for a 100,000-seat 'Wembley of the North'

The way Carrick has been treated in this whole saga has been cruel and a sign of why managers should think twice about taking a job under Ineos

An emergency meeting after a 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last month looked set to be the end for Carrick until Berrada, Wilcox, Ratcliffe and the Glazers surprised the football world and simply did nothing. Everyone just continued with business as usual with no backing for the beleaguered Carrick.

Defeat at Chelsea, coupled with two frantic displays to come from 2-0 down against both Roma and Aston Villa followed. Then came the revelation on Monday that Berrada and Wilcox had settled on a recommendation to the board that they should sack Carrick. But instead of being sanctioned immediately, Carrick spent seven hours at Carrington on Tuesday to take training and watch an Under 17s match.

We are told yet again that Carrick's future will finally be decided on Wednesday at a meeting in Monaco, but in the meantime he must carry on until he gets wind he has been officially sacked.

The way Carrick has been treated in this whole saga has been cruel and a sign of just why managers should – and will – think twice about taking a job under Ineos.

#1462. Prince William asks Aston Villa boss Unai Emery about the team EVERY DAY - as he reveals he's become a bigger supporter since becoming a father to football-mad George

Published: 07:23 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 14:24 EST, 11 November 2026

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery has revealed how passionate Prince William is about his beloved football club and opened up on their relationship.

The Prince of Wales, 44, has been a fan of Villa since his days at Eton when he idolised club legend Paul McGrath - shunning the more conventional Premier League big beasts supported by his schoolmates.

He regularly attends matches at Villa Park and across Europe alongside his son George, and he has been a prominent figure during their success under Emery in recent times.

This included the Prince partying with Villa's squad after last season's Europa League triumph and he watched them against Barcelona in the Champions League at the Nou Camp last week.

And, in a special edition of Country Life magazine, which was guest edited by the 44-year-old, Emery reflected on their relationship and how often they talk about the club.

’During the transfer window, he’s asking about the team every day,' the Villa boss said. 'How is the team? How are you? How are we going to play some players? How are we going to do? He is always so close to us and we appreciate it so, so much.

Unai Emery has revealed how passionate Prince William is about Aston Villa and opened up on their relationship

The Prince pictured alongside his son George at Villa's game against Barcelona last week

A special edition of Country Life, guest edited by the 44-year-old, featured a piece on Emery

’When he’s with us, he’s a fantastic guy. We’ve had lunch together, he’s watched training sessions, we share conversations, everything about football. He shows his humble personality with us - I can’t forget it. For me, it seems unbelievable.

'He’s our boss, but he’s always trying to be at our level, respecting so much everything we are doing here. If he’s sitting with us to have lunch, he asks “Where am I sitting?” Wherever you want! It’s fantastic.

‘We are scoring, he is celebrating, it is fantastic for us. If we can give him good news, good results, good moments in football, we are proud of it.’

In the same article, the Prince of Wales went on to reflect on his love of football and Villa, revealing how he has become increasingly passionate over the years.

He added: 'Football feels like a second family to me, I love the tribal nature of being among others who support the same team. We all experience the highs and lows of following that team together and you get the feeling that you belong somewhere.

'I used to be a defender, usually right back, and I’m hoping to play in a few fathers’ five-a-side matches. Since having children, I’ve become even more fanatical than I thought I would be about the game.

'I wasn’t like this when I was 18 or 20, I kept an eye from a distance. Now, I probably think and talk about Aston Villa every day. I enjoy looking to see what is going on: the stats, the players’ recovery, tactics and matches.'

The Prince is regularly pictured watching his beloved team at Villa Park and across Europe

When asked previously about why he settled on the Midlands club, Prince William shared that it was the thrill of supporting a club without season after season of successes which had brought him to Villa.

'A long time ago at school I got into football big time. I was looking around for clubs. All my friends were either Man United fans or Chelsea fans and I didn’t want to follow the run-of-the-mill teams,' he told the BBC in 2015.

'I wanted to have a team that was more mid-table that could give me more emotional rollercoaster moments.

'Aston Villa’s always had a great history. I have got friends of mine who support Aston Villa and one of the first FA Cup games I went to was Bolton v Aston Villa back in 2000. Sadly, Villa went on to lose to Chelsea (in the final).

'It was fantastic, I sat with all the fans with my red beanie on, and I was with all the Brummie fans and had a great time.

'It was the atmosphere, the camaraderie and I really felt that there was something I could connect with.'

#1461. California votes to give record $8.4 billion to medical research

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Students, researchers and others at the University of California, Los Angeles, have protested over cuts to science funding made by the administration of US President Donald Trump during the past two years.Credit: Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty

Voters in California have approved US$8.4 billion in funding for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history.

The funding proposal, known as Proposition 38, appeared on the ballot for voters in California in last week’s US mid-term elections, but it has taken nearly a week for officials to count enough ballots to declare it a success. The state government will pay for the research — which aims to find treatments that harness or re-engineer the body’s immune system to fight illnesses such as cancer and Alzheimer’s disease — by selling state government bonds. (This is unusual for science funding. Bonds are typically reserved to pay for infrastructure projects such as road construction and require the state to pay back its debt with interest.)

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Supporters of the proposal say that the funding will provide stability for researchers in California, who have been affected by political turmoil. The administration of US President Donald Trump has pushed for massive cuts to science funding; put political appointees in charge of grant decisions at federal science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health; and forced policy change at US universities that receive federal funding, including those in California.

The $8.4 billion “is an advantage to California that is unprecedented”, says Antoni Ribas, a cancer researcher and physician at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), who supported Proposition 38. It will make the state “even more of a global hub for immunology research”.

But the proposal has sparked debate. That’s because it calls for about half of the funding to be given directly to research institutes — and the only institute that matches the criteria called for in the proposal is one co-founded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire medical-device inventor. He wrote the proposition and donated about $45 million of his own funds to get it placed on the ballot and to campaign for its passage.

“I feel like the voters have been taken advantage of,” says Sarah Hill, a political scientist at California State University in Fullerton, who tracks the state’s ballot measures. Michelson did not respond to Nature’s request for comment before this story was published, but has said elsewhere that he will not personally profit from the bond revenue.

In California, citizens can place proposed laws directly on the election ballot by collecting hundreds of thousands of voter signatures.

The state has funded scientific research through this process before. In 2004, after then president George W. Bush restricted federal funding for human embryonic stem-cell research, voters in California approved a $3-billion bond to establish the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, which they then voted to replenish with another $5.5 billion in 2020.

A campaign mailer encouraging California voters to support Proposition 38.Credit: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty

“The model works,” Ribas says. Immunologists have been making great strides with medicines such as personalized treatments called CAR-T therapies, which are revolutionizing care, he says. There has also been a flurry of research into developing vaccines, including the mRNA shots that have been the target of funding cuts by the Trump administration. Proposition 38 will ensure that such research can continue regardless of the political headwinds, Ribas adds.

Around $4 billion from Proposition 38 will fund grants for researchers at select public universities and non-profit institutes in California through a competitive review process. According to the proposal, any commercialized therapies developed through funded research must be sold at a 20% discount to people in California, with 10% of drug royalties returning to the state’s general fund.

#1460. Max Dowman-mania could make League Cup hottest ticket in town

There is an obligation on all of us, from supporters to pundits and journalists, to remain calm and measured about footballers as young as Max Dowman. But, my word, he does make it difficult. Arsenal’s 16-year-old sensation continues to sparkle whenever he steps on to the field, and he did so again with this superb display against Ipswich Town.

"The hype will only continue to grow!"Max Dowman that is delightful! 👏 pic.twitter.com/UfFY1VSyXn

At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again. The forward’s age and inexperience means he is still used sparingly in those high-priority competitions. The League Cup, by contrast, may prove to be his domain over the coming months.

Dowman’s double at Portman Road made him just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side. The first was Wayne Rooney, for Everton against Wrexham in 2002.

The two goals underlined why there is so much excitement around Dowman. The first was a demonstration of his prodigious dribbling ability, as he weaved through Ipswich’s defence and buried his shot with the weaker right foot. The second showed his composure: a slotted finish, rolled in with ease.

Max Dowman nets his second of the game! 😍 pic.twitter.com/XRZ9GqZx3x

As Mikel Arteta approaches the point of signing a new contract in north London, one wonders how much the idea of developing Dowman will excite him as he looks to the future. Which manager would not want to coach a player of such natural ability? Which manager would not want to see how good he could be? The same is true of Marli Salmon, the 17-year-old defender who also impressed on Tuesday night.

“A joy to have him,” said Arteta of Dowman. “It’s remarkable. It’s something very natural for him. He can deliver those actions effortlessly, I would say. What we have to do is look after him. He is 16. You don’t see that in this league. In other leagues in Europe, that’s a totally different context.

“Having two teenagers playing for Arsenal at this level is so fulfilling. Because I’ve been there and just to be able to contribute to somebody’s career and dream, to be able to experience a game like tonight, is phenomenal. And yeah, medium and long term, we know that if they continue to develop in the way that they are, we are going to have two tremendous footballers.”

"He was brilliant, he made the difference - we need to look after him" 🌟Mikel Arteta says Arsenal need to "be really cautious" with 16-year-old Max Dowman after he scored twice in Arsenal's 4-2 win over Ipswich 🔴 pic.twitter.com/1msJAEkK8z

Dowman’s two goals, along with strikes by Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino, secured a comfortable victory for Arsenal against Premier League opponents. Ipswich scored a goal of their own, through Anis Mehmeti, but never seemed likely to cause the visitors too much bother. A late strike from former Arsenal player Chuba Akpom was only a consolation. “We found a way to fight back into it,” said Gary O’Neil. “Losing by two goals to them isn’t a dreadful effort.”

Dowman is already developing a trademark goal, of sorts. His first strike for the club, against Everton last season, came after he left an opponent face-down on the turf at the Emirates Stadium. He inflicted the same pain here upon poor Cédric Kipré, who tried to tackle the teenager in the seventh minute but ended up with a mouthful of grass.

It was an image that encapsulated Arsenal’s dominance in the early exchanges, as was the sight of Madueke firing in the second. The chance came after Bruno Guimarães and Merino, majestic in midfield, had monstered Ipswich’s attempts to play out from the back. Merino was dominant throughout, winning tackles with steel and then spinning away opponents with style. “He’s unbelievable,” said Arteta.

Arsenal’s long-term relationship with the League Cup is not a particularly healthy one. For a club of their stature, it is a source of mild embarrassment that they have not won this competition since 1993. They came close last season, reaching the final at Wembley, but were defeated by Manchester City.

Given the depth of Arteta’s squad, Arsenal really should reach the final again. If this is a tournament for the B-team, at least in these early stages, then Arsenal probably have the best B-team in the country. They started this game without any of Bukayo Saka, Declan Rice, Martin Odegaard, and Kai Havertz but were still extraordinarily strong in midfield and attack.

The only pre-match concern was their defence, which has been weakened by a couple of early-season injuries. Arsenal started with Salmon at centre-back and the teenager was in direct combat with the physical, sharp-elbowed threat of Ipswich striker Zian Flemming. He stood up to the challenge with determination and class.

Ipswich had made 10 changes following their victory at Crystal Palace at the weekend, which was an indication of where the Carabao Cup sits in their priorities. They were able to get into Arsenal’s penalty area but never gave the impression they could really hurt the Premier League champions, apart from when Mehmeti converted Jack Clarke’s low cross.

Akpom struck in the 91st minute to encourage O’Neil, but by then the game had been lost. Arsenal’s work, and indeed Dowman’s work, had been done.

On managing the hype that surrounds Dowman, Arteta said: “What we have to do is look after him. He’s 16 years old, you don’t see that in this league. In other leagues in Europe, that’s a totally different context, but in this league, with the demands... We need to make sure that every time we throw him in it’s in the right context with the right preparation.”

Conor Coady shares his thoughts on Arteta’s role in Dowman’s development:

"He'll know how to nurture him!" 🗣️Conor Coady says Mikel Arteta is the perfect manager for Max Dowman 👏 pic.twitter.com/YdgLxfKiOf

Asked about Dowman’s two-goal performance, Arteta said: “A joy to have him, Marli [Salmon] as well. Seventeen years old, to play at that level with the physicality they have to be able to handle that level, it’s remarkable. Max, yeah, it’s inevitable to talk about him when he scores and he creates the moments he has created tonight. It’s normal.”

He added: “He is coping better and better and better, he did the action where he regains the ball and wins it in the first goal, he loses his man... He’s an unbelievable player because of the character that he has and how much he loves to play on the biggest stage and still handles the situation with such naturality.”

Speaking in his post-match press conference, Mikel Arteta said: “Really pleased with a lot of things we did tonight, the way we attacked the game, how dominant, fluid and aggressive we were, right from the beginning to try to influence the result. We scored two very early goals that gave us obviously a great platform for the game.

“Individually some big performances as well. Some debuts tonight which is great to see as well, so we take a lot of positives from tonight.”

Gyokeres ended up making 18 touches across the 90 minutes.

The Swede is not the type of player to take scores of touches (his average in the league last year was 18.14, so today was about on par for him), but you feel that there were opportunities for him to work into the half-spaces a bit more, as he did towards the end of the match.

Arteta’s side are through to the fourth round of the League Cup.

Plenty of talking points: Dowman, Salmon and an ominous Arsenal showing... Leave your thoughts on the match and join the conversation in the comments section beneath this live blog.

Ipswich Town 2 Arsenal 4 (Akpom) Davis picks out Akpom who swivels to deceive Konsa before sweeping home. There was perhaps a foul in the build-up as Lewis-Skelly appeared to get held back by the goalscorer as he scrambled to get back.

There will be two minutes of time added on.

Dowman seemingly makes history with every touch of the ball. A remarkable talent.

Arsenal are finishing this match with a 16-year-old, 17-year-old and two 18-year-olds on the pitch. A good evening for the academy.

And right on cue, Salmon picks up the ball on the halfway line and drives forward, eventually forcing a foul from Nunez who goes into the book for his troubles.

Gyokeres finally gets a sniff at goal but Greaves is wise to his movement in behind and times a slide-tackle perfectly to poke the ball off for a corner.

Ibrahim comes on for Zubimendi before it is taken and joins the crew congregated at the far post but Walton punches Odegaard’s delivery away.

A really assured performance from Salmon, who has completed all 61 one of his passes and marshalled Flemming and Akpom with maturity beyond his years.

Chance! A high regain puts Mehmeti into a promising position in the right half-space, but his cross in to Akpom comes to nothing.

Tzolis, who is booed by the home fans owing to his Norwich connections, has a glimpse at goal but is immediately closed down before Ipswich earn a corner after a swift transition but it is easily dealt with.

There is an appeal for a handball off an Arsenal defender in the second phase of the set-piece but Egeli is offside so it matters not.

Just the 13 touches for Gyokeres tonight, make of that what you will...

Arteta shuffles the pack again, taking off Eze and Madueke for Tzolis and Odegaard.

Florentino tries his luck from the edge of the box, but his effort is comfortably saved by Kepa despite taking a slight deflection off Konsa’s Achilles.

It has been a relatively quiet night for Eze as Arsenal have prioritised attacks down the right. He twists this way and that and escapes the clutches of Furlong but his eventual effort sails well over.

Davis gets his teeth into the action right away. He swings in a cross from the left but it’s smothered by Kepa.

Ipswich’s substitutes have breathed some life into their attack. Akpom fires a cross-cum-shot towards goal but strikes the side-netting.

Another couple of substitutions for O’Neil, who will now be thinking about Everton next weekend. Davis and Walle Egeli are on for Ouattara and McAteer.

For those who are into your statistics, another Dowman goal here would create some history...

The record for the youngest hat-trick scorer across all professional tiers of English football belongs to Trevor Francis.

Playing for Birmingham City against Bolton Wanderers in Division Two on February 20, 1971, Francis scored four goals in a 4-0 win at just 16 years and 307 days old.

Guimaraes makes way for 18-year-old Julienne.

Ipswich Town 1 Arsenal 4 (Mehmeti) Clarke makes an immediate impact, bursting down the left before cutting the ball back to Mehmeti who had just held his run and is able to beat Kepa from 10 yards out.

Ipswich have been outgunned in the centre of the park, with Arsenal seemingly always creating plus-one and even plus-two situations.

O’Neil makes a pair of changes, replacing Philogene and Flemming with Clarke and former Arsenal striker Akpom.

Ipswich Town 0 Arsenal 4 (Merino) Arsenal work the ball infield from the right in instalments, Madueke feeding Zubimendi who passes through Dowman to Merino on the edge of the box who opens up his body before guiding the ball around Walton.

Arsenal are FLYING!Merino puts another goal away for the Gunners 🔥 pic.twitter.com/nrzHHk1bou

Max Dowman was first spotted by Arsenal at four years old. He’s been running past opponents and scoring goals ever since. Now he’s just doing it on the professional stage, in front of the watching world, but it still looks completely normal to him.

Chance! It could, and maybe should, have been four. Merino threads a wonderful through-ball beyond Ipswich’s final line of defence and Madueke steals in to poke the ball across the face of goal with the outside of his left boot. Gyokeres was in the middle but could not divert the ball goalwards.

Kepa stretches to claim a looped Flemming cross which had echoes of the Spaniard’s game-defining error in last year’s League Cup final. This time he collects with a minimum of fuss. That Flemming was so far out on the left will be of concern to O’Neil.

Ipswich Town 0 Arsenal 3 (Dowman) Madueke picks out Zubimendi in the box who in turn finds Dowman in the right half space and he gallops on to the ball before arrowing the ball past Walton. The assist had grazed Greaves’ outstretched arm and would surely have led to a penalty had Dowman not done the honours.

Max Dowman nets his second of the game! 😍 pic.twitter.com/XRZ9GqZx3x

Arsenal’s kick-off routines caused a stir last season, but this term they have mixed things up once more. Here, Zubimendi lays off Lewis-Skelly, who punches in a line-breaking pass to get Arsenal on the front foot from the off.

Zubimendi gets us going again for the second 45 minutes. Konsa has replaced Gabriel at the interval.

Such is the midfielder’s versatility, his heat map tonight paints a wildly different picture to that from his 45 minutes at the Stadium of Light over the weekend. He has played the midfield-sentry role in Suffolk and has executed it well.

It is further evidence as to why Arteta was hell bent on signing him in the summer. You would imagine his all-conquering presence will relieve pressure from Rice and Zubimendi’s shoulders. They were out on their feet by the end of the last campaign.

Liverpool are ahead against Spurs at Anfield thanks to this strike from Mac Allister:

Pick that out!! 🇦🇷Alexis Mac Allister hits a beauty into the roof of the net 🔴 pic.twitter.com/G7OT27CA8P

Arteta’s nine changes are looking fairly sensible now. He will be particularly pleased to have seen fringe players like Dowman and Madueke get on the scoresheet so emphatically. Arsenal will need their full squad to achieve their lofty goals this season and that half will give Arteta confidence that they have enough firepower to last the course.

We’ll play one minute of time added on...

Arsenal inject a bit of calm to proceedings with a healthy spell of possession. Their horizontal and vertical rotations (Lewis-Skelly is now minding to drop into that Rice role alongside the centre-backs) are proving tricky for Ipswich to track.

Gyokeres gets a shot away after a clever run in behind by Merino but cannot get enough pace behind his strike to trouble Walton.

Mehmeti brings down a searching ball from deep and faces up to Gabriel as he enters Arsenal box. Such is the Brazilian’s poise, though, that even when the Ipswich forward appears to have worked a yard of space, he telescopes in his leg and stops Mehmeti’s advances with perfunctory ease.

Ipswich are getting more bodies forward, with both full-backs bombing on. The ball is worked out to Furlong out on the right but, in a promising position, he loses his footing and the ball rolls out of play.

Next comes a foray down the left, Philogene beats Salmon on the outside but Kepa gets down smartly to cut out his cross. The next goal will naturally go a long way to determining how this tie plays out.

Ipswich are in the ascendancy and Greaves heads goalwards off a corner but does not get the requisite contact to beat Kepa. Arsenal launch a swift counter which is snuffed out by McAteer, illegally, and he goes into the book.

Ipswich might have thrown the towel in at 2-0 but they are pushing quite hard here and have caused Arsenal a few problems since the second goal. Philogene looks particularly dangerous on the left flank.

Outtara has been Ipswich’s best attacking outlet and he threads another lovely ball into the path of Philogene who is just beaten to it by Gabriel. The subsequent corner is punched away by Kepa.

Kepa goes long and Greaves misjudges the flight of the ball. Madueke looks to be in, but Ipswich’s centre-half recovers well and is able to block the eventual effort.

Merino picks out Dowman between the lines and the teenager is straight into Ipswich’s backline. His effort is well-struck but is charged down and cleared to safety.

Better from Ipswich! Their best shot at getting back into this contest is through counters when Arsenal are not set, and here Outtara bursts down the left before swinging in a deep cross to Flemming who cuts the ball back to Mehmeti who fires the ball just over the crossbar.

Guimaraes is slotting in between Arsenal’s split centre-backs in Arsenal’s build-up and Ipswich are not prepared to go three vs three that high up the pitch meaning the Brazilian has all the time in the world to dictate play from there. We’ve seen this all season long from Rice.

Arsenal are in complete control. Madueke flashes a delivery across the face of goal which is just cut out by Kipre before Gyokeres can get a foot in.

Arsenal’s midfield is so powerful and they showed it there, as Guimaraes slammed into one tackle and then Merino followed up with another to create the chance for Madueke. Arsenal are completely dominant here.

A flurry of chances for Ipswich. Philogene’s lopping cross is tipped away by Kepa but the ball falls to Flemming at the back post and his effort pinballs around a thicket of Arsenal limbs before reaching Florentino on the edge of the box, whose effort sails over the bar.

Ipswich Town 0 Arsenal 2 (Madueke) That is goal of Ipswich’s own making. Walton’s loose pass out is picked off by livewire Guimaraes, and Merino spins in a ball in behind for Madueke to stride on to and spear beyond Walton into the bottom corner.

Arsenal are flying 🔥Noni Madueke adds a second for the Gunners 🔴 pic.twitter.com/gAVmAI3odx

Florentino’s loose pass is picked off by Dowman and the youngster earns a free-kick as the Ipswich midfielder attempts to recover. It’s taken quickly and Eze bursts into the box - there is a half-hearted shout for a penalty as the ball appears to strike Ouattara’s arm but the contact appears incidental and the referee waves play on.

Max Dowman’s second goal for Arsenal is quite similar to his first, scored so thrillingly against Everton last season. On both occasions he has put an opposition defender face-first in the turf before scoring the goal. Outrageous ability with the ball at his feet.

"The hype will only continue to grow!"Max Dowman that is delightful! 👏 pic.twitter.com/UfFY1VSyXn

Ipswich earn a free-kick on the left by-line but Gyokeres does his job at the near post and heads away Nunez’s delivery.

Ipswich Town 0 Arsenal 1 (Dowman) Simply majestic. A simple one-two with Eze on the left has Dowman running at Ipswich’s defence. He drops his shoulder and sells Kipre a dream before stroking the ball beyond Walton. “1-0 to the champions” sing the travelling fans.

Lewis-Skelly bursts down the left and picks out Dowman on the edge of the box. He attempts to tee up Guimaraes but Nunez gets a toe in and is able to avert the danger.

Early indications suggest Zubimendi will play in the nominal right-back position, inverting into midfield when Arsenal build up.

Madueke picks up the ball on the right flank and drifts inside before Guimaraes’ effort from the edge of the box is blocked.

Flemming gets us started. Ipswich kicking from right to left.

The players emerge from the Portman Road tunnel, Ipswich in their customary home blue shirts and white shorts, Arsenal in red and also white shorts. Last week Arsenal were made to change into red shorts to avoid a similar clash with Napoli, but apparently that’s no problem tonight. Modern football for ya!

Arsenal are warming up with Eze on the left, Madueke on the right and Dowman as the No 10 behind Gyokeres. In defence it looks like Zubimendi at right-back. The formation in the warm-up is not always the formation in the match, though...! They have played that trick before.

"You have to be patient with him" 🗣️Jamie Redknapp and Conor Coady on Max Dowman's potential for Arsenal 🙌 pic.twitter.com/O2bU0SQoJn

Arsenal have won the League Cup twice – in 1987 and 1993 – meaning eight clubs have better records, including Aston Villa (five titles), Tottenham Hotspur (four), Nottingham Forest (four) and Leicester City (three).

Their rather modest haul is a far cry from their record-setting 14 FA Cup titles. In the 33-years since Arsenal’s most recent League Cup triumph, the competition’s title sponsor has changed hands four times (kudos to anyone who can name all five!).

No team has scored more goals through substitutes in the Premier League than Ipswich, which is a nod to the promoted club’s depth and work in the summer transfer window.

It has meant that Gary O’Neil has had to leave established players out of match-day squads. “It was really tough leaving out Darnell [Furlong] and Anis [Mehmeti] from the squad [against Crystal Palace],” he said. “Doing that to good people is one of the toughest parts of the job. But I have faith in them, it’s just that everyone’s fit at the moment and we’ve had to recruit a strong squad to get us through an unbelievably challenging season.

“On Tuesday, whoever I pick, I have 100 per cent faith that they’re ready and that they’re going to represent what we do and how we go about it.”

On Hincapie’s omission from the match-day squad:

“Some players were carrying some fatigue, some little issues that we have to look after and some other players are available, fresh and in better conditions to play.

On Timber being left out of tonight’s squad:

“Everything is fine, but obviously he has played much more than we would have wanted. He played 53 minutes [against Sunderland] after five months. I will need to look after him.”

When asked if Arsenal will set up with a back three tonight:

Alan Davies, the actor and comedian who is a famously passionate supporter of Arsenal, recently told a story about a charity event he once attended with former captain Tony Adams. Speaking on The Tuesday Club podcast, Davies said Adams revealed his football philosophy to be: “You need seven.”

The “seven” in question, Adams explained, are seven members of the team who are ready and willing to fight the opposition in the tunnel after the game. Once a team have those seven individuals, Adams said, everything else flows from there.

For much of the past two decades, Arsenal have not had seven. In some years in the latter stages of Arsène Wenger’s tenure, they probably did not even have three or four. But that has all changed in recent seasons under Mikel Arteta, to such an extent that the Premier League champions would now undoubtedly bring considerably more than seven combatants to any touchline scrap or tunnel bust-up.

Saturday’s gritty 2-0 victory away to Sunderland provided evidence that Arsenal have added two more of these characters to their squad this summer.

Tonight will be a good test for young Marli Salmon, the 17-year-old defender who is the latest high-class graduate of the Arsenal academy. Arsenal have extremely high hopes for Salmon, who made four senior appearances last season. He could be in the centre of defence or at right-back tonight. I suspect Ipswich striker Zian Flemming might try to target Salmon with some physical challenges, especially in the air. Let’s see how he handles it.

Ipswich Town Walton; Furlong, Kipre, Greaves, Ouattara; Florentino, Nunez; McAteer, Mehmeti, Philogene; Flemming

Substitutes Palmer, Davis, O’Shea, Walle Egeli, Enciso, Clarke, Lukic, Maeda, Akpom

Arsenal Kepa; Zubimendi, Salmon, Gabriel, Lewis-Skelly; Guimarães, Merino; Dowman, Eze, Madueke; Gyokeres

Substitutes Meslier, Calafiori, Konsa, Tzolis, Odegaard, Ibrahim, Julienne, Saka, Havertz

Max Dowman announced himself last season, showing off his gilded footwork in impressive cameos off the bench. Who could forget that lung-busting run and goal against Everton?

And while the 16-year-old winger featured in Arsenal’s pre-season, these will be his first minutes of senior football in the season proper. His only game time thus far has come in the Premier League 2 under-21s competition and he was not included in the match-day squad at the Stadium of Light on Saturday.

When asked about Dowman after the victory at Sunderland, Arteta said: “I wish we could have him here, but we have the limitation with the numbers that we can have. He will have his chance, he will have his minutes and he will have to earn them like anybody else. We know the talent that we have, we know the players that we have there and we need to help him and find a way to make sure he continues to develop and help the team.”

Although keeping Ipswich in the Premier League must be Gary O’Neil’s primary goal, he has insisted that the club will embrace opportunities in the cups.

When asked how he would approach tonight’s tie, O’Neil said: “We’ll have a strong side, we’ve worked our socks off in the transfer window to give ourselves a strong squad. Of course, a different level to Arsenal, but we’ll be strong on Tuesday and we’ll do our best to win the game.

“The club has worked so hard to have these moments and of course it’s a cup game, but to have Arsenal and Liverpool come to Portman Road a week or so apart is what everyone has worked so hard for in recent years, so we’re going to enjoy it, we’re going to have a right go and worst thing that can happen is we lose to Arsenal.”

Good evening from Portman Road, where it’s a gorgeous night for football. Ipswich have made 10 changes, which is an indication of where this competition sits in their list of priorities. Arsenal have made nine.

The Arsenal line-up is quite hard to decipher. It looks like it might be Martin Zubimendi at right-back or centre-back. I’ll keep an eye on the warm-ups and report back shortly.

Gary O’Neil wins the rotation battle, raising Arteta’s nine changes with 10 of his own. Greaves the only survivor from last weekend’s win at Selhurst Park.

Your Town tonight! ✊ pic.twitter.com/EEYjPFww4Y

Young defender Marli Salmon comes into the starting XI as Mikel Arteta makes nine changes to the team that started against Sunderland on Saturday.

🔴 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 ⚪️Introducing your Carabao Cup Gunners starting XI ✨🤝 @deel

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of the Carabao Cup third-round tie between Ipswich Town and Arsenal. Mikel Arteta’s side have won all six of their matches so far this season, but travel to Portman Road fresh off an incident-filled win over Sunderland which thrust officiating back into the spotlight after Ezri Konsa conceded a penalty having been – in Arteta’s words – “judo-rolled” by Dan Ballard.

After the match, the Arsenal manager said: “I watched [the incident] 20 times and I cannot find a way to understand how to even think to give a penalty in this situation or the way the VAR has to intervene. So I don’t know what to think, really. But I’m sad, that we have to discuss, after such a beautiful game, something at this level that has the gravity of that because that changes the course of the season and it can cost you the championship… This cannot happen.”

Arteta may be pleased that VAR is not in use at this stage of the Carabao Cup, and all eyes will be on Peter Bankes who takes charge of tonight’s match against Ipswich.

This season Arsenal hope to arrest a startling League Cup record. It has been 33 years since they last lifted the trophy, during which time they have been runners-up seven times. Losing last year’s final will have also added fuel to Arsenal’s fire, and Arteta may resolve he must field a strong starting XI. In fact, he may not have much choice in his backline as Ben White has emerged as a serious injury doubt after picking up an injury at the Stadium of Light and may join Cristhian Mosquera and William Saliba on the treatment table. This would likely mean starting Jurriën Timber, who is only just returning from a long-term groin issue. There is more scope for rotation in advanced positions, with Noni Madueke, Viktor Gyokeres, Eberechi Eze and Mikel Merino contenders to start.

A 90th-minute Zian Flemming winner against Crystal Palace on Saturday helped Gary O’Neil’s Ipswich to their second win in four Premier League games, a feat they required 16 matches to achieve the last time they were in the top flight. Heavy investment into Ipswich’s squad has proved fruitful thus far, though in-form striker Emersonn is expected to sit out tonight having taken a knock at Selhurst Park.

#1459. Liverpool Confidential: Why Will Wright is the breakout star of Reds academy - LEWIS STEELE reveals club's plans for 6ft 3in hat-trick hero, his rise from Euxton Villa to Anfield and why coaches believe he's Andoni Iraola's next big thing

Published: 12:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 16:17 EST, 11 November 2026

On Will Wright’s last two trips abroad, he has needed to check in some extra baggage on the return flight.

Two UEFA Youth League away games, two hat-tricks and a pair of match balls to go with them. It’s now 13 goals for the season for 18-year-old Wright after his treble in a 5-3 win at Fenerbahce last week, and he has earned a first England youth call-up to boot.

Another hat-trick in one of those three games for the Young Lions? You wouldn’t bet against it – but Wright is used to these rapid rises.

Eighteen months ago, the 6ft 3in striker signed for Liverpool on a Friday, passed his driving test at 8am the next morning and then played for the first team the day after in a friendly at Anfield.

Now, the former Salford City striker is the name on everyone’s lips around Kirkby – with many thinking he could be the next cab off the rank from Liverpool’s famed academy.

Will Wright has lit up the academy goal charts this season for Liverpool, scoring a pair of hat-tricks in the UEFA Youth League

The Under 19s captain struck a brilliant treble against Fenerbahce last week to take his season tally to 13

Wright was first spotted by Salford scouts when playing for local side Euxton Villa, a ninth-tier club who have two England internationals among their alumni in David Unsworth and Sam Johnstone. Wright’s father, Mark, coached at Euxton and is an ex-professional for Preston North End.

It was an unusual path as most future stars are normally signed up by their mid-teens but Wright had injury issues amid a growth spurt that took him to the lanky frame that now bullies defenders. He had heel issues and has worked with a specialist on fascia problems.

Wright made his Salford debut in an 8-0 FA Cup defeat by Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City in January 2025 but scouts had already been alerted by his 50-goal haul at youth level. Arsenal, led by then-academy chief Per Mertesacker, launched an aggressive approach to sign him.

At one point, Liverpool signalled to Wright and Salford that they were pulling out of the deal, given Arsenal’s interest was so advanced. But the Reds soon returned to prevent the Gunners signing their next ‘Wrighty’.

The deal was worth peanuts in the grand scheme of things, around £300,000. It is good money for League Two Salford, though, and they will be set for additional payments for first-team appearances, honours and future national team caps.

Wright, who has a younger brother and is a Nike athlete, is a throwback No9. It is easy to reach for comparisons to current players but the way he combines pace, power and prolific finishing is not too dissimilar to Erling Haaland.

He is a strong dribbler and scored a fantastic solo goal for Liverpool's Under 21s against Rochdale in the EFL Trophy in September, receiving possession on the touchline around halfway, tricking his way past two defenders and curling a sumptuous effort into the top corner.

He is the captain of the Under 19s team and I have watched him play live several times, including one game last season where he was clearly targeted by Atletico Madrid defenders. The striker was clattered, suffered a medial ligament injury and was sidelined for several months.

He is a strong dribbler and scored a fantastic solo goal for Liverpool's Under 21s against Rochdale in the EFL Trophy in September

Coaches have pinpointed hold-up play and heading as two things to work on, as well as instructing Wright not to ‘rise to the bait’ of bigger defenders who might try to ruffle him up

He has returned with a vengeance, with a hat-trick against LASK last month and then last week's effort against Fenerbahce. What impressed more in the latter was not his goals – one a penalty, the other two both true poachers’ finishes – but his assist.

Wright was on a hat-trick at the time but, instead of shooting, he played a ball to Finn Inglethorpe – son of academy director Alex – to score. Earlier, Wright and Josh Sonni-Lambie had argued over who was to take a penalty. Wright won the row and scored.

Under 21s boss Rob Page told the pair later that he would rather them show hunger to score and passion rather than shy away. Page is a huge fan of Wright and said: ‘There was a real maturity about his performance. One of the parts of the development for all the forwards is being unselfish in their actions.

‘As much as he wants to see the headlines and be successful himself, it is all about sharing that. Will has done that really well today with a hat-trick, a complete performance.’

Pressed on how far away Wright is from the first team, Page replied: ‘He doesn’t have to worry about that. Just bring the best version of yourself every day in training, give absolutely everything in games as he does. The rest will take care of itself.

‘He’s got a great support around him. His family are very supportive. Alex (Inglethorpe) is there to lean on, he’s got myself and Jay (Spearing, academy coach). He never gets carried away.’

Coaches have pinpointed hold-up play and heading as two things to work on, as well as instructing Wright not to ‘rise to the bait’ of bigger defenders who might try to ruffle him up. They have also worked on his off-the-ball runs to the back post.

So, what next? It is understood a January loan is being considered. Liverpool think toughening up Wright in a senior league could be a step worth taking, having used him in each of the last two pre-seasons. His agent was at the AXA Training Centre on Tuesday and there will be no shortage of clubs willing to take him on.

Liverpool think toughening up Wright in a senior league could be a step worth taking, having used him in each of the last two pre-seasons

Wright got six minutes off the bench against Como in a friendly at Anfield in August, coming on for Alexander Isak up front

Andoni Iraola will be consulted, too. He has called up the likes of Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and Luke Chambers this season and is eager to use young stars.

Iraola is in frequent dialogue with youth staff such as Page, Inglethorpe, plus Luiz Fernando Iubel who is often cited as the ‘link’ between the academy and first team.

The Brazilian has been spotted at several academy games this term, including for Wright’s hat-trick in Turkey where Iubel sat alongside sporting director Julian Ward and loans manager Gary Probert.

Whether a first-team breakthrough comes now or in the future, the future for Wright looks bright.

Dominik Szoboszlai’s participation with Hungary this week remains in the balance with the national team doing all they can to get their captain fit for crunch games.

The Hungarians take on Georgia and Northern Ireland in must-win Nations League matches – and may have to go without their star man. Szoboszlai hurt his knee in the win at Crystal Palace and, after an injury-hit six weeks, could do with a rest.

But he will try his best to be fit for national team duty and a decision will not be made until the 11th hour.

It comes after Virgil van Dijk pulled out of Dutch duty with a minor muscle issue. It is believed he has been managing the problem for at least a month and was surprised to be substituted on to the field against LASK — which might explain the team conceding three after he came on!

Virgil van Dijk (left) has pulled out of international duty and Dominik Szoboszlai (right) could be set to follow him

Confidential readers will recall our musings on Harvey Elliott a fortnight ago, with Valencia sources telling us that the La Liga outfit might consider cancelling his loan in January.

The English midfielder had struggled in Spain for fitness and form. He was then sent off against Villarreal but, as we reported, Valencia would give him another chance to prove his worth.

He has started well, scoring a free-kick in what was his first start for any club in 285 days. It was part of a notable 6-0 win in the Copa del Rey.

Elliott ran over to fans and put his arms aloft appearing to apologise, which adds to his comments a week ago about the red card where he said: ‘I made a mistake and I’m truly sorry. It won’t happen again.’

#1458. Crystal Palace sack Pierre Sage after disastrous 16-game spell - this is how his reign unravelled over late, intense sessions, dinner at the training ground and an unpopular assistant manager

Published: 10:17 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 07:52 EST, 12 November 2026

Crystal Palace have sacked Pierre Sage after players and club chiefs grew frustrated over his training methods, Daily Mail Sport can reveal.

A 3-1 defeat by Liverpool on Sunday saw Palace drop to bottom of the Premier League for the first time in nine years and proved to be the final straw for club bosses.

Daily Mail Sport understands that while the Palace players got on well with the 47-year-old, they were frustrated by his late training sessions – with some not starting until 4pm. The regimented routine required players to stay at the training ground for dinner on the night before matches, with some not returning home until 8pm ahead of a 2pm kick-off the following day.

The club's hierarchy, meanwhile, expressed concerns early in the Frenchman's tenure that he was not doing enough defensive work on the training pitch.

Sage's philosophy was that the best way to defend was having the ball, meaning training sessions focused on running, pressing and possession rather than defensive structure.

But the lack of focus led to a poor defensive record, with Palace conceding 30 goals in 16 matches across all competitions. Defending set-pieces and counter-attacks has been a persistent problem for Sage’s side, and he won just two of his ten Premier League games in charge.

Pierre Sage has been sacked by Crystal Palace after a dismal start to the season saw them win just two of their first ten games

Palace sit rock bottom of the Premier League, their leaky defence having conceded 24 goals

Daily Mail Sport understands many players voiced fears they were being pushed too hard in training, with sessions the day before a game particularly intense. There were also significant concerns about the quality of Sage's backroom staff, with his assistant Jamal Alioui proving especially unpopular among the players.

There has also been considerable turnover among senior executives, with six departures over the past 18 months. Chief financial officer Mitesh Velani is set to add to that number in the coming months. One well-placed source told Daily Mail Sport that the disruption to the club’s business operations has the hallmarks of a club heading for relegation.

As Palace look to bail themselves out of trouble, Daily Mail Sport understands talks are progressing with former Brentford and Tottenham boss Thomas Frank, who is expected to take over ahead of crucial games against Coventry and Hull after the international break.

Palace chairman Steve Parish first contemplated sacking Sage over his lack of defensive nous in September, but gave him a stay of execution after Palace kept a clean sheet in a spirited performance away at Leeds on the eve of the international break. However, that display proved an anomaly as Palace shipped 19 goals in the following nine games.

Palace have won just once in their last eight matches in all competitions, beating Fulham 1-0 in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

In September, Daily Mail Sport revealed tensions had emerged between Sage and Parish when the latter took a dim view of the decision to drop teenage defender Jaydee Canvot for their defeat by Ipswich Town.

Palace paid French club RC Lens £4million in compensation to appoint Sage in June after he won the French Cup, finished second in Ligue 1 behind Paris Saint-Germain and was named manager of the season last term. It was the first time in 10 years that Palace had paid compensation to appoint a manager.

Palace chairman Steve Parish (right) first contemplated dismissing Sage in September over a lack of defensive nous

Palace players found Sage’s training sessions too intense and struggled to adapt to the late schedule

Succeeding Oliver Glasner, Palace's greatest manager, proved too big a task for Sage.

Following Palace's loss to Liverpool, Sage insisted the Eagles have been playing better than their league position suggests and pleaded for more time. Those appeals fell on deaf ears.

'A lot of times I’ve said we deserved better and it was the case again (on Sunday),' said Sage. 'My job is not the most important thing, as I always said from the beginning. The most important thing is to find an efficient solution for the team and for the club.

‘I know how important it is for the club to stay in the Premier League. The club just have to believe in (me), and if it's not the case, they will take a decision. I always have confidence in myself because it's a big, big mistake to not be 100 per cent involved in what I have to do.

‘We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions and more efficiency and I think it will be OK.’

#1457. Why your physics project needs an anthropologist

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jaco de Swart is a historian and anthropologist of science at the University of Cambridge, UK.

The TAMBO team assesses suitable observatory sites in the Andes Mountains of Peru.Credit: Jaco de Swart

It is uncommon for a social scientist to have a seat at a meeting about an astronomical observatory, let alone for them to jointly lead one. For one-quarter of attendees to be social-science scholars is almost unprecedented. But that’s exactly what happens at meetings about the Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO), a proposed detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes to look for cosmic particles called tau neutrinos.

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Tau neutrinos are elusive fundamental particles that are transmitted through space from black holes and other distant sources. When these particles interact with rocks on Earth, they can produce a shower of other, short-lived particles. The idea behind TAMBO is that if such a shower were emitted from one side of a deep canyon, it could be picked up by an array of 5,000 detectors on the other side (TAMBO collaboration. Nature Astron. 10, 947–951; 2026). The Andes Mountains of Peru contain many promising sites.

For those who live in the area, however, the case for TAMBO is less clear. The Andes are a sensitive ecological environment and home to Indigenous farming communities that consider the mountains sentient beings that are integral to their society. The area is also affected by legal and illegal mining, large-scale infrastructure projects and legacies of colonialism. This all leads to scepticism towards large projects that are developed by people from outside the area.

I am the co-principal investigator of the TAMBO collaboration, alongside Peruvian neutrino physicist Carlos Argüelles at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. I lead the social-science and ‘responsible siting’ side of the project. Having received funding to build a proof-of-principle experiment called TAMBITO, we are searching for a potential location for the observatory.

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Since 2024, the TAMBO collaboration has built partnerships with 11 Peruvian institutions, which are involved in the design and development of the telescope. Scientific links are an important starting point, but they are not enough. No matter what their discovery potential is, big scientific experiments are not beneficial to everyone. For example, construction of the Thirty Meter Telescope has been stalled since 2015 because of protests triggered by objections to its planned site on Maunakea in Hawaii — a mountain that is sacred in Native Hawaiian culture.

To integrate environmental care into the project and build good relationships with the communities that might host the telescope, TAMBO brought in experts on the Andean region. In 2024, the collaboration held a workshop at Harvard’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, at which scholars and policymakers discussed what equitable astrophysics in Peru would look like. This led to the formation of a responsible-siting team that includes geographers, sociologists and anthropologists who have worked in the Andes.

IceCube just won a Nobel prize. Protect astroparticle physics projects with the same potential

IceCube just won a Nobel prize. Protect astroparticle physics projects with the same potential

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03623-w

The current, initial phase of the TAMBO project is made possible by a grant from the John Templeton Foundation.

#1456. Man United set to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as head coach: Club make formal approach to US Soccer after agreeing personal terms - with Michael Carrick's exit confirmed on Thursday

Published: 03:10 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 12:15 EST, 12 November 2026

Manchester United are set to name Mauricio Pochettino as head coach to replace Michael Carrick following a day of talks over both men.

United moved closer to putting Pochettino in charge at Old Trafford after reaching a verbal agreement with the US national team boss on Wednesday. The club then made a formal approach to US Soccer.

Meanwhile, the club’s chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox flew back from Monaco, where minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe was expected to ratify their decision to sack Carrick with the blessing of co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer.

Carrick’s departure could be confirmed on Thursday, but official confirmation of Pochettino’s appointment may take a little longer with more talks planned overnight on Wednesday.

Pochettino is currently at the US Soccer base outside Atlanta preparing for a CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final double header against Haiti, and is due to speak to the media on Friday.

It’s unclear if he will remain in charge for those games, with United said to be relaxed over the Argentine taking the team. It is possible he could stay for the first leg in Kingston, Jamaica at the weekend and then travel to Manchester.

Manchester United are set to name Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager - but he took training as usual on Wednesday

Pochettino, who has managed Southampton,Tottenham, and Chelsea, will succeed Michael Carrick

Carrick checked in at Carrington at 7.45am on Wednesday with his fate in the balance

He was pictured leaving Manchester United's training base at around 1.15pm

Pochettino is pictured working on United States national team duty on Tuesday (Source: X/USMNT)

The second leg is Cincinnati is not until the early hours of Thursday, and Pochettino may even would only take over at United on Friday with a huge game against Liverpool at Anfield 48 hours later.

It’s understood that the US Soccer Federation are ready for this contingency and have a succession plan in place should he leave.

It will cost Pochettino around £7million to buy himself out of his contract with the US Soccer Federation, with United ready to foot the bill.

The cost of bringing in his back-room team, including trusted assistants Jesus Perez and Miguel D’Agostino, will take the cost above £10m.

The 54-year-old only signed a new deal after the World Cup meaning that United could have got him for nothing in the summer.

Amid the secret talks between United and Pochettino’s camp on Wednesday, there was more intrigue when the federation cancelled media access to the players at late notice but allowed cameras to film an open training session.

Sources said the decision was made out of respect for Veterans Day in America, but it also meant the players didn’t have to field any awkward questions over their coach’s future.

Bournemouth midfielder Tyler Adams was quoted by the US media as saying: ‘Why would his name not be on it (United’s list)?

The United execs meet in Monaco today (Pictured is the Casino Monte-Carlo in Monaco)

‘I mean, the credibility, the resume speaks for itself. It goes to show for us how lucky we are to be able to work under a manager of his quality and the person he is.’

Meanwhile, Berrada and Wilcox flew back to Manchester from Nice on Wednesday with United expected to announce Carrick’s departure imminently after 10 months in charge.

The 45-year-old took training at Carrington for the second day running, arriving at 7.45am and leaving shortly after 1.30pm.

#1455. Spurs finally score... but still lose

They scored. Would you believe it? Tottenham Hotspur, the team with more zeroes than an England Ashes batting collapse, found the back of the net but still frustration persists for Roberto De Zerbi.

It could have been something different. The sight of the Italian dashing down the touchline in hailstones, grabbing his head in disbelief in the final seconds, showed this was not a straightforward tale of misery but, ultimately, the misery endures.

“I think this is five or six games we have been for sure not lucky,” De Zerbi lamented, but sympathy did not extend too far. Liverpool deservedly moved into the next round of the Carabao Cup, the gloss on Andoni Iraola’s most enjoyable night provided by Dominik Szoboszlai’s goal-of-the-season contender.

THAT'S MAGNIFICENT! 💥🔴Outrageous strike from Dominik Szoboszlai 👏👏👏 pic.twitter.com/meQ7nilsz6

Liverpool were abject against Fulham on Saturday but with 10 changes to the starting line-up, infused with the exuberance of novices Rio Ngumoha and the terrific Lewis Koumas, Iraola’s team were invigorated and only a lapse of concentration enabled Tottenham to make a fist of it.

Yes, they went down swinging, as their noisy fans demanded. But carelessness cannot be excused and while De Zerbi complained about bad luck, a bad miss from Lucas Bergvall in the 10th minute was the fork in the road for the tie. Tottenham stalled and Liverpool never looked back.

“We have to shoot more times and we have to shoot better,” De Zerbi harrumphed. “We have to finish better the clear situations. We are sorry for the result, disappointed and frustrated. I think it was unfair but we have to be stronger in these unlucky moments.”

Rather than fizzing his drive into the net, Bergvall succeeded only in firing straight at Giorgi Mamardashvili, when he had the whole target in front of him. It was, in all fairness, a brilliant save but he should never have been allowed to make it.

Big save from Giorgi Mamardashvili! 💪Lucas Bergvall is denied by the Liverpool goalkeeper. pic.twitter.com/fKUbfGLMku

The miss changed the atmosphere, as suddenly Liverpool grasped the need to be competitive. At the heart of it all were Ngumoha, James McConnell, Trey Nyoni and Koumas, the last-named a nuisance to Tottenham’s defenders in the way a wasp is to picnickers on a summer’s afternoon.

For all the money that has been lavished by this club over the past 14 months, the one thing that the locals buy into more than anything is the basics done properly: hard work, tackling, a refusal to take second best. Iraola did not want Koumas to go anywhere this summer and it was obvious why.

“I see him training every day,” Iraola said. “He knows very clearly what he needs to do, what the team needs. And also the energy he shows is contagious for the rest. When you see the runs up front, giving everything, you are kind of forced to go behind and use the same intensity levels.”

Simple tenacity enabled Liverpool to get back on an even keel and laid the foundation for them to take the lead. It was a terrific goal, started with a raking pass from Joe Gomez that Cody Gakpo controlled instantly on his chest before scuttling inside and inviting Ngumoha to charge forward.

Whether it was the winger or Destiny Udogie, who was sliding to make a challenge, that ended up playing the ball to Alexis Mac Allister is immaterial, all that mattered is that the Argentine effortlessly placed his shot into the top corner, leaving Martin Dubravka planted and helpless.

Pick that out!! 🇦🇷Alexis Mac Allister hits a beauty into the roof of the net 🔴 pic.twitter.com/G7OT27CA8P

Is Mac Allister playing with a point to prove? Possibly, given his comments about not being offered a new contract last week. Will Iraola be bothered? Not in the slightest. All he wants is top players at the top of their game and Mac Allister is climbing towards the levels he showed two years ago.

What De Zerbi would do to have a player in such form, but Tottenham are a skittish bunch, not the type of team who respond well in the face of adversity and their head coach, dressed in black with his oversized white trainers, regularly shook his head in exasperation.

His mood was not helped just before the interval, when Mohammed Kudus blasted over from eight yards following a zipped-in cross from Udogie, but he would not have called it truthfully if he had suggested Tottenham deserved parity at that stage. Soon Liverpool’s advantage would be doubled.

The buffer they sought arrived in the 54th minute and, again, it was another genuinely attractive goal, with possession being kept until it sped up when Ngumoha scurried forward, found Milos Kerkez, who played it to Mac Allister, who in turn gave Gakpo the opening he craved.

His touch was excellent, his finish was even better and away in the distance Iraola rattled his fists in delight. That is two goals and four assists to start the campaign for the Dutchman and yet Liverpool were ready to sell him to Manchester City two weeks ago. What on earth were they thinking?

Ruthless!! 🔥Cody Gakpo doubles Liverpool's lead against Spurs 🔴 pic.twitter.com/qlaaynMuwM

From that point, it seemed inconceivable that Liverpool would finish living on their nerves, but De Zerbi’s decision to introduce Andy Robertson – given a hero’s reception on his first return to Anfield – and Mateus Fernandes wrestled back some impetus. There was also a significant helping hand.

Unsurprisingly, Andy Robertson gets a great reception from the Liverpool fans on his return to Anfield 👏 pic.twitter.com/uNM6A00k5F

Mamardashvili had made some important saves, including one from Kudus that he celebrated on his own, but he is vulnerable at set-pieces and Fernandes’s looping corner gave Conor Gallagher the easiest headed opportunity in three years to change the dynamic.

Spurs have scored! ⚪️Conor Gallagher brings Roberto De Zerbi's side back into the game! pic.twitter.com/52zSCqClw4

“We were under pressure at the end, but I don’t think we were nervous,” Gakpo said.

He was right. Try as they might, Spurs could not quite get the opening they needed and as they chased in vain, Szoboszlai administered the final blow in mesmerising fashion, thrashing a bouncing ball into the Kop net from 30 yards. And as De Zerbi realised in the sodden conditions, with Tottenham it never rains. It only pours.

"A Steven Gerrard type of strike" 😍Jamie Redknapp and Conor Coady analyse Dominik Szoboszlai's wondergoal 🪄 pic.twitter.com/h9QTuP8lZc

🗣️ "The young players give us energy" 💪Andoni Iraola is very pleased with the way the Liverpool youngsters played after beating Spurs 3-1 at Anfield 👏#ITVFootball | @Carabao_Cup | @markpougatch | @Robbie9Fowler pic.twitter.com/bHjOrmccH2

Mamardashvili does well to save from a deflection, like he did a few minutes ago. Mamardashvili did not cover himself in glory for Tottenham’s goal but has made some great saves tonight.
