For immunoprecipitation, acetylated-lysine antibody (Cell Signaling Technology: 9441S) was used at 1 µg per 100 µg of lysate.

For immunofluorescent staining (COMET-mIF) and PLA assay, the following antibodies were used: p300 (Invitrogen: 33-7600, 1:150); CBP (Invitrogen: PA5-27369, 1:150); AR (Abcam: ab133273, 1:400); H3K27ac (Cell Signaling Technology: 8173S, 1:100); Ki-67 (Abcam: ab243878, 1:300); H2BK20ac (Abcam: ab177430, 1:250); CK8 (Abcam: ab53280, 1:50); ERG (Abcam: ab92513, 1:200); PSA (Cell Marque: 324M-16, 1:50); and MYC (Abcam: ab32072, 1:50).

For ELISA, the following antibodies were used: p300 (Cell Signaling Technology: 86377S, 1:1,000); and AR (Thermo Fisher Scientific: MA5-13426, 1:50).

VCaP cells were seeded at a density of 10,000 cells per well, and all other prostate cancer cell lines were seeded at 3,000 cells per well in poly-d-lysine-coated 96-well plates (Corning) and maintained at 37 °C with 5% CO2. After 24 h, cells were treated with a serial dilution of test compounds, with 6 replicate wells for each concentration. Following 120 h of incubation, cell viability was determined using the CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Luminescence was measured on an Infinite M1000 Pro plate reader (Tecan) and data were analysed using GraphPad Prism (v10; GraphPad Software).

A total of 4,000 VCaP cells or 1,500 LNCaP cells per well were seeded into poly-d-lysine-coated 96-well plates. After 24 h of incubation, cells were treated with a fixed concentration (100 nM) or serial dilutions of compounds and incubated for 4 h. The medium was then removed, and cells were washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) before fresh medium containing either vehicle or compounds was added. Phase-contrast images were collected every 4 h, and cell proliferation was quantified by measuring the percentage of confluence (phase object area).

Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 1× Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and denatured in NuPAGE 1× LDS sample buffer containing a reducing agent (Invitrogen) by incubation at 70 °C for 15 min. Protein concentrations were determined using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of protein (15–30 µg) were resolved on NuPAGE 3–8% Tris-Acetate or 4–12% Bis-Tris protein gels (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and transferred onto 0.45-µm nitrocellulose membranes (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the iBlot 3 Dry Blotting System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Membranes were blocked in TBS-T (Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20) containing 5% non-fat dry milk for 1 h at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies. After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and imaged using an Odyssey CLx Imager (LI-COR Biosciences). Supplementary Figure 1 shows the full, uncropped blots with molecular weight markers for all immunoblot experiments.

The binding affinities of test compounds to AR and CBP/p300 were measured using fluorescence polarization-based competitive binding assays. AR binding was assessed using the PolarScreen Androgen Receptor Competitor Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A15880) following the manufacturer’s instructions.

CBP/p300 fluorescence polarization assays were performed in 96-well plates (MTP96VPWB-EP, Eppendorf) using a CLARIOstar microplate reader (BMG Labtech). Serial dilutions of test compounds were incubated with fluorescein-labelled tracer (2 nM final) and CBP/p300 protein (20 nM final) in assay buffer (PBS pH 7.4 supplemented with 0.01% BGG, 0.01% Tween-20, and 2 mM DTT) to a final reaction volume of 100 µl per well. Plates were mixed for 15 min and incubated at room temperature for 1 h to reach equilibrium. Fluorescence polarization (mP units) was measured at 485 nm excitation and 530 nm emission.

For both AR and CBP/p300 assays, data analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism 10 using nonlinear regression. IC50 values were determined by fitting competition curves, and inhibition constant (Ki) values for competitive inhibitors were derived using nonlinear regression based on the Kd of the tracer and the concentrations of tracer and protein in the reaction. All fluorescence polarization experiments were conducted in duplicates across three independent biological replicates.

VCaP or LNCaP cells were seeded in poly-d-lysine-coated 100 mm culture dishes (Corning) and incubated overnight. Cells were incubated with the DMSO control or indicated compounds for 4 h at 37 °C before being collected and washed once with PBS. The cell suspension was then distributed into PCR tubes (50 µl per tube) and exposed to a predefined temperature gradient for 3 min using a Veriti Thermal Cycler (Applied Biosystems). Following equilibration to room temperature, cells were lysed by three freeze–thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen. Insoluble protein aggregates were pelleted by centrifugation at 20,000g for 20 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants containing soluble proteins were recovered for western blot analysis.

All modelling and simulations were performed with Schrödinger 2025-2 (Schrödinger). Because co-crystal structures of the LBD of AR in an open antagonist conformation were not available, we used our previously reported pseudo-open model58. The bound AR ligand was modified to generate JZY3221, the AR ligand used in our design of DALTACs. To model the p300-BRD interaction with GNE-049, we used the CBP-BRD–GNE-781 co-crystal structure (Protein Data Bank (PDB) 5W0E) as the starting structure59. CBP and p300 are highly homologous proteins, especially in their BRDs, which share conserved sequence and structures. Both proteins were prepared for further modelling using the Protein Preparation Wizard60.

We used the following structures as inputs to generate the initial AR–DALTAC-1–p300 complex: (1) AR in complex with JZY3221; (2) the p300 complex with GNE-049; and (3) JZY3032 (DALTAC-1) prepared with LigPrep module61. These inputs were submitted to Generate Degrader Complex (default settings: MCMM 10,000 steps, maximum clashes 5, maximum poses 50) to construct the ternary AR–JZY3032–p300 complex. The top 20 predicted complexes were further refined using Prime62. The top-scoring ternary complex was then selected for molecular dynamics simulations.

To perform molecular dynamics simulations, the predicted ternary complex was solvated in an explicit water box with periodic boundary conditions. A cubic box was constructed with a 10 Å buffer between solute and box edge and filled with TIP4P water63. The OPLS4 force field was used for all components. Production dynamics used a RESPA integrator with a 2 fs time step. Temperature was maintained at 300 K with a Nosé–Hoover chain thermostat64 (relaxation time 1.0 ps). Pressure was controlled at 1 atm with a Martyna–Tobias–Klein barostat65 (relaxation time 2.0 ps). Long-range electrostatics used a 9 Å real-space cutoff with particle–mesh Ewald for reciprocal space66. One continuous 1-µs simulation was performed without restraints.

Root-mean-square deviation analysis of protein backbones and ligand position indicated that the system equilibrated after approximately 750 ns. Accordingly, trajectory analysis focused on the last 250 ns. Protein–protein interface features were defined as minimum heavy-atom distances between AR and p300. Contacts shorter than 0.5 nm (5 Å) were retained. Principal component analysis was applied to these interface distances, and components explaining 95% of the variance were kept. The reduced data were clustered with HDBSCAN (min_cluster_size 25, centroids enabled)67. For each cluster, the frame closest to the centroid in principal component analysis space was saved as a representative PDB. Cluster occupancies are reported as percentages of frames per cluster. Protein–protein interaction fingerprints were computed with Schrödinger’s analyze_trajectory_ppi.py. Clustering in this reduced dimensional space revealed two dominant populations, with the most prevalent state comprising nearly 80% of the ensemble. The interaction analysis was performed on snapshots representative of this dominant state.

MM-GBSA binding energies were estimated using Prime MM-GBSA (Schrödinger Release 2025-2; thermal_mmgbsa protocol) with the OPLS4 force field and the VSGB 2.0 implicit-solvent model68,69,70. Snapshots were sampled evenly from the final 250 ns of each trajectory, after which water molecules and ions were removed and each complex, receptor, and ligand were locally energy-minimized. The MM-GBSA binding energy was calculated as ΔGbind = Ecomplex − Ereceptor − Eligand, where ΔGbind is the estimated MM-GBSA binding energy and Ecomplex, Ereceptor and Eligand are the calculated MM-GBSA energies of the complex, receptor and ligand, respectively. For compound binding, DALTAC-1 was defined as the ligand and AR, p300, or AR + p300 as the receptor. For p300 association with the ternary complex, p300 (residues 1049–1160) was defined as the ligand and AR + DALTAC-1 as the receptor. To isolate the direct AR–p300 contribution in the induced geometry, DALTAC-1 was deleted from the same ternary snapshots, with p300 defined as the ligand and AR as the receptor. MM-GBSA values were used as model-dependent interaction-energy estimates to compare the relative stability of the modelled complexes and were not interpreted as experimental binding affinities.

AR protein was expressed according to the manufacturer’s protocol for the Expi293 PRO Expression System Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A40003643). In brief, Expi293 PRO cells were transfected with the HA–AR expression plasmid and cultured for 24 h before the addition of 1 μM R1881. The cultures were then incubated for an additional 24 h, and cells were collected 48 h post-transfection. Cell pellets were washed and collected by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The cells were resuspended in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881 and 0.5% NP-40, supplemented with cOmplete EDTA-free Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Roche, 4693159001). Cells were lysed by sonication, and the lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 40 min at 4 °C. The clarified lysate was incubated with anti-HA magnetic beads (Thermo Scientific, 88837) for 3 h at 4 °C. After binding, the beads were washed three times with wash buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.05% NP-40. Bound AR protein was eluted twice using elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881 and 0.05% NP-40) supplemented with 2 mg ml−1 HA peptide (Thermo Scientific, 26184). The eluted protein was further purified by size-exclusion chromatography using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) pre-equilibrated with gel filtration buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881, and 0.05% NP-40. Peak fractions containing purified AR protein were pooled to a final concentration of approximately 0.5 mg ml−1 and used for all subsequent studies.

For each reaction, 15 μl of anti-HA magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 88837) was blocked with 0.3% BSA in PBS for 1 h at 4 °C and washed three times with AR protein buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0; 150 mM NaCl; 0.05% NP-40) for 5 min per wash. Purified HA-tagged full-length AR (1 μg) was incubated with the blocked beads for at least 4 h at 4 °C. The beads were then washed three times with p300 protein buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl, 0.04% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM TCEP) for 10 min per wash and incubated overnight at 4 °C with purified Flag-tagged p300 (Active motif, 81858) (200 ng or 1 μg) in 350 μl of p300 protein buffer containing the indicated compounds or an equivalent volume of DMSO. Beads were subsequently washed at least three times with p300 protein buffer containing the corresponding compounds for 10 min per wash. Bound proteins were eluted in SDS–PAGE loading buffer and analysed by immunoblotting.

Anti-Flag IgG biosensors (Sartorius, 18-5187) were pre-equilibrated in assay buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-NaOH (pH 7.5), 300 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.04% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM TCEP. N-terminal Flag-tagged full-length recombinant p300 protein (1 μg; Active Motif, 81858) was immobilized onto the biosensors at 25 °C until the binding signal reached a plateau. After immobilization, the biosensors were washed in assay buffer to remove unbound protein and minimize nonspecific binding.

The biosensors were then incubated with recombinant GST–His-tagged AR-LBD protein (Invitrogen, A15675) at varying concentrations in assay buffer containing either 10 μM DALTAC-1 or an equivalent volume of DMSO. The association phase was monitored, followed by transfer of the biosensors into assay buffer to measure dissociation. Binding data were analysed using Octet Analysis Studio 13.0 (Sartorius). Sensorgrams obtained in the presence of DMSO were used as reference controls and subtracted from those obtained with DALTAC-1. The reference-subtracted data were globally fitted to a 1:1 binding model to determine the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd).

PLA was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Navinci Diagnostics) using the Naveni TriFlex Cell kit for cultured cells (AR–p300) and the NaveniFlex Tissue Red kit for VCaP-CRPC tumour sections.

Cultured cells (Naveni TriFlex Cell) were fixed, permeabilized and blocked per kit protocol instructions. Primary antibodies against AR (1:400) and p300 (1:200) were applied in antibody diluent and incubated as recommended. After washes, Naveni proximity probes were added, followed by ligation and rolling-circle amplification steps according to the vendor’s workflow. Slides were counterstained with DAPI and mounted in antifade medium. PLA signals were visualized on a Zeiss LSM900 fluorescence microscope under identical exposure settings across conditions.

For formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour sections (NaveniFlex Tissue Red), sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated and subjected to heat-induced epitope retrieval as specified by the kit. After blocking, primary antibodies against AR (1:1,000) and p300 (1:100) were applied in antibody diluent and incubated per protocol. Following washes, NaveniFlex proximity probes, ligation and amplification were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, slides were mounted and images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM900 microscope using matched acquisition parameters.

Where indicated, PLA puncta were quantified as foci per nucleus using standardized thresholds across groups.

VCaP cells were plated in 96-well plates (50,000 cells per well) and cultured for 3 days in medium containing 5% charcoal-stripped FBS. Cells were treated with a serial dilution of DALTAC-1, Neg-1, or Neg-2 compounds for 3 h. Following treatment, cells were lysed in 1× AlphaLISA SureFire Ultra Lysis Buffer (PerkinElmer) for 30 min at 4 °C with gentle mixing.

For detection, high-binding MaxiSorp 96-well plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were coated overnight at 4 °C with 50 µl of anti-AR antibody (clone AR441, Thermo Fisher Scientific) diluted 1:50 in PBS. After washing with TBS-T and blocking with 5% BSA for 2 h at room temperature, 50 µl of cell lysate was added to each well and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Plates were washed three times with TBS-T and then incubated overnight at 4 °C with rabbit anti-p300 (D8Z4E, 86377, Cell Signaling Technology) antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer.

After washing, HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Bio-Rad, 1706515; 1:10,000 dilution) was added and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Plates were washed seven or eight times with TBST, and chemifluorescent signals were developed using QuantaRed Enhanced Chemifluorescent HRP Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Fluorescence (excitation 570 nm, emission 585 nm) was immediately measured using a Tecan Infinite M1000 Pro plate reader, with readings taken at 5 and 15 min.

Cells (50 million) were washed once with ice-cold PBS, scraped, and pelleted at 500g for 5 min at 4 °C. The cell pellet was resuspended in 2 ml hypotonic buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 0.1% Triton X-100, 15 mM β-mercaptoethanol) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors and rotated for 1 h at 4 °C. Nuclei were collected by centrifugation at 2,000g for 5 min at 4 °C, the supernatant (cytoplasmic fraction) was discarded, and nuclei were washed once with hypotonic buffer.

The nuclear pellet was lysed in 1 ml nuclear lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 0.5% Triton X-100, 15 mM β-mercaptoethanol) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors and rotated for 1 h at 4 °C. Benzonase (500 U ml−¹; Sigma-Aldrich E1014) was added during lysis to digest nucleic acids. Lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 16,000g for 20 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected and precleared with 50 µl Dynabeads Protein G magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher 10004D). Protein concentration was determined using the Pierce 660 nm Protein Assay (Thermo Fisher 22660).

For each immunoprecipitation, 400 µg of precleared nuclear lysate was incubated overnight at 4 °C with either anti-androgen receptor antibody (Abcam ab108341) or anti-p300 antibody (Active Motif 61401). Antigen–antibody complexes were captured with 30 µl Dynabeads Protein G for 2 h at 4 °C. Beads were washed three times with wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2).

For immunoblotting, bound proteins were eluted in 1× NuPAGE LDS Sample Buffer (Thermo Fisher NP0007) supplemented with 50 mM DTT and subjected to SDS–PAGE. For mass spectrometry, washed beads were flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C for subsequent on-bead trypsin digestion.

Total RNA was isolated using QIAzol Lysis Reagent (QIAGEN). In brief, 1 × 106 cells were lysed in 700 µl QIAzol and incubated for 5 min at room temperature to allow for complete dissociation of nucleoprotein complexes. Following the addition of 140 µl chloroform, samples were vigorously mixed and centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min at 4 °C. The aqueous phase was collected, mixed with 1.5 volumes of ethanol, and applied to a RNeasy Mini spin column (QIAGEN) for purification according to the miRNeasy Mini Kit protocol. RNA was eluted in RNase-free water, and the concentration and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

For quantitative PCR analysis, cDNA was synthesized from purified RNA using the Maxima First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. qPCR reactions were performed with SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) on a QuantStudio 7 Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems).

Primers used in this study are listed below: GAPDH forward (F): ACAACTTTGGTATCGTGGAAGG and reverse (R): GCCATCACGCCACAGTTTC; KLK3/PSA F: GACCAAGTTCATGCTGTGTGC and R: CCACTCACCTTTCCCCTCAAG; TMPRSS2 F: GTCCCCACTGTCTACGAGGT and R: CAGACGACGGGGTTGGAAG; NKX3-1 F: CCCACACTCAGGTGATCGAG and R: GAGCTGCTTTCGCTTAGTCTT; MYC F: CCTGGTGCTCCATGAGGAGAC and R: CAGACTCTGACCTTTTGCCAGG; CCND1 F: GCTGCGAAGTGGAAACCATC and R: CCTCCTTCTGCACACATTTGAA.

Tandem mass tag (TMT) proteomic analysis was performed as previously described8, with minor modifications. VCaP cells were treated with DMSO or DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) in three independent biological replicates. Cell lysates were prepared, and protein concentrations were determined. For each sample, 75 µg of protein was reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol, alkylated with 15 mM 2-chloroacetamide, precipitated with ice-cold acetone, and digested overnight with a trypsin/Lys-C mixture at a 1:50 protease-to-protein ratio. Peptides were labelled with TMTpro 16-plex reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A44521), with DMSO replicates assigned to channels 126, 127N and 128N and JZY3032 replicates assigned to channels 130C, 131C and 132C. Labelled peptides were pooled and separated into 12 fractions by high-pH reversed-phase chromatography.

Fractions were analysed at the University of Michigan Proteomics Resource Facility using an Orbitrap Ascend Tribrid mass spectrometer equipped with a FAIMS source and coupled to a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system. Peptides were separated on an Easy-Spray PepMap Neo C18 column, and data were acquired using two FAIMS compensation voltages (−45 and −65 V) and a MultiNotch MS3 method to minimize reporter-ion ratio distortion. Data were processed using Proteome Discoverer v3.0 and searched against the Swiss-Prot Homo sapiens protein database (TaxID 9606; version 5 February 2025). Peptide-spectrum matches and proteins were filtered to a false-discovery rate of ≤1%. TMT quantification was based on high-quality MS3 spectra with an average signal-to-noise ratio of ≥10 and isolation interference of <50%.

VCaP cells were treated with DMSO, 100 nM DALTAC-1 for 4 or 12 h, or a combination of p300/CBPi and ARi for 12 h, each in three biological replicates. The cells were then subjected to acetyl-lysine proteomics analysis as previously described8. In brief, total proteins were extracted, digested with trypsin, and acetylated peptides were enriched using anti–acetyl-lysine antibody–conjugated beads. Enriched peptides were analysed by nano-liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (nanoLC–MS/MS) on a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and raw data were processed using MaxQuant (v2.3.0.0) with acetyl-lysine and protein N-terminal acetylation set as variable modifications.

In-solution digestion: VCaP cells were treated with 100 nM DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) or DMSO for 4 h. Co-immunoprecipitation assays were performed as described above. The beads were resuspended in 50 µl of 0.1 M ammonium bicarbonate buffer (pH ~8). Cysteines were reduced by adding 50 µl of 10 mM DTT and incubating at 45 °C for 30 min. Samples were cooled to room temperature and alkylation of cysteines was achieved by incubating with 65 mM 2-chloroacetamide, under darkness, for 30 min at room temperature. An overnight (~16 h) digestion with 1 µg sequencing grade, modified trypsin was carried out at 37 °C with constant shaking in a Thermomixer. Digestion was stopped by acidification and peptides were desalted using SepPak C18 cartridges using the manufacturer’s protocol (Waters). Samples were completely dried using a vacufuge. The resulting peptides were dissolved in 8 µl of 0.1% formic acid/2% acetonitrile solution, and 2 µl of the peptide solution was resolved on a nano-capillary reverse phase column (Acclaim PepMap C18, 2 µm, 50 cm, Thermo Scientific) using a 0.1% formic acid/2% acetonitrile (buffer A) and 0.1% formic acid/95% acetonitrile (buffer B) gradient at 300 nl min−1 over a period of 180 min (2–22% buffer B in 110 min, 22–40% in 25 min, 40–90% in 5 min followed by holding at 90% buffer B for 5 min and requilibration with buffer A for 25 min). The eluent was directly introduced into the Orbitrap Fusion tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) using an Easy-Spray source. MS1 scans were acquired at 120K resolution (AGC target = 106; max IT = 50 ms). Data-dependent collision induced dissociation MS/MS spectra were acquired using the Top speed method (3 s) following each MS1 scan (NCE ≈ 32%; AGC target = 105; max IT 45 ms).

Proteins were identified by searching the MS/MS data against the UniProt human database (sp_canonical TaxID=9606, v2025-02-05) using Proteome Discoverer (v3, Thermo Scientific). Search parameters included MS1 mass tolerance of 10 ppm and fragment tolerance of 0.2 Da; two missed cleavages were allowed. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was considered a fixed modification and oxidation of methionine, deamidation of asparagine and glutamine were considered as potential modifications. The false-discovery rate (FDR) was determined using Percolator, and proteins or peptides with a FDR of ≤1% were retained for further analysis.

VCaP cells were treated with 100 nM DALTAC-1 or a combination of 100 nM p300/CBPi and ARi for 4, 12 or 24 h, each in two biological replicates. The cells were then subjected to RNA-seq as previously described8. In brief, total RNA was extracted, and ribosomal RNA was removed using the RiboErase module of the KAPA RNA HyperPrep Kit (Roche). rRNA-depleted RNA was used for library preparation following the manufacturer’s protocol, and libraries were quality-checked on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer before sequencing on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform (paired-end, 2× 100 bp). Sequencing reads were quantified with Kallisto (v0.50.1), normalized with edgeR (v3.34.1), and analysed for differential expression using limma-voom (v3.58.1). GSEA was performed using fgsea (v1.28.0), and data visualization employed tidyverse, gplots, ggplot2, gtable (v0.3.0), and EnhancedVolcano (v1.15.0) packages in R.

ChIP–seq was performed as previously described8. In brief, cells were cross-linked in 1% formaldehyde, quenched with glycine, and lysed for chromatin extraction. Chromatin was sheared to 200–600 bp fragments using a Bioruptor (Diagenode) and subjected to immunoprecipitation with antibodies against transcription factors (AR, FOXA1, p300, ERG and BRD4) or histone marks (H3K27ac, H2BK20ac and RNA Pol II) using the iDeal ChIP–seq Kit (Diagenode). Drosophila spike-in chromatin (Active Motif, 53083) and spike-in antibody (Active Motif, 61686) were added during the overnight incubation. After reverse cross-linking and DNA purification, sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform. For PR, SRC2, and CBP ChIP–seq, we performed double-cross-linking. In brief, 10 million cells were cross-linked with 250 μl of 200 mM DSP (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 22585) for 30 min at room temperature. PBS was then added to a final volume of 9 ml, followed by 40 μl of 0.5 M EDTA. Formaldehyde (250 μl, 37%) was added, and the cells were incubated for an additional 10 min at room temperature. Cross-linking was quenched by adding 1 ml of 1.25 M glycine and 200 μl of 10% Tween-20, followed by incubation for 5 min. Samples were then processed according to the ChIP–seq protocol described previously.

ChIP–seq reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic (v0.39). Alignment was then performed separately to both the human genome (hg38) and the Drosophila genome (dm6) using BWA (v0.7.17-r1198-dirty). Low-quality and duplicate reads were filtered with SAMtools and Picard, respectively. Normalization ratios were calculated based on the lowest amount of uniquely aligned reads per ChIP target to each genome as recommended on the vendor’s website. Reads were then downsampled per the normalization ratios. Peak calling was then performed with MACS2 (v2.1.1.20160309) using narrow or broad settings depending on the target, and blacklisted genomic regions were removed using BEDTools with the ENCODE exclusion list. Motif enrichment analysis was performed using HOMER (v4.10). Processed data were converted to BigWig format using UCSC wigToBigWig for visualization.

Read density heat maps and average enrichment profiles were generated using deepTools. For histone marks, signals were plotted within ±2.5 kb of the reference point, and for transcription factors within ±1 kb. The parameters --skipZeros, --averageType mean, and --plotType se were applied. ENCODE blacklist regions (ENCFF356LFX) were excluded from analysis. Genomic interval operations were performed using the IRanges Bioconductor package (v2.36.0), and non-promoter regions were defined using the ChIPseeker R package tool annotatePeak excluding ±1 kb windows surrounding annotated gene transcription start site regions. Peak overlap and annotation analyses were additionally performed using the ChIPpeakAnno R package (v3.6.5).

Mouse prostate organoids and patient-derived xenograft organoids were established and maintained following previously described protocols41,71. In brief, organoids were cultured in 50 µl Matrigel domes and overlaid with prostate organoid medium, with media changed every 2–3 days and passaging performed weekly. For growth and drug-response assays, organoid fragments were dissociated into single cells and used to generate new organoids (1,000 cells per dome for standard viability assays) in complete organoid medium. Cell viability was measured using the CellTiter-Glo 3D assay (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

All animal procedures were approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC; protocol PRO0001291) and performed in accordance with institutional guidelines. Male CB17 SCID mice, 4–6 weeks old, were procured from the breeding colony at the University of Michigan and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions on a 12 h light:12 h dark cycle, with ambient temperature maintained at 18–23 °C and relative humidity maintained at 40–60%. Only male mice were used, as prostate cancer is specific to males.

Sample sizes for efficacy studies (n = 7–20 tumours per group) were chosen prospectively based on a power calculation: with >7 tumours per group, the study had an estimated 92.3% power to detect a 50% decrease in mean tumour volume or metastatic burden, assuming a coefficient of variation of 40%. No animals or data points were excluded from analysis. Mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups prior to dosing. Histopathological evaluation and immunohistochemistry-based scoring for drug toxicity studies were performed in a blinded manner by two independent pathologists; blinding was applied to other end-points (for example, tumour volume measurement). Per IACUC protocol PRO0001291, tumour burden was not permitted to exceed 4,186 mm3, and this limit was not exceeded in any experiment reported here.

Male SCID mice (6–8 weeks old) were obtained from the breeding colony at the University of Michigan and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions. All animal procedures were approved by the University of Michigan IACUC (protocol PRO0001291). Subcutaneous xenograft tumours were established by injecting 3 × 106 VCaP cells suspended in serum-free medium mixed 1:1 with Matrigel (BD Biosciences) into both dorsal flanks. Tumour growth was monitored weekly using digital calipers, and volumes were calculated as (π/6) × (length × width2). At study end-points, mice were euthanized, and tumours were excised and weighed.

The castration-resistant VCaP model was generated as previously described8. In brief, mice were castrated once tumours reached 150–200 mm³, and treatment with DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1 intraperitoneally or 60 mg kg−1 orally), combination of p300/CBPi (30 mg kg−1 orally) and ARi (10 mg kg−1 orally), or vehicle was initiated after tumour regrowth to baseline size for 24 days.

A tissue microarray (TMA) was created according to a design involving 8 unique cases from 4 different subgroups: vehicle (n = 2), p300/CBPi + ARi (n = 2), DALTAC-1 intraperitoneal (n = 2) and DALTAC-1 oral administration (n = 2). Two independent samples were selected from each subgroup. To ensure data reliability and representativeness, a replicate core from each sample was included in the TMA, resulting in a focused 16-core TMA. Technical details are as follows: in brief, FFPE donor blocks for the selected samples were chosen by two study pathologists (R.M. and S.M.) after reviewing the haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The pathologists then annotated the H&E slides to identify the most representative tumour area of interest (AOI) on the surface of each donor block. The Semiautomatic tissue arrayer from Beecher Instruments (Sun Prairie) was used to punch 1 mm-diameter cores from each marked region. These cores were carefully transferred into a recipient acrylic block in a grid-like pattern. Once transferred, the recipient block was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min to ensure proper fusion of the cores within the paraffin. The prepared TMA block was then sectioned at 4-μm thickness and stained with H&E to assess the quality of the final TMA.

Four-micrometre-thick sections from the PDX TMA, mounted on positively charged slides, were cut and prepared according to the guidelines and recommendations. Subsequently, the slides were deparaffinized using a standard xylene and graded ethanol series, followed by heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER) as per the Lunaphore COMET protocol to unmask target epitopes72. Automated sequential immunofluorescence (seqIF) staining was performed on the COMET instrument (Lunaphore) to enable highly multiplexed protein detection with the target primary antibodies. This process involved cycles of staining, imaging, and elution managed by the COMET Control software through controlled temperature and microfluidic reagent delivery. Each cycle included incubation with unconjugated primary antibodies, followed by species-specific fluorescently conjugated secondary antibodies (for example, Alexa Fluor 555 and 647), automated image acquisition including DAPI counterstaining, and complete antibody removal via elution. After the final staining cycle, the COMET Control software (v1.5.0.0) automatically stitched, aligned, and stacked images to produce a single OME-TIFF file for each sample. During post-processing, autofluorescence background was systematically subtracted using reference images acquired from unstained tissue sections at the beginning of the protocol.

The raw prostate TMA data included single-cell measurements across multiple markers along with their spatial locations. Markers were grouped into two panels based on biological relevance, as shown in the plots. To normalize marker expression and reduce skewness, a log1p transformation (log1p(expression)) was applied. Outliers were identified and removed separately for each marker within each group. Outliers were defined as values exceeding ±5 median absolute deviations from the group-specific median. The median absolute deviation is a robust measure of statistical dispersion that calculates the median of the absolute deviations from the median, making it less sensitive to extreme outliers than standard deviation. This approach preserves most of the data while minimizing the impact of extreme values.

The prostate cancer PDX models MDA-PCa-146-12 and MDA-PCa-183 were established and maintained as previously described8. MDA-PCa-146-12 is an AR+ and ERG+ adenocarcinoma PDX derived from the adenocarcinoma region of a primary prostate tumour with mixed adenocarcinoma–neuroendocrine morphology. MDA-PCa-183 is an AR+ and ERG+ adenocarcinoma PDX derived from a bone marrow aspirate of a treatment-naive patient with metastatic prostate cancer. Both models harbour PTEN loss and TP53 loss-of-function alterations. In brief, tumour fragments (~2 mm3) were implanted subcutaneously into the dorsal flanks of six- to eight-week-old male SCID mice bred in-house and propagated by serial passage. Once tumours reached approximately 200 mm3 using the formula (π/6) × (length × width²), mice were randomized into treatment groups. Mice bearing MDA-PCa-146-12 tumours received vehicle or DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1, intraperitoneally three times per week). Mice bearing MDA-PCa-183 tumours received vehicle, DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1, intraperitoneally three times per week), ARV-766 (10 mg kg−1, orally, 5 times per week), or enzalutamide (10 mg kg−1, orally, 5 times per week). Tumour volumes were measured weekly, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC, protocol PRO0001291).

All experimental procedures and statistical analyses were performed as previously described8. In brief, key experiments were independently repeated at least three times, with most quantitative assays carried out in biological replicates as noted. Representative images and immunoblots reflect reproducible results, and the number of biological replicates is provided in the figure legends. No data were excluded from analysis. For in vitro experiments, sample sizes were not predetermined by a statistical method and randomization was not applicable, as cells were allocated to experimental conditions under homogeneous culture conditions. For animal studies, sample sizes were determined prospectively (see Methods), and mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups. Histopathological and immunohistochemical scoring for drug toxicity studies were performed in a blinded manner by two independent pathologists; all other data collection and quantification relied on automated instruments or standardized computational pipelines and were therefore not blinded. Two-sided statistical tests were used unless otherwise stated. Comparisons between two groups used unpaired t-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, and multiple comparisons were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. Exact P values are reported in the figure legends.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

All data are available in the manuscript and Supplementary information. Raw sequencing data (RNA-seq and ChIP–seq) have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession numbers GSE310948 and GSE310949. This study used the following public databases and reference datasets: human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38), used for ChIP–seq read alignment (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/assembly/GCF_000001405.26/). Drosophila melanogaster reference genome (dm6), used for ChIP–seq spike-in normalization (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/assembly/GCF_000001215.4/). The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifiers PXD084247, PXD084250 and PXD084305. Protein Data Bank (PDB) entry 5W0E (CBP-BRD–GNE-781 co-crystal structure) was used as the structural template for computational modelling of the p300-BRD–GNE-049 interaction. No restrictions apply to the availability of these data. Source data are provided with this paper.

No custom code or software was used in this study. All computational analyses were performed using publicly available software and code, which are described in Methods.

Y.Q., J.C.Y.-T. and J.L. performed all of the organoid and animal efficacy studies with assistance from S.E., Y.Y. and A.J.T. E.Y. and S.L. carried out all of the bioinformatics analyses with assistance from A.P. J.T. and J.Y. performed the computational modelling of the AR–p300–DALTAC-1 complex. R.M. and S.M. carried out all of the histopathological evaluations of drug toxicity as well as quantified all of the histology-based data. R.M. and S.M. carried out all of the immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence staining. R.S. and A.R. conducted quantification of sequential multiplex immunofluorescence datasets. X.C. and F.S. performed sequencing. J.Y., W.X., M.W., S.J. and S.W. designed, synthesized and performed initial evaluations of a large number of DALTAC molecules, leading to the discovery of DALTAC-1, as well as Neg-1 and Neg-2 control compounds. J.L., J.Y., S.J.M., J.C.Y.-T., S.W. and A.M.C. wrote the manuscript and organized the final figures.

Pharmacokinetic parameters of compound 7 (JZY3031) and DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) in mice following intravenous (i.v.; 2.0 mg kg−1) or oral (p.o.; 5.0 mg kg−1) administration. The table reports terminal half-life (t1/2), maximum plasma concentration (Cmax), area under the concentration–time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC0–24), steady-state volume of distribution (Vss), clearance (CL) and oral bioavailability (F). d. Chemical modifications of DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) used to generate the inactive analogues JZY3137 (Neg-1; impaired p300/CBP binding with retained AR binding) and JZY3138 (Neg-2; impaired AR binding with retained p300/CBP binding). g. Dose–response curves from fluorescence polarization (FP) assays measuring p300 binding for Neg-1, Neg-2, GNE-049 (p300/CBP bromodomain inhibitor), JZY3221 (AR binder), JZY3222 (p300/CBP binder), and DALTAC-1. Viability of GEMM-derived mouse organoids treated with DMSO or DALTAC-1 (100 or 1000 nM) for 7 d using 3D-CTG assay (mean ± s.d.; n = 4 replicated wells; two-sided t-test performed separately for each model, three independent experiments). b. a. Schematic illustrating the design, treatment schedule, pharmacodynamic, and endpoint analyses of the DALTAC-1 efficacy study using the VCaP-CRPC xenograft model. b. Endpoint tumor weights in the VCaP-CRPC model treated with vehicle, DALTAC-1 i.p., DALTAC-1 p.o., or combination of p300/CBPi and ARi p.o. Data are mean ± SEM; n  =  14 tumors for vehicle, oral DALTAC-1, and p300/CBPi + ARi, and n = 16 tumors for i.p. DALTAC-1. P values were calculated using a two-sided t-test. c. Individual tumor volume changes after 24 d from VCaP-CRPC study. d. Tumor volume curves of individual tumors from the VCaP-CRPC study. e. Representative COMET multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) images of the indicated targets in PD5 tumors from the VCaP-CRPC study. A tissue microarray comprising eight biologically independent tumors from four treatment groups (n = 2 tumors per group), with two replicate cores per tumor, was analyzed. The TMA staining experiment was performed once. Scale bar, 20 µm. f. Violin plots showing the log10-transformed expression levels of individual targets across single cells based on Seq-mIF staining from PD5 tumors in the VCaP-CRPC study (n = 462,056 cells for veh, n = 501,827 cells for p300/CBPi+ARi, n = 597,031 cells for DALTAC-1 i.p and n = 464,670 cells for DALTAC-1 p.o). The violin outline represents the kernel density estimate; grey dots indicate individual cells; and the central white line denotes the median. g. Graph depicting the tumor volume curves of MDA-PCa-146-12 CRPC PDX tumors treated with vehicle or 30 mg/kg DALTAC-1 i.p. Data are presented as mean +/− SEM (vehicle: n  =  16 tumors, DALTAC-1 i.p.: n = 7 tumors). P values were calculated using a two-sided t-test. h. Tumor volume curves in the MDA-PCa-183 PDX model treated with vehicle or DALTAC-1 (30 mg/kg, i.p., 5×/week during the first week, then 2×/week for an additional 4 weeks). Data are mean ± SEM; n = 8 in vehicle group and n = 7 in DALTAC-1 treated group. P values were calculated using a two-sided t-test. i. Tumor volume curves of individual tumors from the MDA-PCa-183 PDX study shown in Extended Data Fig. 9h. j. Waterfall plot showing the percentage change in individual tumor volumes from baseline after 35 days of treatment in the MDA-PCa-183 PDX study. k. Kaplan–Meier survival curve of MDA-PCa-183 PDX–bearing mice, with survival defined as the time for tumors to reach threefold the initial volume. Statistical significance was assessed using a two-sided log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test.

#1407. Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying

Never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

It will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

Russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian said. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

Still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

At the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”

This was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he said he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

“It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”

No. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9

Tomorrow’s race will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start on the front row together. It is a reasonable run down to turn one and there are overtaking opportunities through the first few corners at Sepang, with it being similar to the configuration in China, with plenty of lines and moves on offer.

Respect between two great champions 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/fbZ6aoKRyw

“Very difficult to understand. We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is the different to all the (other) tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

On Kimi Antonelli’s track limits breach in Q2:

“Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”

Lewis Hamilton says this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). My understanding is the Bahrainis are organising the race this year, while local forces are handling the traffic outside the circuit.

“The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”

“I love this energy [from the crowd]. Big, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

“I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”

A reminder that Isack Hadjar will drop from third to eighth after his grid penalty.

QUALIFYING CLASSIFICATIONCan't wait for Sunday! 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/qqi8hPDcKA

“It is fantastic. We have been trying many grand prix to get pole. Sometimes a bit closer than others but to finally get it, from where we started the season, pretty incredible. I am happy with today and, for sure, I am going to try and win tomorrow. When you start first, that is the target.”

Big disappointment that for Russell. After his win in Baku, where he said he finally felt hooked up to the car, he was desperate to build the momentum. P8, four places behind Antonelli, was not what he would have had in mind. Has it all to do in the race tomorrow.

Excellent (though not unexpected) pole for Verstappen, and a very good P2 for Hamilton. Could be some fireworks on the front row tomorrow.

*Hadjar’s three-place grid penalty will drop him down to eighth place for the race tomorrow.

Neither of the Red Bulls can improve in the first sector but it is those behind them who need significant improvements. The two Ferraris are going along nicely at the start of their final flying laps. Hadjar is unable to improve despite a purple final sector. Verstappen then goes fastest in the final sector and improves his advantage at the top.

Hamilton meanwhile went fastest in the middle sector and goes second fastest overall. Piastri cannot improve but stays ahead of Russell.

Norris is the final man across the line but is only fast enough for P6. That means that Verstappen takes pole in Malaysia, which is the first time this season that Red Bull have taken pole position. Hamilton is second with Hadjar third, although the Frenchman has a five-place grid penalty.

MAX VERSTAPPEN TAKES POLE FOR THE BAHRAIN GRAND PRIX IN MALAYSIA!! 👊#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/NgtaCAZacL

The two Red Bulls, who are one and two at the moment, will be the first two drivers across the line on these final efforts.

The other nine drivers in Q3 are in the pits so young Antonelli has the track to himself as he sets his one and only flying lap of Q3. He is over four tenths down on Verstappen through the first sector and has plenty of work to do.

The championship leader sets a decent middle sector where he loses no more time to Verstappen. As it stands he would put himself third before the others do their final runs. He comes across the line in P3 but will have the likes of Hamilton, Piastri, Leclerc, Norris and Russell trying to surpass him.

Russell is the first across the line and sets a time of a 1:36.032. He does not last long at the top as he is immediately displaced by Hadjar, who is half a second quicker.

Hamilton then comes over the line in second, just ahead of his teammate Leclerc. Piastri puts himself between the two Ferraris.

What about Verstappen? The man who won here the last time we were in Malaysia continues his great form today and goes quickest by more than three tenths.

Antonelli now heads out and will have the track to himself really. This is going to be the championship leader’s only flying lap of Q3.

Russell is the first man to head out for his first flying lap in Q3. Antonelli has remained in the pits with just one new set of softs remaining. Verstappen, who right now feels like the favourite for pole, will be one of the last across the line in these first attempts of Q3.

The fight for pole position in Sepang begins now as the green light is on at the end of the pit lane to get Q3 going.

Antonelli, due to that lap time deletion in Q2, has just one new set of softs for Q3, which could prove costly in his attempts to try and take pole.

P12 the best qualifying result of the season for Alonso. It was only his second time in Q2 after Hungary (P16).

I should add, P14 was also Lance Stroll’s best qualifying result of the season. His first outing in Q2 this year.

11. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls)12. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)13. Carlos Sainz (Williams)14. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)

With grid penalties already on their way, neither Colapinto nor Lindblad set lap times in Q2.

Verstappen, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris, Hadjar and Russell all remain in the pits. A bit of a risk for Russell down in eighth but his time should be enough to get into Q3.

Lindblad, who will start tomorrow’s race at the back of the grid after penalties, gives his teammate Lawson a tow down the back straight and it works as Lawson just sneaks into the top ten.

Can Bortoleto get back ahead though of Lawson? Yes he can and he will take the final place in Q3. Lawson thought he might be through but the tow was not enough.

Lindblad, who's taking a grid penalty for Sunday's race, gave team mate Lawson a tow but it wasn't quite enough to send the Kiwi into Q3#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/IMlrqg4ENv

As the young Italian starts his flying lap, there is no-one else out on track so no traffic. He is a lot more cautious at turn six this time than last time, when he had his lap time deleted.

He has not set blistering first and second sector times but a purple final sector puts him into second and the Italian is safely into Q3.

Plenty of other drivers are now heading around the track for their final flying laps of Q2.

11. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)12. Carlos Sainz (Williams)13. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)14. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)

Mercedes have put a brand new set of softs onto Antonelli’s car as he heads out promptly, with no lap time to his name so far. Antonelli is still disputing the lap deletion over team radio but his team tell him the images show he exceeded track limits. This is now a lot of pressure on the championship leader; any mistake now and he will not make Q3. His teammate Russell is only in seventh.

Antonelli was fourth fastest but has had his lap time deleted for exceeding track limits at turn six. That is a big moment in Q2 and could prove problematic if he gets into Q3. Antonelli appeared to be confused when he was told about his lap deletion over team radio but the on-board view looked pretty clear-cut.

Piastri then comes across the line in third.

Here's the moment Kimi ran wide 👀#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/E0VdWdBt8x

The Dutchman looks in a great spot at the moment to take pole position today and his 1:35.696 is very quick. He is nearly four tenths quicker than Antonelli.

How about the Ferraris? Leclerc was quickest in the middle sector but is nearly three tenths down on Verstappen. Hamilton puts himself into third place. Russell is more than half a second down on Verstappen.

Verstappen has been shown a black and white flag for driving unnecessarily slowly. I doubt he will get a grid penalty for that but it will be a warning for the Dutchman.

Anyway, the drivers, other than Colapinto and Alonso, are on flying laps, with Verstappen currently fastest inthe first sector.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and the second part of qualifying is under way. Like the start of Q1, it is hardly a stampede to go out.

17. Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)18. Oliver Bearman (Haas)19. Esteban Ocon (Haas)20. Alex Albon (Williams)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

The Aston Martin of Stroll improves significantly from 20th and is set to make Q2, as is his teammate Alonso. A bit of a surprise to see the Aston Martins improve and make it into Q2.

Go Fernando! 🤩 Go Lance! 🤩First double Q2 appearance this season 🙌#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/xjiWYv6ycr

That has seen the Audi of Hulkenberg drop into the drop zone and the German is out. For contrast, his teammate improves to go into eighth place! Hulkenberg had a big lock up into turn 14, which proved very costly.

As it stands, eight of the top nine are remaining in the garage. Russell is in ninth and has not gone out but Gasly above him in eighth has. You would imagine Russell is perfectly safe.

17. Esteban Ocon (Haas)18. Alex Albon (Williams)19. Oliver Bearman (Haas)20. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

Ocon, in 17th, is quite far off Hulkenberg in 16th and needs more than four tenths to usurp him.

The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

The two Ferraris are on medium tyres but Leclerc still puts himself into second place. He is then displaced by Hamilton, who slots in behind Verstappen. Good times from the Ferraris on the mediums.

What about the McLarens? Norris goes sixth fastest but is more than six tenths down on Verstappen. Then comes Piastri, who goes fourth fastest, just under four tenths off Verstappen.

Arguably the three favourites for pole; Antonelli, Russell and Verstappen, are all on flying laps.

The first sector goes the way of Verstappen, who is purple, and then the Dutchman goes purple in the middle sector.

Antonelli is two tenths faster than his teammate Russell but Verstappen is over half a second quicker than the Mercedes. Hadjar is then second fastest to show the pace in the Red Bull this weekend.

Most of the teams waited and waited to come out and then suddenly lots of drivers are sent out, resulting in a queue in the pits! With the high track temperatures and high degradation, the drivers are crawling around on their out laps to preserve these soft tyres.

Bumper to bumper in the pit lane! #F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/ff8JO9kB1g

The two Haas drivers have a free track to themselves whilst everyone else bides their time. In theory, as the hour of qualifying goes on, the track temperature should decrease and the more rubber that is laid down the faster the track should get.

Finally, just before the two Haas drivers finish their first flying laps, the rest of the grid is starting to emerge, led by the Mercedes duo.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and Q1 is officially under way. The two Haas drivers are the first to head out. Other than that, it is a quiet start to Q1.

The top four teams; Mercedes, Red Bull, Ferrari and McLaren, all have a genuine chance of taking pole in Sepang today. I think the true favourites though have to be the Mercedes duo and Max Verstappen but with how close it between all four of the teams you cannot rule anything out.

It is 33 degrees celsius air temperature, with the track temperature up at 58 degrees.

Not long to wait now until qualifying begins. It is hot, humid and dry in Sepang right now. As we know in Malaysia, the weather can change quickly and thunderstorms can roll in quite quickly but it looks like today’s qualifying will be a dry one. This will be one of if not the hottest qualifying sessions of the season, so much so that we are seeing umbrellas going up to get some shade from the sun rather than sheltering from any rain.

This will be important to consider after qualifying finishes as there will be some shuffling around:

Isack Hadjar (Red Bull): five-place grid penalty- new internal combustion engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): ten-place grid penalty- new engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): five-place grid penalty- causing a collision in BakuArvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls): back of the grid- complete power unit change

Hadjar has looked good since returning from his wrist injury so could be fighting it out near the front of the grid, although his five-place penalty will drop him down. We know Lindblad will be at the back and is very likely to be joined there by Colapinto, who is not going to be qualifying high up in the top ten in his Alpine.

Haas have announced that Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave at the end of this season. Ocon now faces an uncertain future, with it difficult to see a spot for him on the F1 grid next season. There are suggestions that the 30-year-old’s replacement will be Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, although nothing has been confirmed on that front. 21-year-old Camara currently leads the Formula 2 championship.

TGR Haas F1 Team and Esteban Ocon will part ways at the conclusion of the 2026 season. With plenty of racing ahead, our focus remains on working together to maximize every opportunity through to the final race of the year.#HaasF1 #F1 pic.twitter.com/4iQAuqnSyA

Aston Martin have now confirmed their driver line-up for next season, retaining both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. There had been reports that Alonso had been contemplating retirement but the 45-year-old will continue into another season.

Aston Martin Aramco confirms Lance and Fernando will continue as the team's drivers in 2027. Read more: ​https://t.co/ePyjJdyAIB pic.twitter.com/VogFUEbNxy

Other than the second seat alongside Ollie Bearman at Haas, the only other team to keep an eye on is Racing Bulls, with no definite confirmation on their exact driver line-up for next season.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, said the Scuderia had decided to issue a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

“Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti said. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”

“It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

“The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

Almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. Here they are and who they were racing for:

Max Verstappen (Red Bull) Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes) Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes) Esteban Ocon (Force India)Nico Hulkenberg (Renault)Sergio Perez (Force India)Fernando Alonso (McLaren)Lance Stroll (Williams)Carlos Sainz (Toro Rosso)Pierre Gasly (Toro Rosso)

With Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a new floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car update since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

This race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

#1406. The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Eukaryotic genomes are exposed to numerous sources of DNA damage that impede replication. Only a decade ago, repriming by the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL was identified as a pathway that enables cells to tolerate DNA damage1,2,3,4. However, the molecular mechanism that underlies repriming remains poorly understood, and it is unclear how PRIMPOL is precisely targeted to stalled forks, where along single-stranded DNA PRIMPOL binds and how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize error-prone DNA synthesis. Here, to dissect the molecular basis of repriming, we perform real-time single-molecule imaging in nuclear extracts that recapitulate genome maintenance. We directly visualize how stalled forks restart through repriming. We show that PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS (CMG). This facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. At near-physiological concentrations, PRIMPOL reprimes leading strands in a CMG-dependent manner and polymerase ε extends those primers. This primary mode of repriming does not require DNA damage checkpoint signalling. PRIMPOL overexpression and checkpoint activation promote a secondary mode of repriming, whereby PRIMPOL restarts DNA synthesis far from CMG and polymerase δ extends those primers. Our data reveal a simple yet effective mechanism that directs PRIMPOL’s activity to stalled forks awaiting restart, and suggest a strategy to inhibit the repriming pathway.

Multiple pathways maintain genome stability during replication stress (RS)5, including fork reversal and translesion DNA synthesis (TLS)6. In 2013, a new RS response pathway called repriming was identified in eukaryotes1,2,3,4. PRIMPOL performs repriming and enables cells to tolerate diverse DNA lesions1,2,3,4,7,8. As it lacks proofreading, PRIMPOL has an error rate comparable to that of TLS polymerases (10−2−10−4)9,10. PRIMPOL-deficient cells and mice are hypersensitive to several DNA-damaging agents8,11,12,13, underscoring its role in genome maintenance. While repriming enables cancer cells to tolerate RS induced by oncogenes14 and chemotherapy15, PRIMPOL generates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps16,17 that sensitize cells to PARP inhibitors18,19,20. Blocking fork reversal enhances repriming, suggesting that cells favour high-fidelity pathways to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis7,21,22.

The replicative helicase CMG unwinds parental DNA23 and is functionally coupled to polymerase ε (Pol ε)24, which synthesizes the leading strand. The lagging strand is primed and extended by primase–polymerase α (Pol α) and polymerase δ (Pol δ), respectively24. Damage on the lagging strand is readily bypassed due to the discontinuous nature of Okazaki fragment synthesis25,26. This is not the case for leading strand DNA lesions, which stall Pol ε while CMG continues to unwind DNA25,26,27. This CMG uncoupling exposes ssDNA that is rapidly coated by replication protein A (RPA)28. The notion that PRIMPOL may reprime leading strand synthesis was hypothesized at the time of its discovery2, and discussed in later work7,16,29, but there is no direct evidence for this idea.

Although repriming is a major RS response pathway and PRIMPOL is an attractive therapeutic target, key mechanistic aspects of repriming remain unclear. For example, although RPA recruits PRIMPOL to ssDNA30,31, it is unclear why PRIMPOL acts at stalled forks, but not on ssDNA generated by other processes (transcription, recombination). One study reported that high RPA concentrations inhibit PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA in vitro30, presumably because RPA fully coats ssDNA and prevents PRIMPOL’s access to the template. Another study found that RPA stimulated PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA long enough to accommodate the simultaneous binding of both proteins, that Pol ε can extend PRIMPOL’s primers in vitro and that RPA stimulates PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity in synergy with Pol ε31. It remains unclear how repriming occurs in the nucleus, where RPA is abundant and rapidly coats exposed ssDNA. Although PRIMPOL is a known target of checkpoint kinase 1 (CHK1)22, how the DNA damage checkpoint regulates repriming remains poorly understood. Finally, it is unclear how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis during repriming.

To address these questions, we used single-molecule imaging to directly visualize PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart in Xenopus egg extracts. We found that PRIMPOL preferentially binds near stalled forks, suggesting that it interacts with fork-associated proteins. We identified an interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG that is required for targeting PRIMPOL to stalled forks and for efficient fork restart in nuclear extract and in human cells. Our data indicate that the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the leading strand polymerase Pol ε, therefore minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. Finally, in conditions that mimic PRIMPOL overexpression, we found that PRIMPOL can reprime DNA synthesis far from the replicative helicase, and those primers are extended by Pol δ. Our findings support a simple-yet-elegant mechanism that targets PRIMPOL’s activity specifically to stalled forks and suggest a strategy to inhibit repriming.

To investigate the mechanism of PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we used nuclear extract prepared from Xenopus laevis eggs32. This extract contains all soluble nuclear proteins, supports efficient DNA replication and recapitulates several RS response pathways33. We could not detect frog PRIMPOL in egg extract using mass spectrometry (MS) or western blotting (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Table 1). To reconstitute repriming, we supplemented nuclear extract with recombinant human PRIMPOL, which displayed robust enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d).

To visualize PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart in real-time, we adapted a single-molecule assay called kinetics of eukaryotic replication via molecular imaging and tracking (KERMIT)25,34. A biotinylated linear DNA template was double-tethered onto a streptavidin-coated coverslip in a microfluidic flow-cell (Fig. 1a). DNA was incubated with high-speed supernatant—an extract that supports origin licensing but not origin firing, mimicking G1 (ref. 32) (Fig. 1a). The flow-cell was washed with buffer to remove any soluble proteins while retaining DNA-bound MCM2–7. Licensed DNA was incubated with nucleoplasmic extract—an extract that supports origin firing, elongation and RS response, mimicking S phase32 (Fig. 1a). Replication was monitored in real-time using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy.
