#1397. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? https://t.co/DuSpvymZfu

The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

“We suffered in the game but every situation of the game. I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat. We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. Today he was captain because he deserved it, especially in this moment because he suffer because Tottenham didn’t score or win any games. He is a great guy, great player and we are behind him.

“We have to believe in ourselves and this football way. If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don’t play as a team, it is impossible.”

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford.

If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

The spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after big-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1396. Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4,5,6,7,8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

#1395. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b

Was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. He made no mistake with a powerful, first-time finish.

Doku soon added a second, a sublime strike, as he dribbled goalwards, defenders backing off, and he arced a right-footed shot high beyond Alisson Becker’s grasp.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

In a letter to fans, a defiant Khaldoon Al Mubarak, City’s chairman, expresses complete confidence that his club would be vindicated.

“There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club,” he writes. “We will not give them that opportunity.”

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

Hull City owner Acun Ilicali then likens City’s transgressions to “doping” before Mauricio Pochettino, whose Spurs side were often in the hunt with City for major trophies during his time as manager, says that football has “lived through a period of deception”.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

An unblinking Soriano then features in a video statement published by City in which he claimed their guilty verdict was based on “a single false accusation”.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1394. EFL asks clubs to stop targeted 'banter' on social media amid fears over reputational damage in the wake of 'Spygate' fallout

Published: 09:54 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 11:40 EST, 12 November 2026

The EFL has written to clubs calling for a halt in reputationally damaging social media posts disguised as ‘banter’ - believing the line has been blurred when it comes to regulatory matters.

The letter expressed concern over a ‘growing pattern of posts that use disputes, disciplinary matters, alleged wrongdoing or rival Clubs as material for public “banter”.’

A letter, seen by Daily Mail Sport, has been sent by EFL chief executive Trevor Birch to club chairs and executives following a board meeting.

‘While any one post may be viewed as an isolated lapse, taken together they risk creating a culture in which short-term engagement is prioritised over judgement, responsibility and long-term reputation,’ the letter read.

‘This is not about removing humour, personality or rivalry from Club channels. It is about recognising when content becomes disparaging, prolongs a dispute, targets an individual, or calls the integrity of a Club or the competition into question.

‘The impact extends beyond the Clubs directly involved. Repeated public exchanges can inflame relationships, undermine confidence in the fairness and professionalism of our competitions, and weaken the collective EFL brand.

The EFL have called for clubs to halt 'banter' social media posts. Pictured: Wrexham owners Rob Mac (left) and Ryan Reynolds (right) spoofed Southampton's Spygate case in September. Source: X/Wrexham_AFC

Wrexham were among the clubs to mock the case by putting a not to 'check training ground for unauthorised visitors' prior to their match with Southampton on fixture release day. Source: X/Wrexham_AFC

Birmingham City also referenced the case by revealing the date for their fixture by showing the club badges cut into hedges and visible through binoculars. Source: X/BCFC

‘Recent media interest in perceived public disputes between Clubs illustrates how quickly individual posts can become a wider reputational issue.’

Daily Mail Sport understands the EFL are keen to avoid being seen as killjoys. Rather, they are taking a preventative approach to posts that could end up breaching FA or EFL rules.

The Southampton ‘Spygate’ scandal is among the most prominent disputes that have been referenced by clubs in social media content in recent months.

Both Birmingham City and Wrexham shared posts on the Championship fixture release date in June, using the case to highlight the dates of a fixture with Southampton.

Birmingham’s official X account posted a graphic of both clubs' badges cut into hedges which were viewed through binoculars. The account added: ‘One of the other key fixtures to keep an eye on...’

Wrexham’s calendar for their matches in September included a reminder to 'check training ground for unauthorised visitors’ two days before they played Southampton. An image of a man behind a tree was included in the Southampton badge.

The club also included their Hollywood owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac in a spoof video in the build-up to the match. The actors were seen behind a tree similar to one which Southampton intern William Salt was caught spying near ahead of their play-off semi-final with Middlesbrough.

Following the revelations by Daily Mail Sport, Southampton were eventually thrown out of the play-offs.

Last week, Blackburn hit back at a video of West Ham manager Scott Parker declaring he ‘didn’t see a Blackburn fan’ by showing images of their supporters celebrating goals in their 2-1 win over the Hammers.

Blackburn hit back at West Ham boss Scott Parker last week after he declared he ‘didn’t see a Blackburn fan', with the club then showing supporters celebrating goals. Source: X/Rovers

The EFL reminded clubs in their letter that regulations called for clubs to ‘to act towards one another with utmost good faith’. The organisation called for clubs to consider whether their content is ‘punching down’ or ‘targeting a specific Club or individual’, adding they would likely cross the threshold if it does.

The organisation stressed that its preference is for ‘engagement and prevention’ and was not requesting clubs to make ‘bland or risk-free’ content.

However, the EFL warned it is prepared to take ‘proportionate and consistent action’ where ‘conduct which doesn’t meet the standards we expect is repeated or serious.’

Clubs have been asked to ensure a senior leader owns the standard applied to the club’s content, as well as formalising approval arrangements, briefing relevant people and exercising restraint.

#1393. Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1,2,3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

The physical characteristics of the cell nucleus are extraordinarily diverse, exhibiting distinct shape and mechanical phenotypes across tissue types, physiological states and disease conditions. Fragile or misshapen nuclei are hallmarks of cancer, cardiomyopathy and premature ageing4,5. Nuclei in stem cells gradually stiffen during differentiation4,5,6,7. While these changes are widely recognized as consequences of altered nuclear composition and chromatin dynamics, they also influence genome organization and transcription8,9,10. Despite the importance, the physical state of the nucleus at the earliest stages of mammalian development, when life begins, remains unclear.

During the first few cleavages, nuclei undergo extensive epigenetic reprogramming, enabling the zygote to initiate a new developmental program. In mice, this transition occurs within the first approximately 48 h after fertilization and is associated with a surge in new transcript production, known as major zygotic gene activation (ZGA)11,12,13. Major ZGA occurs during the mid-to-late two-cell stage, and embryos that impair ZGA fail in subsequent development. Around the time of ZGA, chromatin exhibits distinct structural and biochemical changes accompanied by histone modifiers and transcription factors14,15. By contrast, whether the nucleus organizing chromatin undergoes any crucial changes that drive ZGA is not known. In somatic cells, nuclear shape and mechanics depend on lamins, which line the inner nuclear membrane16,17. Lamins are long-lived, enriched in eggs and are crucial for mammalian development18,19,20. Previous studies have documented that, of the two major types, A-type lamins exhibit cell-lineage-specific differential expression patterns, whereas B-type lamins are constitutively expressed throughout development16. However, their dynamics and transiency, as well as the underlying core regulatory mechanism, during the earliest embryonic stages are poorly understood. Likewise, how the nuclear lamina, which forms a structural meshwork, controls nuclear mechanics and genome dynamics during this critical transition is unknown. Investigating physical nuclear characteristics necessitates direct quantification and manipulation of their mechanical properties. However, achieving this without compromising cell viability poses a challenge.

To investigate physical nuclear properties, we first performed high-resolution confocal scanning of fertilized mouse eggs during early cleavages (Fig. 1a). Our three-dimensional (3D) images of nuclei with H2B–mCherry, expressed without perturbing development (Extended Data Fig. 1a), revealed their distinct shape features, showing uneven local deformation at the two-cell stage in contrast to their predominantly spherical appearance at the one-cell and four-cell stages (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1b). Timelapse imaging revealed that one-cell nuclei remained spherical during the cell cycle (Fig. 1d). Two-cell nuclei underwent slow, incremental deformation, which started at around 21 h post-insemination (h.p.i.), peaked at 24–26 h.p.i. and then gradually regressed by 32–36 h.p.i. (Fig. 1e). At the four-cell stage, nuclei were again spherical (Fig. 1f) (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Videos 1−3). Before the onset of deformation, two-cell nuclei had fully swollen and reached steady sizes; once deformed, the altered nuclear shapes persisted for hours (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Similar deformation was observed using emerin–eGFP for the nuclear envelope (Fig. 1g) or mCherry–NLS for the nuclear interior (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

a, Schematic of early-stage mouse embryos. b,c, Representative 3D images of nuclei visualized using H2B–mCherry (b) and quantification of nuclear sphericity (c). F, female; M, male. d–f, Time courses of 2D nuclear deformation during the one-cell (d), two-cell (e) and four-cell stages (f). Live imaging was performed at 1 h intervals over around 52 h for n = 9 embryos; the mean (orange) and s.d. (shaded area) of nuclear deformation, calculated as shown in the inset in d, are plotted. g, Nuclear membranes were imaged using emerin–eGFP (green) and analysed for 2D nuclear deformation. The arrowheads indicate prominent deformation sites. h, Schematic of nanocapillary-based mechanical measurement. An embryo is held with a holding pipette, while a pressure-controlled nanocapillary captures and stretches the nucleus to measure nuclear elasticity and stiffness. i, Snapshots of nuclei subjected to the nanocapillary-based measurement (red, H2B–mCherry; overlay with bright field). Representative from four (8 and 24 h.p.i.) and two (48 h.p.i.) independent experiments. j–l, Maximal nuclear deformation (j), nuclear stiffness (k) and the degree of elasticity (l) analysed from experiments as in i. S0, Smax and Sr are as in i. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. For c, g and j–l, statistical analysis was performed using Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s-multiple comparisons test; the thick horizontal bars represent the mean values (red or black). Scale bars, 10 μm (b, g and i).

This finding prompted us to develop a biophysical setup that quantitatively characterizes the mechanical properties of early embryonic nuclei in situ (Fig. 1h). The setup equipped a pressure-controlled nanocapillary, of which the tip was inserted into a fertilized embryo to capture the nuclear surface. A weak, constant suction pressure (2.1 × 101 kPa) pinched the surface, which was then stretched through axial translocation of the nanocapillary. The nuclei could be gradually strained, resulting in tension, and the strain reached a maximum just before the detachment (Fig. 1i). The analysis could be performed from the one-cell to four-cell stages, over which the predominantly fluid-like cytoplasm minimally influenced the measured mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 2a–f). Measurements were also insensitive to nuclear markers and were comparable to label-free imaging results (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h).

Our analysis revealed that two-cell nuclei were significantly more deformable than one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1j). The deformable nature persisted throughout the cell cycle (from 21 to 32 h.p.i.) even as DNA doubled at about 24 h.p.i. Nuclear stiffness, as estimated based on the nanocapillary pressure and the extent of nuclear deformation, transiently lowered at the two-cell stage (one-cell, 5.0 ± 1.3 nN µm−1; two-cell, 2.0 ± 0.5 nN µm−1; four-cell, 4.6 ± 1.9 nN µm−1; n = 18, 38 and 13 embryos, respectively) (Fig. 1k). The stiffness values varied between male and female pronuclei (30.7 ± 21.3%, n = 8 pairs) and between blastomeres of each two-cell embryo (23.5 ± 14.5%, n = 16 pairs), while the differences were pronounced among the developmental stages (Extended Data Fig. 2i). Two-cell nuclei also exhibited significant plasticity, in contrast to more elastic one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1l) (shape recovery, 91.0 ± 4.3% for one-cell; 66.9 ± 8.0% for two-cell; and 87.9 ± 4.6% for four-cell). The deformable two-cell nuclear stiffness was consistent when embryos were examined using lower nanocapillary pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). An alternative capillary-based approach, using an incremental suction pressure that aspirated nuclei, yielded consistent results (n ≥ 12 embryos per stage) (Extended Data Fig. 2l–n). These corroborate the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus.

Our nanocapillary-based assay at 1.2 × 101 kPa minimally perturbed development, enabling us to relate two-cell nuclear stiffness with embryos’ developmental competence (Fig. 2a). We found that all fertilized embryos that timely reached the blastocyst stage had soft nuclei (2.0 ± 0.6 nN µm−1; n = 66 of 66 embryos), while nearly half of the embryos that impaired development had stiff nuclei (n = 7 of 15 embryos; defined as more than twice the mean nuclear stiffness of the normal development) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Detecting embryos with stiff nuclei was infrequent (8.6%; n = 7 out of 81 embryos). The outcome was regardless of the fluorescent tag type and marker expression levels (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). A similar mechanical feature was observed for cloned embryos created through somatic cell nuclear transfer (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3a,d,e) (n = 46 embryos). Thus, deformable two-cell nuclei are a signature of normal preimplantation development.

a, Schematic of the assay. Embryos prepared through in vitro fertilization or through somatic cell nuclear transfer were subjected to the nanocapillary-based mechanical measurement during the two-cell stage using a pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k), after which the embryos resumed standard culture. b, The relationship between two-cell nuclear stiffness and the frequency of development to the blastocyst stage at 96 h.p.i. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. For b, statistical analysis was performed using Mann–Whitney U-tests (two-sided); the thick horizontal bars (red) represent the mean values.

We next explored the molecular mechanism underlying the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus. Using immunofluorescence, we first examined four major lamins, A/C, B1 and B2, and found that lamin B1 transiently cleared from the two-cell nuclear envelope, nearly paralleling nuclear softening (Fig. 3a,b). The clearance was rapid and substantial, with an approximately 70% decrease in peripheral signal during the early-to-mid two-cell stage (21 to 24 h.p.i.; Fig. 3b). Lamin A/C and B2 levels also changed, but their trends were gradual and monotonic, with only a minor decline, if any, during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Another nuclear envelope protein, Lap2β, also changed little (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Live-embryo imaging confirmed the clearance of lamin B1 from the two-cell nuclear envelope with a decay time constant of 86 ± 44 min (n = 5 embryos; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). An immunoblotting assay revealed a reduction in lamin B1 during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3d), suggesting degradation.

a, Immunofluorescence images of endogenous lamins in early embryos (h.p.i. are as in Fig. 1j–l). Representative images are shown from six independent experiments. Identical imaging conditions were used. b, Quantification of lamin B1 at the nuclear envelope from assays in a. c, Live-imaging data showing mEGFP–lamin B1 signals at the two-cell nuclear envelope, acquired under conditions that minimized photobleaching and phototoxicity. d, Immunoblotting of lysates from two-cell embryos for lamin B1; β-actin was used as the loading control. Two independent experiments with similar results. e, Diagrams of the lamin B1 constructs used in this study. The red ticks indicate mutated sites. aa, amino acid; LIR, LC3-interacting region. f, Endogenous lamins in embryos (24 h.p.i.) expressing sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ, visualized using immunofluorescence. Representative images are shown from three to five independent experiments. g, Quantification of lamins at the nuclear envelope from assays in f, analysed as in b. h, Developmental rates of embryos expressing sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ versus the non-injection control. i, Live-imaging analysis was performed to quantify mCherry-fused WT and mutant lamin B1 signals at the two-cell nuclear envelope. j, Colocalization of lamin B1 (red) with lysosomes (green) at 24 h.p.i. Nuclei were out of the image plane. k,l, Total counts of lamin B1 foci (k) and lysosomes (l) from the assays in j. m, A model illustrating LC3-mediated lamin B1 clearance during the two-cell embryonic stage. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. Statistical analysis was performed using Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s multiple-comparison test (b, g, k and l) and χ2 tests (h). The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the means (b, g, k and l). For c and i, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bars, 10 μm (a, f and j). Source blot data are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1. Additional image data are provided in Extended Data Figs. 4c and 5a.

Our pilot assay using wortmannin implicated that autophagy promotes lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Autophagy is active in early embryos and is essential for preimplantation development21. In live-embryo imaging, the autophagy factor LC322 was diffusive at the one-cell stage and accumulated in the two-cell nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Our antibody microinjection targeting LC3 suppressed lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Cell cycle progression as monitored by EdU was normal (Extended Data Fig. 4g). We therefore designed a construct that interferes with the endogenous interaction between lamin B1 and LC3, using a short fragment of lamin B1 carrying LC3-binding domains and an intrinsic nuclear localization signal23 (hereafter, sfLB1; Fig. 3e). When expressed in embryos, this fragment was predominantly nucleoplasmic (Extended Data Fig. 4h), while a major autophagy substrate p62 maintained stable protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Our analysis revealed that the clearance of lamin B1 was suppressed by sfLB1, whereas lamin A/C and B2 remained largely unperturbed (Fig. 3f,g). An accumulation of lamin B1 was detectable in western blot analysis of lysates (Extended Data Fig. 4j). A sfLB1 variant (sfLB1Δ), which was nucleoplasmic but with abrogated LC3 binding23 (Extended Data Fig. 4h,k), had little influence on lamin B1 clearance (Fig. 3f,g). The development of embryos was impaired by sfLB1, but not by sfLB1Δ (Fig. 3h).

To understand the mechanistic basis of lamin B1 clearance, we constructed fluorescent reporters based on full-length lamin B1 fused to mCherry. Consistent with the results shown in Fig. 3a–c, the wild-type (WT) construct (flLB1wt; Fig. 3e) localized to the nuclear envelope and exhibited rapid lamin B1 clearance (T1/2 = 83 ± 44 min, n = 18) (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 5a). The other three constructs carried mutations near or at an LC3-interacting region core motif (flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A)) or at the major N-terminal CDK1 phosphorylation site for nuclear-envelope breakdown24 (flLB1(S24A)) (Fig. 3e). These constructs also localized to the two-cell nuclear envelope (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Notably, the mutations that abrogated LC3 interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5b) suppressed the lamin B1 clearance, whereas the mutation at the CDK1 site did not prevent the clearance (Fig. 3i). The mutations in flLB1(5A) were at the site targeted for autophagic degradation of lamin B1 during oncogene-induced cell senescence23. The selectivity of lamin B1 over lamin A/C and B2 was also consistent with the phenomenon reported in senescent cells23.

Our assay further suggested that lamin B1 is degraded through an autophagy–lysosome pathway. This was confirmed by tracking the fate of flLB1wt and identifying its predominant lysosomal localization and formation of foci (n = 18 embryos; Fig. 3j,k). flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) localized much less to lysosomes (n = 12 and 14 embryos; Fig. 3j,k), while the numbers of lysosomes remained comparable (Fig. 3l). We did not observe prominent lamin-B1-positive structures bulging from the outer nuclear membrane23 nor an accumulation of lysosomes on the nuclear surface25 within the timescale examined. Collectively, our mechanistic view of lamin B1 clearance is shown in Fig. 3m.

We next examined the effect of lamin B1 on two-cell nuclear stiffness. Nanocapillaries indicated that two-cell nuclei of which the envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1 were stiffer and less plastic than controls (4.2 ± 1.3 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (sfLB1; Fig. 4a–d). These nuclei were as stiff as normal one-cell and four-cell nuclei (~5 nN µm−1, Fig. 1k). We next overexpressed lamin B1. As WT lamin B1 rapidly dissociated from the nuclear envelope, we used flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) to compensate for the clearance. Whereas excess loading of these lamins resulted in collapsed nuclei, titrating expression levels preserved the overall nuclear shape, with lamin B1 loaded to the nuclear envelope at a level comparable to that using sfLB1 (Fig. 4a,b). We found that flLB1(F454A/L457A) profoundly increased nuclear elasticity and stiffness (4.0 ± 1.1 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (Fig. 4c,d), while overall autophagic activity as assessed by LC3 signal26 was maintained (Extended Data Fig. 5c). The phenotype quantitatively mirrored the embryos perturbed through sfLB1. By contrast, flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, which lacked the carboxy-terminal CaaX motif for farnesylation16 and remained nucleoplasmic, did not significantly alter nuclear shape and mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 5d). These data indicate that two-cell nuclear stiffness depends on the nuclear envelope localization of lamin B1.

a–e, Two-cell nuclear mechanics with lamin B1 enrichment. OE, overexpression. a, Representative immunofluorescence images at 24 h.p.i. from two independent experiments. b, Quantification of peripheral lamin B1 signals. c,d, Nuclear stiffness (c) and elasticity (d) were measured using nanocapillaries. e, Lamin B1 stability at the two-cell nuclear envelope. n values represent the numbers of isolated nuclei exposed to a high salt. f–k, RNA-seq results (28 h.p.i.; three biological replicates). f–h, Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) for the following comparisons: non-injected (non) versus flLB1(F454A/L457A) (f), flLB1(5A) versus flLB1(F454A/L457A) (g) and non-injected versus flLB1(5A) (h). FC, fold change; Padj, adjusted P. i, The overlaps among the sets of genes indicated (as assigned in DEGs, versus the non-injected controls). j, Expression levels of major ZGA genes in each embryo group. k, Expression levels of Obox genes15. ps, pseudogenes. l, H3K4me3 signals in broad H3K4me3 domains, as determined by Cut&Tag (28 h.p.i., two biological replicates). m, Expression levels of histone demethylases as determined by RNA-seq. Plots are individual biological replicates (three to seven per condition). FPKM, fragments per kilobase million. n–r, Tether-based nuclear stiffening. n, Live confocal imaging, showing the engineered tether–anchor proteins localized at the nuclear periphery. INM, inner nuclear membrane; ONM, outer nuclear membrane. o, Nuclear stiffness with the tether–anchor WT and deficient tether mutants. p, Lamin B1 signals at the tether-stiffened nuclear envelope. q, Lamin A/C and B2 signals are shown in Extended Data Fig. 9e. Expression levels of major ZGA genes with and without the tether–anchor (28 h.p.i., 3 biological replicates). r, The overlaps among the sets of downregulated genes indicated (as assigned in DEGs, versus the non-injected controls). n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. Control data pooled from four independent experiments (Fig. 1k,l) were used for comparisons in c, o and d (Methods). Statistical analysis was performed using Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s multiple-comparisons test (b–d and o), Tukey’s honest significant difference tests (m) and Mann–Whitney U-tests (two-sided) (e and p). The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the mean values (b–d, o and p). For e and m, data are mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 10 µm (a, e, n and p).

Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) showed nuclei of which the shape remained largely deformed as in normal two-cell embryos (Fig. 4a). These nuclei were soft and plastic (1.6 ± 0.4 nN µm−1, n = 10 embryos), despite their comparable level of nuclear envelope loading to sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4b–d). The minimal mechanical impact of flLB1(5A) was probably due to its poor assembly competency at the nuclear envelope for the following reasons: first, our nuclear isolation assay indicated that flLB1(5A) was more soluble than flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4e). Second, sfLB1(5A) showed comparably slightly higher affinity for LC3 than sfLB1(F454A/L457A) (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Finally, our expansion microscopy (ExM) analysis revealed a less-uniform peripheral localization of flLB1(5A) in comparison to endogenous lamin B1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A)27 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–g). The difference in peripheral DNA signals appeared less pronounced between perturbed embryo groups (Extended Data Fig. 6h). Our nanocapillary-based assay further suggested an early reduction in nuclear stiffness before lamin B1 clearance (Figs. 1k and 3a,b). Collectively, our data suggest that lamin B1 controls two-cell nuclear stiffness depending on their assembly stability at the nuclear envelope and that the stability depends on the site to which LC3 binds.

We next examined whether the observed nuclear changes impact the two-cell transcriptional reprogramming. We analysed the above embryos using RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq; Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 1). The first cleavage and following cell cycle progression were normal in those embryos; the overexpressed protein levels were stable and comparable among conditions (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Our analysis indicated that the transcriptomes of flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos were distinct from those of the flLB1(5A) and non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified more than 3,000 downregulated genes in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos compared with the non-injected controls (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Table 2). The downregulation was evident even when compared with flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4g), whereas very few DEGs were detected between flLB1(5A) embryos and the non-injected controls (Fig. 4h). Importantly, the genes downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) overlapped more with major ZGA and two-cell-activated genes than with minor ZGA and one-cell-activated genes28 (972 out of 3,763 (25.8%) versus 251 out of 3,763 (6.7%); P < 0.01, Fisher’s exact test) (Fig. 4i). The overlap was even greater when compared with another major ZGA gene list29 (1,338 out of 2,508, 53.3%) (Fig. 4i,j). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC embryos did not show an appreciably altered transcriptome at comparable expression levels (Extended Data Figs. 5g and 7e). Our analysis also indicated perturbed expression of key transcriptional regulators Obox15 in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos but it was not prominent in flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4k). The profiles of maternal and zygotic Obox genes suggested a failure in minor-to-major ZGA transition15.

We next analysed how ZGA is altered when the nuclear envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1. Analysing embryos overexpressing sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ, along with the non-injected controls, we found that thousands of genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated through sfLB1 (Extended Data Fig. 7f–l and Supplementary Table 3). Many downregulated genes identified as DEGs were shared between sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos (71.1%; Fig. 4i (bottom right)). Developmentally essential genes were enriched among the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7m). Analysing published chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) datasets further indicated sharp H3K4me3 signals around the transcription start sites of the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7n). We therefore performed genome-wide profiling of H3K4me3 through an optimized cleavage under targets and tagmentation (Cut&Tag) analysis. By establishing a condition that maintained the nuclear structure, reproducible signals were obtained that agreed with previously published ChIP–seq data14,30 (Extended Data Fig. 8a–e). Our analysis indicated that H3K4me3 is more abundant at transcription start sites in sfLB1 embryos than in the non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 8f). It has been demonstrated that broadly spread noncanonical H3K4me3 is removed by histone demethylation for major ZGA14. Indeed, H3K4me3 remained accumulated in broad-domain H3K4me3 (bdH3K4me3) in sfLB1 embryos, whereas H3K4me3 enrichment in lamina-associated domains unchanged (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 8g). Analysing the expression levels of histone methylation-related enzymes, key lysine demethylase (KDM) genes, which are needed to eliminate bdH3K4me314, were downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) and sfLB1, but the changes were not significant through flLB1(5A) and sfLB1Δ (Fig. 4m). These data suggest that the establishment of histone methylation status2 failed in embryos when lamin B1 stiffened the two-cell nuclear envelope.

There was a marked difference in nuclear stiffness between the embryo groups that failed in major ZGA and those that were transcriptionally less perturbed. To test whether nuclear stiffness per se was inhibitory to ZGA, we developed a molecular tether–anchor system that targets the nuclear envelope and stiffens nuclei (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 9a). The tether comprised an elastic I27 module of titin31 of which the ends were fused to a pair of GFP nanobodies. The anchor was made based on a minimal KASH domain fused to mEGFP for outer-nuclear-envelope localization32. When co-expressed, the tether was recruited to the anchor-coated nuclear envelope and increased nuclear stiffness by around twofold (4.3 ± 1.5 nN µm−1, n = 20 embryos; Fig. 4n,o and Extended Data Fig. 9b). Nuclear plasticity and deformation decreased accordingly (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Importantly, in the tether-stiffened nuclei, lamin B1 levels were as low as in normal mid two-cell embryos (Fig. 4p). Lamin A/C and B2 also remained largely unperturbed (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Our mRNA microinjection into late zygotes minimally affected pronuclear stiffness, first cleavage and cell cycle progression (Extended Data Fig. 9f–i). Moreover, our two mutant tether derivatives, one that weakened its affinity to the anchor (tether LaG16(5A)) and one that impaired its elastic force-generating property (tether titin(W34E)), showed no appreciable impact on nuclear shape and mechanics (Fig. 4o and Extended Data Fig. 9b–d,j). In contrast to the WT, neither of the two mutants significantly impaired development (Extended Data Fig. 9k). Thus, our tether–anchor system increases two-cell nuclear stiffness and perturbs embryonic development when it binds to the nuclear envelope and exerts force.

Our RNA-seq analysis revealed that embryos in which the nuclei were stiffened by the tether WT (tWT) exhibited distinct transcriptomes compared with those expressing the LaG16(5A) tether mutant and the non-injected controls (Extended Data Fig. 10a). A total of 634 genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated in the tWT embryos, while much fewer DEGs were identified in tether-mutant embryos (Fig. 4q and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e; versus the non-injected controls). Furthermore, the expression of the Obox cluster and other major ZGA genes was dampened (Extended Data Fig. 10f). Downregulation of key ZGA genes and transcriptional repression were detectable in quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) and 5-ethynyl-uridine (EU) incorporation analyses (Extended Data Fig. 10g,h). Whereas the impact on ZGA was broader and less variable for flLB1(F454A/L457A) than for tWT (972 versus 168 genes; Fig. 4i versus Extended Data Fig. 10e; Fig. 4j versus Fig. 4q), 82.2% of the downregulated genes in tWT embryos were shared with those perturbed through sfLB1 or flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4r). Together, we conclude that deformable two-cell nuclei are integral to the execution of proper ZGA.

We next examined the effect of lamin B1 persistence on early development. As a result, approximately 50% of the embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) did not progress beyond the two-cell stage (Extended Data Fig. 5h), comparable to those perturbed through sfLB1 (Fig. 3h). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC did not significantly affect development, indicating that the effective site of lamin B1 is at the nuclear envelope. Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) also showed impaired development, despite their nearly normal transcriptome (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Our analysis indicated that those embryos accumulated DNA damage as detected through phosphorylated H2A.X (γH2A.X) foci (Extended Data Fig. 5i), a developmental impediment33. By contrast, DNA damage levels in embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) were as low as those of non-injection control. Our results do not exclude the possibility that the suppressed ZGA and basal DNA damage combinatorially impaired development. Nonetheless, our data indicate that embryos with stiff two-cell nuclei are unable to facilitate proper ZGA and early development. Embryos with tether-stiffened nuclei also exhibited a two-cell arrest (Extended Data Fig. 9k), supporting the necessity of nuclear softness for development.

Given the impact of nuclear stiffness on ZGA, we examined chromatin dynamics in deformable and non-deformable nuclei. Our ExM images at 24 h.p.i. showed peripheral layers of DNA and lamins, with the overlap comparable to those analysed using electron microscopy34 (~150 nm; Extended Data Fig. 6i). Our imaging further revealed a preferential localization of DNA near concave regions of the two-cell nuclear envelope (Fig. 5a–c and Extended Data Fig. 6j). Lamin B1 signals also exhibited a weak negative correlation with nuclear deformation35 (Fig. 5b,c). However, the biased DNA localization was shared among deformable nuclei regardless of lamin B1 enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 6k–m), suggesting that nuclear deformation is associated with peripheral DNA organization.

a–c, ExM analysis. a, Representative image of a two-cell nucleus (left) and its enlarged section (white dashed rectangle) at 24 h.p.i. with linescans (white dashed curve) from two independent experiments. b, DNA and lamin B1 profiles along the deformed nuclear surface. c, Dependence of DNA and lamin B1 signals on local nuclear deformation (Pearson’s r = –0.38 ± 0.18 and –0.20 ± 0.26, respectively). d–h, Pol II localization. d, 3D-rendered two-cell nuclei at 21 and 24 h.p.i., with immunostaining signals of Pol II Ser2P foci (red; top 10% signal) with DNA (green). Representatives are shown from two independent experiments. e, The distributions of Pol II Ser2P foci from the nuclear periphery (at least 10 foci per embryo). f, The percentage of Pol II Ser2P foci near the concave nuclear surface (Pearson’s r = –0.57; grey ellipsoids, 95% confidence intervals). g, Pol II Ser2P focus size at 21 and 24 h.p.i. (the plots show the mean values; at least 10 foci per embryo). h, DNA mass volume at 21 and 24 h.p.i. i–l, 3D DNA FISH. i–k, The locations of the Kdm5b (i), Obox6 (j) and Gabarapl1 (k, for control) genes (green) in two-cell nuclei at 21 and 28 h.p.i. Representatives are shown from three independent experiments. l, Clustering analysis of the positions of Obox6 and Kdm5b locus pairs. Coloured plots indicate major clusters with boundary (grey shade) (alpha shape algorithm: α = 0.6). n values represent the numbers of embryos (a–h) and loci (i–l) analysed. Statistical analysis was performed using Mann–Whitney U- tests (two-sided) (h–k) and Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s multiple-comparison test (g). Scale bars, 10 μm (a, d and i–k).

We next examined how deformable nuclei are linked to gene expression regulation during ZGA. In 3D images, large fluorescent foci positive for elongating RNA polymerase II (Pol II Ser2P) shifted their distribution towards the nuclear periphery, as nuclear deformation increased from 21 to 24 h.p.i. (Fig. 5d,e). Notably, the majority of the Pol II foci became more frequently associated with nuclear concavity (Fig. 5f). The focus sizes increased over time, and their growth was suppressed by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5g). Concomitantly, DNA mass volume decreased by 14.7 ± 6.5% (Fig. 5h). We next performed sequential 3D fluorescence in situ hybridization (3D FISH) analysis36 to examine the link between peripheral transcriptional activity and ZGA (Fig. 5i–l). We analysed the genomic loci of Kdm5b and Obox6, along with Gabarapl1 as a non-ZGA control and found that their distributions were broad and changed from the early to the mid-to-late two-cell stage, but the average distance remained 2–3 µm from the nuclear periphery around the time of major ZGA (2.7 ± 2.0, 2.0 ± 1.6 and 2.1 ± 1.3 µm, respectively; 28 h.p.i.) (Fig. 5i–k). Pol II Ser2P intensities were greater when the Obox6 and Kdm5b loci were positioned >1 µm from the nuclear periphery, while DAPI signals remained unchanged, suggesting that the increased local transcriptional activity was not merely a consequence of higher chromatin density (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j). This trend was not observed in Gabarapl1 (Extended Data Fig. 10i). Our sequential FISH further enabled us to determine the locations of multiple gene loci within the same nucleus (Fig. 5l). Our data indicated a widespread positioning of Obox6 and Kdm5b loci at 21 h.p.i. and a change in the localization of gene loci at 28 h.p.i., with a frequent incidence of their concomitant presence near the nuclear periphery. This locus distribution was disrupted by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5l). Notably, Pol II Ser2P intensities at Obox6 loci depended on the nuclear stiffening, while their changes at Kdm5b loci appeared less pronounced (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We therefore performed sequential 3D DNA–RNA FISH analysis to detect nascent Kdm5b transcripts and found a surge in the production around 2–4 µm from the nuclear envelope, and it depended on peripheral nuclear stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 10l–n). In summary, our data suggest that soft and plastic two-cell nuclei ensure the formation of active transcription sites a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope and enable the coordinated positioning of key ZGA gene loci around the sites for expression.

Our study reveals physical characteristics of early embryonic nuclei and their distinct changes that facilitate ZGA. Our data show that the autophagy factor LC3 and lamin B1 clearance confer nuclear plasticity and softness, and that deformable nuclei are key to robust zygotic transcription. Extensive studies have profiled epigenetic states of chromatin and provided a genome-centred view of this critical developmental transition. Our study highlights the importance of physical nuclear state for this transition and underscores the need for integration of diverse embryonic parameters, including their subcellular material properties.

Our work identifies a transient phase of nuclear deformability that manifests as cells transition through a totipotent state (Fig. 1). Notably, this nuclear change marks normal preimplantation development and contributes to transcription and gene locus movement (Figs. 2, 4 and 5). Notably, the sites of active DNA transactions appear a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope, often associated with local negative curvature, suggesting the generation of inward forces around these sites (Fig. 5d–h). During ZGA, chromatin undergoes dynamic remodelling and compaction37,38,39, while maintaining contact with the nuclear lamina40. A flexible nuclear envelope may accommodate these internal and peripheral chromatin activities, mediating a mechanical conflict for the consolidation of functional genome architectures. Our analysis also suggests that intense transcriptional activity near the deformable nuclear envelope enables the full activation of key ZGA genes that shape the two-cell epigenome14 (Fig. 4l,m). Such mechanical control may also operate in naive embryonic stem cells, in which soft nuclei are linked to pluripotency and priming for differentiation41.

We find that the embryonic mechanism governing lamin B1 clearance shares similarities with nuclear autophagy activated during oncogene-induced cell senescence23 (Fig. 3). As autophagy is accompanied by an increase in intracellular calcium levels and is independent of mTORC1 in early embryos21,42, the clearance is most likely developmentally programmed. Our data suggest a role of nuclear translocation of LC3 and its distinct effect on nuclear shape and mechanics. Further analysis of its regulated nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling43 should reveal the mechanistic basis behind the physiological and pathological nuclear remodelling.

Our findings also raise several interesting questions for future studies. First, our imaging assay detected diluted lamin B1 at convex regions of the nuclear envelope35 (Fig. 5b,c). It remains to be explored whether the clearance of lamin B1 merely contributes to nuclear softening or controls DNA organization by sensing local nuclear curvature. Second, as lamins influence transcription44,45 and the chromatin–lamina contacts change during development40, understanding the interplay between mechanical cues and biochemical factors that ensures robust transcriptional control will be an essential next step. Third, soft and transcriptionally active nuclei, yet enriched with lamin B1 at the nuclear envelope, were prone to DNA damage (Extended Data Fig. 5i). As excess lamin B1 can cause persistent DNA damage46, autophagic clearance of lamin B1 may be necessary to protect against such damage. It would be interesting to dissect nuclear actin in two-cell nuclei47, as per its involvement in DNA damage repair48.

Physical nuclear stability is likely important for early embryos, given the potential mechanical challenges they face during passage through the uterine tube49. Yet this period coincides with a transient state in which nuclei become less mechanically resilient. Early mammalian embryos are also prone to DNA lesions and chromosome missegregation50,51,52. Understanding how embryos navigate the vulnerable state may reveal principles underlying developmental robustness.

Mice (ICR and B6C3F1/Jc1 or slc (BCF1)) aged 5–15 weeks53 were purchased from CLEA Japan, Japan SLC or Kiwa Laboratory Animals, maintained in light-controlled (light: 08:00 to 20:00; dark: 20:00 to 08:00), air-conditioned rooms (ambient temperature: 23 °C ± 1.5 °C, humidity: 50 ± 10%) at each facility and used for experiments. All mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation and all efforts were made to minimize suffering and to reduce the number of animals used.

To obtain oocytes, female mice were superovulated by intraperitoneal injections of 7.5 IU of pregnant mare serum gonadotropin (PMSG; ASKA Animal Health), followed by 7.5 IU of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG; ASKA Animal Health) at 48 h after PMSG injection. After the female mice were euthanized at 15–16 h after hCG injection, oocytes were collected from the oviducts by an abdominal operation and transferred to a pre-heated medium of Human Tubal Fluid (HTF; ARK Resource). Sperm were collected from the caudal epididymis of male mice for in vitro fertilization (IVF). For fertilization, freshly prepared or cryopreserved sperm were incubated in HTF medium for 1–1.5 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2 to allow for capacitation. Subsequently, the sperm suspension was mixed with the medium containing the oocytes, and fertilized eggs were collected 1–2 h after insemination followed by removal of cumulus cells with 0.1% hyaluronidase. The eggs were then transferred to drops of preheated KSOM medium (ARK Resource) and cultured at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2.

Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) was performed as described previously54. In brief, enucleation of cumulus-free MII oocytes was performed in drops of CZB medium including 5 μg ml−1 cytochalasin B. One donor cumulus cell in CZB medium with 6% deionized-BSA was transferred to the perivitelline space of an enucleated oocyte together with a small amount of HVJ-E (GenomeONE-CF; Ishihara Sangyo) by tightly attaching the donor cell to the enucleated oocyte. The oocyte was then cultured in KSOM medium for 1 h at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2 for the cell fusion. The reconstructed oocytes were activated in KSOM medium containing 5 mM SrCl2, 2 mM EGTA and 5 μg ml−1 cytochalasin B (Sigma-Aldrich) for 6 h at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2. The activated SCNT embryos were cultured at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2 in KSOM medium.

Pharmacological inhibition experiments were performed by treating embryos with the following chemicals in KSOM medium containing 0.5% (v/v) DMSO: 10 µM wortmannin (19545-26-7, AdipoGen); and 200 nM bafilomycin A1 (SML1661, Sigma-Aldrich). Wortmannin treatment was started at 12 h.p.i. and terminated before fixation at 32 h.p.i. Bafilomycin treatment was started at 15 h.p.i. and terminated before fixation at 28 h.p.i. The mock control also contained 0.5% (v/v) DMSO throughout assays.

For immunoblotting assays, the following antibodies were used: anti-p62 rabbit IgG (PM045MS, MBL), anti-β actin mouse mAb (AC-15, Santa Cruz), anti-GFP chicken IgY (ab13970, Abcam), HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody (32460, Thermo Fisher Scientific), HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG antibody (61-6520, Thermo Fisher Scientific), HRP-conjugated goat anti-chicken IgY-HRP (A16054, Thermo Fisher Scientific), anti-lamin B1 mouse IgG (sc-374015, Santa Cruz), anti-HA antibody (51064-2-AP, Proteintech) and HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG antibody (32460, Thermo Fisher Scientific). For immunostaining imaging assays, the following antibodies were used: anti-lamin A/C mouse IgG2a (39287, Active Motif), anti-lamin A/C mouse IgG1k (sc-376248, Santa Cruz), anti-lamin B1 mouse IgG (sc-374015, Santa Cruz; amino acids 559–586 of lamin B1), anti-lamin B1 rabbit IgG (ab16048, Abcam), anti-lamin B2 rabbit IgG (ab151735, Abcam), anti-lamin B2 mouse IgG1 (68475-1-Ig, Proteintech), anti-RNA polymerase II phosphorylated at serine 2 mouse IgM (920203, BioLegend), anti-phospho-histone H2A.X (Ser139) mouse IgG1 (05-636, Sigma-Aldrich), anti-LAP2Β mouse IgG (611000, BD Transduction Laboratories), anti-BrdU mouse IgG1 (sc-32323, Santa Cruz), goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 488 (A11001, Thermo Fisher Scientific), goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 568 (ab175473, Abcam), goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 647 (ab150115, Abcam), goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 488 (A11008, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 594-labelled donkey anti-rabbit IgG antibody (A21207, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and goat anti-mouse IgM (Heavy chain) Alexa Fluor 594 (A21044, Thermo Fisher Scientific). For antibody microinjection experiments, the following antibodies were used: anti-LC3 mouse IgG (CTB-LC3-2-IC, Cosmo Bio) and normal mouse IgG (sc-2025, Santa Cruz).

Conway (Addgene, 68127)56. pcDNA3.1-H2B-mCherry-polyA, pcDNA3.1-H2B-EGFP-polyA and pcDNA3.1-EGFP-polyA were gifts from K. Yamagata. pcDNA-emerin-eGFP-polyA was used to label the nuclear envelope. pcDNA3.1-EGFP-polyA was used as a backbone or an expression control, while pcDNA3.1-H2B-mCherry-polyA and pcDNA-H2B-EGFP-polyA were used as nuclear markers. Moreover, custom constructs generated in this study for live-embryo imaging and overexpression assays are as follows: pcDNA3.1-sfLB1-polyA, pcDNA3.1-sfLB1Δ-polyA, pcDNA3.1-eGFP-sfLB1-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mEGFP-sfLB1Δ-polyA, pcDNA3.1-eGFP-LC3-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mEGFP-flLB1wt-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1wt-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1(5A)-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1(F454A/F457A)-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1(S24A)-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1(F454A/F457A)ΔC-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-NLS-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mEGFP-KASH-TM-polyA, pcDNA3.1-LaG16-titin-LaG16-mCherry-polyA, pcDNA3.1-LaG16(5A)-titin-LaG16(5A)-mCherry-polyA and pcDNA3.1-LaG16-titin(W34E)-LaG16-mCherry-polyA. For generating each of the WT constructs, the corresponding genetic sequences were amplified by PCR from mouse ovary cDNA, which was synthesized using SuperScript VILO Master Mix (11756050, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with the following primer pairs: flLB1_fp1 and flLB1_rp1 for lamin B1 and LC3_fp1 and LC3_rp1 for LC3 (sequence information is provided below). Amplified fragments were cloned either into downstream of eGFP in the pcDNA3.1-eGFP-polyA vector to create fusion constructs, or used to replace its eGFP sequence. All cloning procedures were performed using the In-Fusion cloning system (Clontech) unless otherwise noted. For mCherry fusion constructs, the eGFP sequence was replaced with mCherry, and a codon-optimized linker sequence (SGLRSRAQA)57 was inserted in between. The plasmids for full-length lamin B1 mutants were generated by introducing substitutional mutations into pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1wt-polyA using the following primer pairs: flLB1_fp2 and flLB1_rp2, flLB1_fp3 and flLB1_rp3, and flLB1_fp4 and flLB1_rp4, for flLB1(5A), flLB1(F454A/L457A) and flLB1(S24A), respectively. For flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, the corresponding CaaX sequence was removed using flLB1_fp5 and flLB1_rp5 followed by ligation. The plasmids carrying sfLB1 were generated by amplifying the corresponding coding sequence (371–459) from the lamin B1 plasmid using the following PCR primers: sfLB1_fp1 and sfLB1_rp1, sfLB1_fp2 and sfLB1_rp2, sfLB1_fp3 and sfLB1_rp3, and sfLB1_fp4 and sfLB1_rp4, and inserting them into a pcDNA3.1 vector. A codon-optimized linker sequence (RDPPVAT) was inserted between eGFP and sfLB1. pDHFR-3HA-LB1, pDHFR-3HA-LB1Δ, pDHFR-3HA-LB1(5A) and pDHFR-3HA-LB1(F454A/L457A) for pull-down assays were generated by cloning out the corresponding coding sequence from the full-length lamin B1 plasmids and inserted them into the DHFR vector (New England Biolabs). For GST-LC3, the coding sequence of LC3 was inserted into a pGEX vector downstream of GST and the PreScission sequence. pcDNA3.1-mCherry-NLS-polyA for nuclear imaging was generated by inserting a codon-optimized SV40 large T antigen NLS downstream of mCherry in pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1-polyA (inverse PCR primers: NLS_fp1 and NLS_rp1). To generate pcDNA3.1-mEGFP-KASH-TM-polyA for nuclear envelope tethering, the KASH-TM sequence (amino acids 6525–6874 of nesprin 2G) was amplified by PCR from the pcDNA nesprin TS vector (Addgene, 68127, gift from D. Conway) using primers KASH-TM_fp1 and KASH-TM_rp1. The amplified fragment was then inserted into a pcDNA3.1-mEGFP vector. pcDNA3.1-LaG16-titin-LaG16-mCherry-polyA was generated as a fusion of titin immunoglobulin domain (I27(V11P))31 flanked by a pair of GFP-nanobody (LaG16)58. First, the coding sequences of LaG16 and I27(V11P) codon-optimized for mouse were synthesized by Eurofins Genetics. The first LaG16, I27(V11P), and the second LaG16 comprising the tether were each amplified by PCR using primer pairs LaG16_fp1 and LaG16_rp1, Titin_fp1 and Titin_rp1, and LaG16_fp2 and LaG16_rp2, respectively, and then inserted in order into a pcDNA3.1-mCherry vector using restriction enzyme digestion (ClaI and HpaI) and sticky/blunt-end ligation with a Ligation Mix kit (6023, Takara). Codon-optimized linker sequences (GGGGS and RDPPVAT) were inserted between the first LaG16 and titin I27 and between the second LaG16 and mCherry, respectively. The DNA fragment of LaG16 mutant (S32A/T56A/V57A/R103A/V106A), designed according to a previous study59, was also synthesized by Eurofins Genetics and used to generate the plasmid in the same way as above. The mutation in titin (W34E)60 was introduced using the primers Titin_W34E_fp1&rp1. All the plasmids were verified by DNA sequencing (Eurofins Genetics).
