For a, fold change ≥ 2 or ≤ 0.5 and p < 0.05, two-sided t-test. For (b and q), p < 0.05. Scale bars, 20 μm (e) and 5 μm (g).

a, Cell death phenotype of RPS4TIR in WT and NbGRP7-KO Nb leaves 36 h post-infiltration (hpi). Color-coded stacked bars display the percentages (in each case) of each cell death score (0-5). 11 leaves were scored. b, Expression of proteins (EV and RPS4TIR-MYC) in WT and NbGRP7-KO Nb leaves were detected by immunoblot using anti-MYC antibody. Actin was detected on a separate blot prepared from the same samples and processed in parallel. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. c, Cell death phenotypes of RPS4TIR in NbGRP7-KO at 56 hpi (n = 17). d, Two independent NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO knockout (NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO) lines were generated using the CRISPR/Cas9 system. The corresponding mutation target sites are shown. e, Cell death phenotype following transient expression of OsTIR in WT and NbGRP7/ NbGRP8-KO leaves at 40 hpi. f, Color-coded stacked bars display the percentages (in each case) of each cell death score (0-5). 11 leaves were scored. g, Immunoblot detection of OsTIR-MYC in WT and NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO leaves using an anti-MYC antibody. Actin was used as the loading control. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. h, Cell death phenotypes of OsTIR in NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO at 68 hpi (n = 24). RPS4TIR and OsTIR-induced cell death assays were performed under laboratory conditions and the greenhouse conditions described in the Methods, respectively.

#1372. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Caicedo rattles the woodwork with a stunning effort! 💥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/CSIM9ogtSp

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

He told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

"Not as good as we wanted." 💬 David Moyes reflects on Everton's defeat to Chelsea 🔵 🎙️ @jules_breach | Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/qPU64VjHYC

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Xabi Alonso gives relatively positive news on Emi Martinez.

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and says, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

On his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that says when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”

With Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really important. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”

Everton playing like a completely Moyes side. At their best, they are dangerous on the counter and solid at the back. When it goes wrong, the lack of creativity hurts Moyes’ sides, but right now they are holding their own.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1370. Mauricio Pochettino to sign two-and-a-half year deal to replace Michael Carrick at Man United - as it emerges he WILL take charge of USA game in early hours of Wednesday, just days before crunch Liverpool clash

Published: 10:58 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 18:28 EST, 12 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino will face a brutal start to life at Manchester United with the prospective Red Devils boss set to manage the United States days before his debut at Liverpool.

United have moved closer to putting Pochettino in charge at Old Trafford after reaching a verbal agreement with the US national team boss on Wednesday. The club then made a formal approach to US Soccer, and he is set to sign a two-and-a-half-year deal.

Daily Mail Sport understands Pochettino will take charge of both of the United States matches during the international window.

The US take on Haiti in the CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final first leg on Saturday, with the second fixture then taking place in Cincinnati on Tuesday evening, but would likely finish at around 2am GMT.

Pochettino would then have to travel to Manchester following the match to link up with the Red Devils' squad for the first time, likely on Thursday.

The Argentine would then have limited time with his players before a daunting trip to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool on Sunday in a blockbuster first match in charge.

Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of the United States upcoming matches against Haiti

Pochettino will coach in the early hours on Wednesday morning in Cincinnati before travelling to Manchester

The Argentine would have limited time to prepare his side for Sunday's match at Anfield

Man United are said to be relaxed over Pochettino taking charge of his final two matches as US boss before starting as their new head coach.

It will cost Pochettino around £7million to buy himself out of his contract with the US Soccer Federation, with United ready to foot the bill.

The cost of bringing in his back-room team, including trusted assistants Jesus Perez and Miguel D’Agostino, will take the cost above £10million.

The 54-year-old only signed a new deal after the World Cup meaning that United could have got him for nothing in the summer.

Pochettino is set to take over a Man United side languishing in the Premier League relegation zone following just one win in their opening ten matches.

The trip to Anfield would be the first of a run of eight matches in 29 days, as Man United juggle Premier League and Champions League football.

Pochettino is set to succeed Michael Carrick, whose departure as the Red Devils' boss was officially announced on Wednesday morning.

Pochettino will face a tight turnaround to prepare his new side for the daunting clash on Merseyside

Carrick arrived at United's training ground at 7.50am this morning and was dismissed. He left at 10.18am, less than two and a half hours later. He is the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season, followed hours later by bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage.

In a statement released at 10.37am, Carrick's sacking was confirmed. United's statement read: 'After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

'Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.'

Carrick's backroom team have also left the club with Pochettino set to bring his own staff to United.

Assistant boss Steve Holland, coaches Jonathan Woodgate, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, and goalkeeping coach Craig Mawson have all gone, although United didn't initially confirm the news because not all of them were at the training ground this morning and had to be told in person.

#1369. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.

A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.

City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1367. 'It's a LIE': Bullish Morgan Rogers hits back at claims Cole Palmer isn't committed to England as Three Lions star appears to suggest Thomas Tuchel is 'wrong' for questioning Chelsea team-mate

Published: 18:35 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 18:41 EST, 12 November 2026

Morgan Rogers has rubbished questions around team-mate and friend Cole Palmer's commitment to England after the Chelsea star was left out of the latest squad.

After missing out on selection for the World Cup, Palmer was called up to the group for the first international break of the season as he continued to monitor his fitness, but dropped out of the squad.

It meant he was again ignored when it came to selection for this fortnight's Nations League games against Croatia and Spain, with manager Thomas Tuchel saying Palmer 'misses too many opportunities to impress' him.

The events have led to criticism of Palmer, who scored for England in the final of Euro 2024, but Rogers has moved to defend his friend.

'It's a lie,' Rogers, who was speaking after starting and scoring for England in their 2-1 win over Croatia on Thursday, said on BBC 5 Live. 'He wants to be here. He wanted to get called up and he wanted to come and represent his country as he always has done. People just see it as news and say the easy thing.

'We all know he had a difficult year last year with injuries and I know personally he's been managing them injuries ever since. He was in quite a low place with his injuries last year and didn't feel 100 per cent himself on the pitch, so he wants to be here and he wants to be the best version of himself. Of course he does, who wouldn't?

Morgan Rogers (right) has rubbished questions around Cole Palmer's (left) commitment to the England team

Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel (right) said Palmer 'misses too many opportunities to impress' him

'But he also has to look at his body. He wants to play for 10 to 15 years, (so) he also has to manage himself. If he has to manage himself in the short term for the greater good then he has to do that and you have to fully support it.

'It has nothing to do with England or not wanting to play with England. It's a nonsense really that people are questioning someone that wants to play for England. You see the joy and smile on his face, how much he loves the game, so I honestly don't get it and he doesn't get it. But it's something he has to deal with but I can assure you he wants to be here and he wants to play for his country.'

Tuchel has accepted that Palmer is 'no exception' to being 'desperate' to wanting to play for England.

But the German claimed he has largely opted to stick with much of the group he ran with in the last international break, despite calling up Jobe Bellingham, James Hill, and Josh King – who plays in Palmer's position – for the first time.

'It's not personal,' the Three Lions boss said on the 24-year-old's omission. 'And of course we will never assume that Cole is not in the mindset to come and desperate to play for his country, but the competition is on and the players who were in camp did an amazing job and kept their place.'

Rogers, though, is desperate to see Palmer back in an England shirt.

'What a player he is,' he added. 'What a person he is and it's someone you want to see in an England shirt.

'He's got so much quality, so much ability. We all know what we can do, what he's done, so of course we want to see him in an England shirt and hopefully sooner rather than later.'

#1366. Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1,2,3. Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival4,5,6,7. Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse.

Gene expression profiles classify breast cancers into luminal A or luminal B (hormone-receptor-positive (HR+)), HER2-positive and basal-like subtypes. Among these, basal-like subtypes largely overlap with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)2,3. These classifications guide treatment management and prognosis. Luminal HR+ breast cancer generally responds to endocrine therapy with favourable outcomes, yet many patients relapse8. Single-cell and spatial studies have revealed substantial intratumoural heterogeneity among subtypes, which potentially drive treatment resistance and recurrence4,5,6,7,9.

Chromatin organization, mediated by DNA and histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), facilitates the acquisition of epigenetically distinct cellular states in genetically identical cells10,11,12. Although single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell chromatin-accessibility sequencing (scATAC–seq) delineate intratumour heterogeneity13,14,15,16, the contribution of chromatin patterns remains unclear17. Single-cell profiling of histone marks, such as trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me3), implicates chromatin states in breast tumour heterogeneity and treatment resistance18,19. However, these methods measure a limited number of chromatin marks, which hinders analyses of complex patterns and interactions. We developed a cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) method to systematically profile multiple histone PTMs and decode population-specific chromatin patterns to examine heterogeneity among cancer cells20,21,22,23.

Tumour epigenetic states are also reflected in blood. Cell-free, plasma-circulating nucleosomes, released mainly by dying normal and cancer cells, retain tissue-of-origin epigenetic patterns24,25,26,27. Our single-molecule imaging platform, epigenetics of plasma isolated nucleosomes (EPINUC), captures multiple epigenetic features on plasma nucleosomes28. This method detects colorectal cancer, including low-burden early-stage disease28, and enables minimally invasive molecular profiling and treatment monitoring of paediatric brain tumours29.

Here we present a holistic epigenetic analysis of primary treatment-naive breast tumours and blood cell-free nucleosomes. Linking recurrent intratumoural epigenetic patterns to circulating nucleosomes connects tumour epigenetic heterogeneity with its potential clinical implications. This work reveals epigenetic alterations as key mediators of intratumour heterogeneity and potential biomarkers for early diagnosis and prognosis.

To assess heterogeneity in breast tumour histone modifications, we performed epigenetic focused CyTOF on fresh, surgically resected tumours from treatment-naive women and quantified histone modifications at single-cell resolution (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). The cohort included mainly luminal HR+ tumours and only one basal triple-negative (TN, HR–) tumour (n = 12; Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1a,b), as standard neoadjuvant therapy excluded most TN cases from treatment-naive eligibility. Following batch correction and normalization, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) analysis of all 12 tumours revealed that tumour cells largely occupied patient-specific regions, whereas stromal cells clustered together across patients. This result aligns with previous studies that measured single-cell genomic differences13,14 (Fig. 1b, Methods and Supplementary Fig. 2a). Partial overlap among luminal tumour cells from different patients probably reflects shared lineage-specific epigenetic programs. As expected, stromal cells expressed vimentin and αSMA, whereas tumour cells expressed the epithelial keratins, EpCAM and E-cadherin (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2b,c). Notably, the basal TN tumour differed from HR+ tumours, showing low expression of the luminal marker GATA3 and high expression of the basal marker cytokeratin-5 (K5; also known as KRT5) and mesenchymal vimentin markers (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2d). Stromal and tumour chromatin patterns also differed, a result that underscores their role in dictating cellular identity (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2e). CyTOF analysis of MCF7 (luminal) and four basal-like TN cell lines validated that GATA3 and K5 expression patterns can differentiate luminal and basal-like identities. Moreover, SHAP analysis30,31 identified these two markers as the strongest discriminators of tumour type (Fig. 1e,f). Using multiple cell-identity markers, we derived a PermCell luminal signature (Methods) that accurately distinguished the identities of the cell lines (Fig. 1g).

a, Schematic of the experiment. Tumours were dissociated, depleted of CD45+ immune cells, stained with metal-conjugated antibodies and analysed by CyTOF (Supplementary Table 1). Ac, acetylation; Me, Methylation; Ub, Ubiquitination. b, UMAP of the CyTOF dataset (1,157,765 cells, n = 12 tumours, mean of 96,480 cells per tumour; Supplementary Table 3). Shown are around 1,000 cells per sample (one replicate per tumour), coloured by sample (left) or marker intensity (right). Dashed outlines indicate HR+, TN and stromal cell regions. c,d, Heatmaps of mean marker levels in stroma, TN tumour (n = 1) and luminal tumours (n = 11); rows are standardized and clustered. e, UMAP of breast cancer cell lines. Shown are 5,000 cells per line, coloured by line (left) or marker intensity (right). f, XGBoost classifier segregating luminal and basal-like cell lines using all cell identity markers (Supplementary Table 1). SHAP scores indicate feature importance. g, UMAP as in e, coloured by a luminal signature score derived from the indicated markers (bottom). Asterisk indicates markers absent from the cell-line panel. h, UMAP of cells from tumour 5 (representative of n = 11) following DBSCAN clustering and noise (unclassified cells) removal, coloured by subpopulation, marker intensity and luminal signature. i, Heatmap of mean marker levels per subpopulation in h, row-standardized as z-scores. Rows and columns are clustered. j, UMAP of two luminal PDX models, coloured as in h. For PDX-1, six tumours were sampled equally to match PDX-2 cell numbers. k,l, Mean CyTOF Ki-67 levels versus the percentage of Ki-67+ cells by IHC (k) or cycling cells by epigenetic signature (l, n = 11). Data show linear fit (lines), 95% confidence intervals (CI, grey), Pearson’s r and two-sided P values. Tumour 20 showed outlier CyTOF Ki-67 levels and was excluded. m,n, UMAP and DBSCAN clustering of MCF7 parental cells (m) and a single-cell-derived clone (n, clone 5, using only epigenetic features, coloured as in h.Results were reproduced in seven independent MCF7 CyTOF experiments and three independently derived clones (Extended Data Fig. 2). Schematic in a created in BioRender; Furth, N. https://biorender.com/twf1psb (2026).

We next examined intratumour heterogeneity, focusing on the cancer cells of each luminal breast tumour separately. UMAP clustering and density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) across all features revealed three subpopulations in each tumour, which we termed cycling, luminal and basal-like (Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). These subpopulations were also conserved in two different luminal patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. This finding validates the observed heterogeneity as an inherent feature of luminal breast tumours and excludes contamination of normal cells (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 1c). MCF7 cells showed similar luminal and basal-like heterogeneity, although most cells were cycling, as expected for a cell line (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In tumours, only a luminal subset cycled and expressed high levels of Ki-67, a result consistent with previous immunohistochemistry (IHC) and scRNA-seq studies14,32. CyTOF Ki-67 levels correlated with pathology estimates (Fig. 1k). Cycling cells also showed high levels of multiple chromatin modifications, both in raw measurements and following normalization to core histones (Fig. 1i, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Fig. 3). We validated this result by repeating CyTOF analyses of two tumours (14 and 18), adding the established cell cycle marker phospho-Rb (pRb). pRb-positive cells showed an increase in core histones, as expected from cycling cells, and a larger increase in histone PTMs (Supplementary Fig. 3). Accordingly, the epigenetically inferred cycling fraction strongly correlated with Ki-67 levels (Fig. 1l).

Most cancer cells strongly expressed GATA3 and scored highly for the luminal signature, consistent with clinical classification (Fig. 1h, Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Moreover, in each tumour, the PDX samples and the MCF7 cells, we identified a minor recurrent subpopulation that acquired basal-like identity, with high K5 expression and a reduced luminal signature (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4a). This phenotypic diversity is consistent with previous single-cell studies of human and mouse breast tumours14,21,33,34. Notably, luminal and basal-like cells also had distinct histone PTM signatures (Fig. 1h–j and Extended Data Fig. 1). Accordingly, UMAP plots based solely on histone modifications revealed separation of the subpopulations, which validated the epigenetic basis of this phenotypic diversity (Supplementary Fig. 4b). In MCF7 cells, epigenetic UMAP and clustering similarly identified several clusters, including a K5hi basal-like population (Fig. 1m). These basal-like cells with reduced luminal signalling appeared closer in UMAP space to the TN cell lines, which provided further support for their basal-like identity (Supplementary Fig. 4c). Independent CyTOF experiments, additional MCF7 parental cell culture and populations derived from independent single-cell clones revealed similar subpopulation patterns, a result that argues against a genetic basis for these effects (Fig. 1n and Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). Moreover, individual PDX tumours derived from the same donor and grown independently in different mice showed similar subpopulation proportions, which provides support for a dynamic and plastic relationship between cell states (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Overall, our data revealed inherent intratumour heterogeneity in luminal tumours, with epigenetic variability between distinct subpopulations.

We further explored the characteristics of the cycling, luminal and basal-like subpopulations. Unsupervised clustering grouped corresponding subpopulations across patients, which confirmed their robustness and similarity (Fig. 2a). Across tumours, luminal cells expressed oestrogen receptor (ER), GATA3 and cytokeratin-8 and cytokeratin-18 (K8/18; also known as KRT8 and KRT18, respectively), whereas basal-like cells downregulated these luminal markers and highly expressed K5 (Fig. 2b). As these subpopulations also exhibited distinct and conserved chromatin patterns, we applied a machine-learning algorithm to predict intratumour classification35. In each tumour, a model trained on a random subset predicted the remaining cells with 94% accuracy, which confirmed the robust differences between subpopulations (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3a). It also assigned 78% of unclustered ‘noise’ cells with >95% confidence, generating classifications that aligned with the original clustering and UMAP positions (Extended Data Fig. 3b). SHAP analysis identified the features driving each subpopulation. In detail, histone PTMs, particularly the four acetylation marks, were leading predictors of cycling cells despite overlap of individual marks with basal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Polycomb-associated H3K27me3 and H2Aub also contributed to the features, a finding consistent with previously observed Polycomb deregulation and pro-proliferative activity in breast cancer36,37,38.

a, The three subpopulations from each HR+ tumour (n = 14, including 3 anchor repeats; Supplementary Table 3) clustered by CyTOF features. The dendrogram shows recurrent patterns across patients. b, Heatmap of mean cell identity marker differences between basal-like and luminal subpopulations (n = 14, as in a). c, Confusion matrix of XGBoost predictions of subpopulations (HR+ tumours, n = 14). Rows are normalized per true class, with 94% accuracy. d, SHAP scores for feature contribution to basal-like versus luminal classification, ranked in descending order. XGBoost accuracy = 92%. e, Heatmap as in b of the top discriminating histone PTMs shown in d; rows are clustered. f, UMAP plots of tumours 4 and 5, luminal PDX models (n = 2) and MCF7 cells, coloured by the basal-like epigenetic signature (Extended Data Fig. 4a). The dashed line indicates the basal-like population. g, Percentage of basal-like cells in HR+ tumours stratified by luminal A (n = 7) or luminal B (n = 4) subtype. Boxes: median and 25–75th percentiles; whiskers indicate 1.5× interquartile range (IQR); and points are individual tumours. Two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. h, Percentage of basal-like cells versus tumour mutational burden (n = 11). Data show the linear fit (line), 95% CI (grey shading), Spearman’s ρ and two-sided P value. i, Levels of luminal identity markers in K5hi and K5low cells from tumour 19. Dots indicate protein intensity (log2) in technical repeats of 200 sorted cells (6–7 wells per population). Two-sided Welch’s t-test, with no adjustment for multiple comparisons. j, Volcano plot of protein expression differences between K5hi and K5low cells, as in i. Axes show protein intensity difference and –log10[P]. P values (two-sided Student’s t-tests) were corrected by false-discovery rate (FDR). Green and pink depict proteins significantly deregulated (fold change > 1.5, q < 0.05). Labelled proteins have fold change >2 and correspond to enriched terms in k. k,l, Functional enrichment of proteins significantly upregulated defined in j. k, MSigDB hallmark terms. l, Mammary epithelial cell (MEC) lineages50 (Supplementary Table 4a). Terms with nominal P < 0.05 are shown (one-sided hypergeometric test). Dot size indicates overlapping proteins, colour –log10[P]. m, CD74 protein expression as in i. n–o, MCF7 cells were sorted by CD74 levels and assayed for Transwell migration towards FBS and EGF (n) or wound healing (o), using n = 3 independently recovered sorted populations from the same experiment. For o, the gap area was quantified relative to day 0. Data are the mean ± s.e.m.; dots indicate replicates. Two-sided Welch’s t-test, Holm-corrected.

Luminal and basal-like separation was similarly epigenetic driven, with H4K20me3, H3K36me3 and H3K9me2 marks having the highest SHAP scores (Fig. 2d). Across tumours, basal-like cells consistently had increased H3K9me2 and H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation, whereas luminal cells had enhanced H4K20me3, H3K36me3, H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 marks (Fig. 2e). These results align with subtype-associated histone PTM signatures39 and reported roles for H3K4 demethylases, such as JARID1B, in luminal–basal transitions40. Both luminal and basal-like cells showed similar pRb distribution, which provide support for the conclusion that these results reflect distinct cell states rather than cell cycle differences (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Similar epigenetic signatures distinguished luminal and basal-like populations in PDX models (Extended Data Fig. 3f). Accordingly, epigenetic-only basal-like PermCell scores accurately captured basal-like cells in tumours, PDXs and MCF7 cells (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 4). Overall, our computational framework confirms that there is recurrent epigenetic heterogeneity in HR+ breast tumours and highlight chromatin patterns associated with basal-like K5hi cells.

Consistent with the CyTOF results, tumours with higher fractions of epigenetically defined basal-like cells had fewer ER-positive and progesterone receptor (PR)-positive cells, as measured by IHC (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b and Supplementary Table 2). Basal-like cells were also more abundant in worse-prognosis luminal B than luminal A tumours. This result is in agreement with studies showing that these tumours exhibit features shared with the basal-like subtype3,41,42,43 (Fig. 2g). Although tumour mutational burden was low across the cohort, it correlated positively with the CyTOF-defined basal-like fraction, which parallels the greater genomic instability typically associated with TNBC44,45 (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Table 2). TP53 mutant tumours likewise contained more basal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 5c), a finding reminiscent of single-cell studies of glioblastoma showing that genetic mutations may affect balance between cellular states46. Overall, these associations between pathological and molecular characteristics link the epigenetically distinct basal-like subpopulation to a more aggressive disease phenotype.

To characterize these cells functionally, we performed FACS to sort cells from tumour 19 and then low-input mass spectrometry. After excluding stroma through pan-cytokeratin staining, cells were sorted according to K5 levels to enrich for basal-like cells compared with the luminal population. K5low cells highly expressed luminal markers and proteins associated with oestrogen signalling, whereas basal-like K5hi cells expressed proteins involved in oncogenic pathways, such as MYC–mTOR signalling (Fig. 2i–k). Moreover, multiple chromatin regulators differed between these subpopulations, including the H3K4me1 methyltransferase SETD7 and histone demethylase KDM4A, consistent with the histone PTM differences observed by CyTOF47,48 (Extended Data Fig. 5d). KDM4A, enriched in K5hi cells, targets H3K9me3 and H3K36me3, which potentially accounts for their reduced levels and H3K9me2 accumulation in the basal-like population49. Comparisons with a normal mammary single-cell atlas50 revealed hormone-sensing programs in K5low cells and an alveolar progenitor signature in K5hi cells (Fig. 2l), a result consistent with their enrichment in luminal and basal TN tumours, respectively50.

To gain a mechanistic understanding of these findings, we sorted MCF7 cells using K5-specific and GATA3-specific antibodies and performed transcriptomic profiling, comparing basal-like cells (K5hiGATA3low) to bulk MCF7 or extreme luminal cells (K5lowGATA3hi; Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Notably, basal-like cells were enriched for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes (P < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 5f). We then focused on differentially expressed cell surface markers to enable live sorting, which revealed that CD74 was significantly upregulated in basal-like cells in both MCF7 and tumour 19 proteomic analyses (Fig. 2m and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Live-sorted CD74hi cells exhibited increased migratory capacity in migration and wound-healing assays, which provided further support for the more aggressive phenotypes of basal-like cells (Fig. 2n,o and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Together, these single-cell and bulk proteomics and functional assays identify epigenetically distinct K5hi basal-like cells in luminal tumours associated with aggressive traits such as reduced luminal signalling, elevated oncogenic signalling and increased migratory potential.

The distinct chromatin and phenotypic states of the basal-like subpopulation led us to explore whether intratumour epigenetic heterogeneity is also apparent in DNA methylation patterns. Thus, we conducted deep whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) on three luminal tumours from our cohort. DNA methylation patterns accurately capture breast cancer subtyping, as shown by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)51. We next jointly deconvoluted the TCGA and our WGBS data into functional archetypes (V1–V3), with each tumour positioned in the deconvolution space. Stratifying the data into three archetypes revealed the expected separation of basal (TN) tumours from luminal (HR+), with archetype V3 associated with basal tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Tumours 18, 19 and 23 from our cohort clustered with the luminal tumours, as expected from their bulk clinical subtyping. Correlation of the archetype contribution with RNA expression confirmed the association of V1 and V2 with luminal transcriptional programs, whereas V3 was associated with EMT, a result consistent with previous studies of TN tumours52,53,54 (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 5a). To improve resolution, we added a fourth archetype (V4). This analysis revealed another layer of diversity: basal TN tumours were strongly associated with V3, which corresponded with reduced oestrogen signalling and increased oncogenic signalling, whereas luminal tumours were more heterogeneous and spread across the V1 axis (Fig. 3a,b and Supplementary Fig. 5b). Notably, V1 was strongly enriched for EMT, thereby potentially capturing an intermediate-transitional state between luminal and basal-like programs. Moreover, the percentage of CyTOF-measured, vimentin-positive cells, indicative of EMT, in tumours 18 and 19 differed accordingly (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 5c). Tumour 19, with a higher V1 contribution, also comprised more vimentin-positive cells, as assessed by CyTOF. These results support the use of WGBS deconvolution to capture functionally distinct cellular states in tumours, such as luminal cells undergoing EMT.

a, TCGA BRCA DNA-methylation dataset (n = 782)51 deconvoluted into four archetypes, with UMAP of archetype composition per tumour coloured by PAM50 subtype (left) or archetype contribution (right). The three tumours (18, 19 and 23) analysed in this study are indicated and vary mainly along the V1 archetype. b, Genes ranked by correlation between DNA-methylation archetypes and matched TCGA BRCA expression data, followed by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) against the MSigDB hallmark collection. V1 differs from the luminal archetypes (V2 and V4) on the EMT axis. Representative normalized enrichment scores (NES) are shown. Black outline indicates Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05. All terms provided in Supplementary Fig. 5b. c, Top, UMAP of CyTOF measurements (tumours 18 and 19, stroma excluded), coloured by vimentin expression, with vimentin-positive cells highlighted. Bottom, the vimentin-positive fraction per tumour. d, Top, scATAC–seq of luminal tumours (n = 9)13 analysed for WIP fraction58 and gene activity. Matrix shows Pearson’s correlations between the WIP fraction and UCell scores per tumour. Bottom, UMAPs of cancer cells from patient 10-R, coloured by WIP fraction or the basal–luminal index (the difference between z-scored luminal and basal gene sets59; higher values indicate more basal-like expression). e, UMAP of H3K4me1 snCUT&Tag data (stroma removed). Cells are represented by a scTransform-normalized gene activity matrix reflecting H3K4me1-associated regulatory activity per gene, with the read count excluded. Louvain clustering and cell numbers per tumour are indicated. f, Differentially H3K4me1-marked genes per cluster in e (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, log2 fold change > 1, adjusted P < 0.01) were analysed for enrichment against MSigDB Hallmark and breast-related collections (Supplementary Table 4). Shown are terms enriched among genes with increased H3K4me1 in cluster 2 in at least two out of three tumours (one-sided hypergeometric test, FDR < 0.05). Circle sizes indicate overlapping genes; colour, –log10[FDR]. g,h, UMAPs of H3K4me1 (g) and H3K4me3 (h) snCUT&Tag data, analysed as in e and f and coloured by UCell scores for signatures comprising genes contributing to the respective enrichments (Gaussian-smoothed). For H3K4me3 enrichment, see Extended Data Fig. 8h. i, Pearson’s correlations between snCUT&Tag read number and UCell scores for the indicated gene signatures per tumour and histone mark. Gene signatures shown in d,f,i are derived from previously published studies (refs. 13,59,85,86,87,88).

To directly link the CyTOF-defined subpopulations with DNA methylation patterns, we sorted K5hi and K5low cells from tumour 5 and tumour 23, followed by enzyme-mediated methylation sequencing (EM-seq). Functional enrichment of differentially methylated promoters revealed hypermethylation of oestrogen-response programs in K5hi cells, whereas genes associated with aggressive and oncogenic features, including KRAS signalling and mesenchymal or basal-state transitions, were hypomethylated (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). We next derived a CpG island (CGI) methylation signature to distinguish the two states using CGIs that were concordantly differentially methylated across both tumours. In TCGA breast cancer data, this signature scored higher in basal-like tumours, which indicated that the K5hi methylation program resembles basal-like tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6e). K5hi samples also showed higher contribution to the basal-associated and EMT-associated archetypes than K5low samples, in both the three-archetype and four-archetype models (Extended Data Fig. 6f,g). Thus, the CyTOF-defined basal-like population exhibits basal-like and EMT-related methylation programs, which reveals another layer of intratumoural epigenetic heterogeneity.

Having identified distinct DNA methylation programs associated with tumour cell states, we next assessed cell-to-cell variability by clustering read-level methylation patterns across 100-bp genomic bins and calculating empirical entropy as an estimation of cell-type heterogeneity55. Genes near high-entropy bins were associated with functional terms related to poor differentiation, tumour aggressiveness and basal compared with luminal identity (Supplementary Fig. 6a). This result suggests that empirical entropy, by capturing diverse DNA methylation states, can be used as a proxy for cell-to-cell heterogeneity and reveal functional differences between subpopulations. We next calculated the mean entropy for each CGI (Extended Data Fig. 7a). As expected, most CGIs were unmethylated across all cells56, thus showing zero entropy. The variable CGIs (entropy > 0) were functionally enriched for EMT and the related Hedgehog signalling pathways, which indicated that these are differentially regulated in tumours57 (Extended Data Fig. 7b). This analysis suggests that intratumour variability in methylation patterns may be associated with cell identity transitions.

To further explore intratumour entropy and its relation to cell identity, we leveraged a published multiomic study of luminal breast cancer that included single-cell expression and chromatin accessibility measurements13. Focusing on cancer cells, we observed intratumour heterogeneity in luminal and basal-like expression patterns, as previously described14,54 (Supplementary Fig. 6b). Using the ATAC–seq modality, we calculated the within-peak (WIP) fraction, a metric of epigenetic noise58, whereby a low-WIP fraction may indicate a destabilized or noisier epigenome, which supports cell plasticity. For each tumour, we correlated the WIP fraction with chromatin accessibility of basal-like and luminal gene signatures. Cells that scored high for EMT and basal-like identity showed lower WIP fraction, a finding reminiscent of the higher DNA methylation entropy associated with these signatures (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 6c). Single-cell multiome analysis of a freshly resected independent luminal tumour reproduced the basal–luminal continuum and association between basal identity and reduced WIP fraction (Supplementary Fig. 6d,e). To explore whether the increased epigenetic noise is associated with higher transcriptional heterogeneity, we divided cells into quartiles according to a published basal–luminal index59 and basal-like and luminal gene sets (Methods). Indeed, across all tumours, cells with a high basal identity showed higher transcriptional heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 7c). In line with these observations, the CyTOF-defined basal-like subpopulation also showed higher epigenetic heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Moreover, read-level methylation entropy was higher in K5hi-sorted compared with K5low-sorted populations in both tumours analysed by EM-seq, with higher variability among the K5hi 200-cell replicates (Supplementary Fig. 6f,g). Together, our analyses across DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility and histone PTMs indicate that the basal-like subpopulation exhibts a noisy epigenetic landscape and increased transcriptional heterogeneity.

Our CyTOF analysis highlighted a global increase in several histone PTMs in the basal-like subpopulation, including H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation (Fig. 2e). To explore the genomic distribution of these marks, we conducted single-nucleus CUT&Tag (snCUT&Tag) on three luminal tumours from our cohort60. Similar to the CyTOF data (Fig. 1b), stroma cells clustered together across patients, showing H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 deposition on fibroblast and endothelial markers. By contrast, tumours clustered separately, which indicated inter-patient variability (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d).

In each tumour, malignant cells clustered into distinct H3K4me1-defined or H3K4me3-defined states (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). Differential analysis of H3K4me1 distribution between clusters highlighted a recurrent group of cells across tumours, annotated as ‘cluster 2’, with significant H3K4me1 enrichment at genes associated with basal-like identity and EMT (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 8g,i). In tumour 15, cluster 1 was also enriched for basal-like genes (adjusted P < 0.05), but not EMT. H3K4me3 similarly identified basal-like subpopulations in all tumours (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Accordingly, peaks associated with these clusters showed enrichment for transcription factor motifs linked to EMT and basal-like identity (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Next, we trained a classifier to identify H3K4me1-marked and H3K4me3-marked genes that contribute to variation between the clusters. For both histone methylations, these genes were enriched in terms related to breast cancer cellular identity, including oestrogen signalling, basal-like and mesenchymal identity (Supplementary Fig. 7b–e). Overall, our analysis provides support for chromatin-defined cell states in luminal tumour cells, including a basal-like state distinguished by H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 distributions.

The above snCUT&Tag results aligned with the heterogeneity observed by CyTOF, which led us to compare the single-cell datasets and integrating both genomic and protein information. CyTOF-defined basal-like cells showed global increases in both H3K4 methylation marks. We reasoned that sequencing reads per nucleus may reflect global levels of the target modification. Single-cell epigenomic analyses generally assume similar global modification levels, discarding read-count information, as in our analysis above61 (Fig. 3e–h). Departing from this convention, we examined whether read counts capture additional aspects of epigenetic heterogeneity. Across all three tumours and both modifications, read counts negatively correlated with luminal identity signatures and positively with basal-like and mesenchymal signatures (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Consistently, cells with high read counts, potentially indicative of elevated global levels of H3K4me1 or H3K4me3, showed less enrichment of these active marks at luminal identity genes. Although requiring further validation, this direct comparison suggests that read counts may serve as proxy for global levels of histone modifications to capture additional aspects of epigenetic variation.

To further integrate these datasets, we label-transferred the CyTOF classification (Figs. 1 and 2) onto the H3K4me1 snCUT&Tag dataset. CyTOF-predicted basal-like populations were enriched in the basal-like clusters identified by H3K4me1 genomic profiling (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 9b). For tumour 15, cluster 1 was also predicted to comprise basal-like cells, consistent with its higher H3K4me1 deposition on basal-like-associated genes (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 9c). CyTOF-predicted basal-like cells also showed higher H3K4me1 deposition at EMT and basal-like gene signatures, which further confirmed their distinct epigenetic and functional features (Extended Data Fig. 9d). To validate these results, we sorted luminal PDX models and MCF7 cells by K5 expression, followed by H3K4me1 CUT&Tag. K5low-specific peaks were enriched near oestrogen signalling genes, whereas K5hi-specific peaks were associated with basal-like and mesenchymal programs, which confirmed the distinct H3K4me1 landscapes between subpopulations (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Together, the protein abundance and genomic distribution data implicate H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 as epigenetic determinants of the basal-like subpopulation in luminal tumours.

The repressive mark H3K9me2 was also identified as a strong contributor to the epigenetic basal-like signature (Fig. 2d,e). Thus, we conducted H3K9me2 snCUT&Tag on tumour 8, which was also profiled for H3K4me1. Given that H3K9me2 occupies large genomic regions, its distribution is not readily interpretable in relation to gene activity, especially in low-coverage single-cell datasets. We therefore leveraged the H3K4me1 data and trained a classifier, assuming opposing genomic distributions of enhancer-associated H3K4me1 and repressive H3K9me2 chromatin62,63, to identify malignant versus stromal cells (Extended Data Fig. 9f). We next clustered tumour cells by H3K9me2 genomic distribution and applied the same H3K4me1-based inference framework. This approach predicted strong enrichment of basal-like cells in cluster 4, consistent with elevated H3K9me2 deposition on oestrogen-related genes (Extended Data Fig. 9g–i). This cluster also showed the highest H3K9me2 read counts per nucleus, which provided support for its correspondence to the H3K9me2hi basal-like cells identified by CyTOF (Extended Data Fig. 9j). Overall, these analyses highlight an epigenetically distinct basal-like population with globally increased and redistributed active and repressive histone modifications over genes associated with luminal-basal identity and EMT.

Our multimodal analysis linked the chromatin landscape to intratumoural cell-state diversity. We next aimed to translate our tissue-level findings to a liquid biopsy test based on our single-molecule EPINUC technology, which profiles the epigenetics of plasma-isolated nucleosomes28,29. We tailored EPINUC for breast cancer by developing single-molecule systems to quantify the breast-tissue-related proteins K5, L1CAM and MUC1, and added the histone PTMs H4K16ac and H4K20me3 (refs. 64,65,66,67) (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Table 5 and Supplementary Fig. 8a–c). Nucleosomes from plasma were captured and their combinatorial modifications imaged by TIRF microscopy, whereas protein biomarkers were quantified in parallel single-molecule antibody-capture assays (Fig. 4a). The expanded 29-parameter panel was applied to a cohort of plasma from 77 women with luminal breast cancer and 30 healthy women, and the results revealed significant differences (Supplementary Table 6). For example, cancer samples contained more H3K9ac and H4K16ac nucleosomes (Fig. 4b). As PTMs were normalized to nucleosome abundance, these differences reflect the epigenetic state rather than tumour burden. We also used EPINUC to measure PTM ratios and co-occurrence, which revealed increased bivalent (H3K4me3 and H3K27me3) nucleosomes, as previously observed in colorectal cancer and pancreatic cancer28. Indeed, bivalency is altered across cancers68, and can prime drug-tolerant persister programs in breast cancer19.

L1CAM and MST1 were also elevated in plasma from patients with breast cancer, a result in agreement with the association of high MST1 with poor prognosis in ER+ tumours69 (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 8d). Multiple parameters differed between healthy individuals and patients diagnosed with early-stage (T1) low-burden tumours, which demonstrated the early detection sensitivity of this method (Fig. 4b). Predictive power scores (PPS) revealed the contribution of the newly measured H4 PTMs, selected on the basis of the CyTOF analysis, which illustrates the value of matched tissue–plasma profiling (Fig. 4c). Principal component analysis (PCA) of predictive features separated healthy individuals from patients with breast cancer, which highlights the ability of EPINUC to capture differences between these groups (Fig. 4d).

We next applied machine-learning-based classifiers to diagnose luminal breast cancer from EPINUC data. SHAP analysis of XGBoost models trained on all patients, or only stage T1 cases, identified multiple histone PTMs and protein biomarkers as informative (Fig. 4e). Notably, both models emphasized combinatorial features, particularly H4K16ac and H4K20me3 co-occurrence, thereby highlighting the ability of EPINUC to quantify such combinations. In particular, H4K16ac activates transcription of transposable elements70, which reside in H4K20me3 heterochromatin71, and because transposable elements are often upregulated in cancer, elevated H4K16ac and H4K20me3 might be a cancer-associated phenomenon. Finally, we applied several classifiers to assess the diagnostic contribution of the expanded EPINUC panel in discriminating healthy individuals from patients with cancer. Use the original 20 EPINUC parameters28 produced an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.85 (Supplementary Fig. 9a), whereas the expanded 29-parameter panel achieved 0.95, including among patients with early-stage T1 cancer (Fig. 4f,g). Unlike mammography, the sensitivity of which declines with dense breast tissue72,73, the features and performance of EPINUC were unaffected by different BI-RADS breast density scores, including patients with heterogeneous and extremely dense breast scores (Supplementary Fig. 9b,c). To assess the robustness of the EPINUC-based classifier, we applied the model trained on the original cohort (MAYO-1; Fig. 4f) to an independent, separately processed set of plasma samples collected 6–12 months later (MAYO-2). Following batch correction (Methods), the pre-trained model accurately distinguished healthy from luminal breast cancer, achieving an AUC of 0.98 and high classification accuracy (Extended Data Fig. 10a,b).

To generalize our findings, we analysed pretreatment plasma from patients with luminal breast cancer at two independent medical centres (Supplementary Table 6). EPINUC distinguished patients from healthy controls with high accuracy in both cohorts and showed comparable sensitivity and specificity in TNBC (Extended Data Fig. 10c–e). Pooling all luminal samples across centres (n = 188), a model trained on 75% of the data achieved an AUC of 0.96 and robustly classified the remaining 25% despite mixed sources and batches, a scenario that reflects real-world clinical settings (Fig. 4h, Extended Data Fig. 10f and Supplementary Fig. 10). Performance was similar for luminal A and luminal B tumours (Extended Data Fig. 10g). Although retrospective, these results support the use of high-resolution, multiparametric plasma epigenetic analyses for cancer diagnosis.

MAYO-1 comprised preoperative samples with at least 5 years of clinical follow-up, which enabled stratification by 5-year recurrence (Fig. 5a). Already at diagnosis, several EPINUC features differed between patients who were disease-free and patients who had relapsed disease. H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation, associated with the aggressive basal-like subpopulation, were elevated in plasma of patients developing recurrent disease (Fig. 5b). H3K27me3 and H3K9ac were also elevated, perhaps reflecting other aggressive tumour or microenvironmental states, such as cycling cells that were particularly high for histone acetylations (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Nucleosomes modified with both H3K9ac and H3K4me1 were higher in the recurrence group, a result that further demonstrates the power of EPINUC in capturing these combinations (Fig. 5b). ER or PR status did not associate with relapse (Fisher’s exact test, P > 0.05), and the epigenetic signature persisted in tumours with the following characteristics: comparable ER and PR levels; only luminal A tumours; low-burden T1–T2 or grade 1–2 disease; and tumours without lymphovascular invasion (LVI). No EPINUC feature was significantly associated with histological grade, which indicates that there is prognostic information beyond known clinical parameters (Extended Data Fig. 11a–f).
