#1353. Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 372–377 (2026) Cite this article

Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

The increasing integration of renewable energy calls for sustainable electrochemical energy storage systems beyond lithium-ion batteries1. Aqueous metal–iodine batteries offer a promising platform for large-scale energy storage by combining earth-abundant electrode materials, aqueous electrolytes and conversion-type iodine chemistry2,3. Unlike intercalation-type positive electrodes, iodine positive electrodes store charge by reversible valence-state changes, offering access to multi-electron redox chemistry with increased capacity and redox potential4. Most studies have focused on the two-electron I−/I0 redox couple, with a theoretical capacity of 211 mAh g−1 at a redox potential of 0.54 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode10. Extending iodine conversion to the successive I−/I0/I+ redox couples doubles the theoretical capacity to 422 mAh g−1 while introducing the I0/I+ redox process at a higher redox potential of 1.07 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode11. However, despite this potential, achieving reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous environments remains a fundamental challenge3,7.

The crux of iodine conversion chemistry lies in interfacial reactions, where electrolyte composition and interfacial microenvironment govern reaction pathways. Electron-deficient I+ is strongly electrophilic and susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water, resulting in hydrolysis and poor reversibility in aqueous environments9,12. Previous studies have achieved four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries by stabilizing reactive I+ through interhalogen complexes (for example, ICl2 or IBr2) in highly concentrated chloride- or bromide-containing electrolytes5,6,13. In these systems, electrophilic I+ coordinates with two nucleophilic halide ions (Cl− or Br−) through non-covalent interactions8,14. However, at water-enriched interfaces, hydration of nucleophilic species (Nuc) competes with these interactions and destabilizes I+ complexes (Fig. 1a). Highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes mitigate this competition by reducing water activity and increasing halide availability, but their high salt contents and corrosivity constrain broader implementation (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1), necessitating new electrolyte chemistry and a mechanistic framework that move beyond reliance on halogen-containing electrolytes and conventional interhalogen stabilization5,8.

a, The mechanism of the competition between halogen bond and hydrogen bond. b, The conventional interhalogen stabilization mechanism in highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes. c, The KA–PA–Nuc framework levering anionic chemistry and halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free electrolytes. IHP, inner Helmholtz plane; OHP, outer Helmholtz plane.

Given the competition between I+ stabilization and hydration at water-enriched interfaces, overcoming this challenge requires simultaneous regulation of the interfacial environment and water–Nuc interactions. Anionic chemistry offers a powerful lever to coordinate these interfacial and molecular interactions15,16,17,18. Herein we establish a kosmotropic anion (KA)–polar anion (PA)–Nuc electrolyte framework for reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes (Fig. 1c). Systematic experiments and theoretical calculations reveal how the synergistic effects of PAs and KAs coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, thereby stabilizing interfacial electrochemical behaviour and promoting reversible four-electron iodine conversion. The applicability of this electrolyte framework is demonstrated across four halogen-free Nuc (urea, acetamide, pyridine and nicotinamide) and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Beyond establishing a halogen-free electrolyte chemistry, this work reveals how electrolyte chemistry governs iodine conversion across interfacial, molecular and electrochemical scales, providing a mechanistic basis for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

Stabilizing I+ against hydrolysis is essential for reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous electrolytes. Previous studies have relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes for interhalogen stabilization19,20, whereas more recent studies have explored specific additive-halogen nucleophilic substitution reactions21,22. These approaches primarily address I+ stabilization through specific molecular interactions, whereas how electrolyte chemistry collectively regulates the interfacial microenvironment, molecular stabilization and the resulting iodine conversion pathways remains less understood. This work establishes a mechanistic framework that integrates anionic chemistry with halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, strong PAs establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interface, whereas KAs weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding to facilitate halogen-bond stabilization of I+. These complementary effects underpin the halogen-free KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, whose composition was subsequently optimized (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4) and exhibits sufficient electrochemical stability (Supplementary Fig. 5) for four-electron iodine conversion.

a, Molecular interplay governed by anionic chemistry and halogen bonding. b, Cyclic voltammetry profiles of iodine conversion reaction using urea as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. c, Cyclic voltammetry profiles using acetamide as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. d, Cyclic voltammetry profiles using nicotinamide as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. e–g, Corresponding GCD profiles for b–d at 1 A g−1, respectively. All electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework was validated in aqueous Zn–I2 batteries across four different Nuc (Supplementary Fig. 6). Electron-deficient I+ can interact with two electron-rich Nuc molecules to form linear Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. These halogen bonds provide the molecular basis for I+ stabilization, as supported by Nuc-free controls, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and theoretical calculations23 (Supplementary Figs. 7–11). Using urea (U) as a representative Nuc, KA–U exhibits only the I−/I0 redox process, whereas PA–U enables further I0/I+ oxidation but with poor reversibility (Fig. 2b,e). The excessive capacity at the second charge plateau is attributed to irreversible iodine oxidation coupled with parasitic water oxidation (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). Combining KA and PA in KA–PA–U produces two reversible redox peaks and corresponding charge–discharge plateaus, demonstrating their synergistic role in enabling reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion (Supplementary Fig. 14). Replacing U with acetamide (AE), nicotinamide (NA) or pyridine (PD) shows the same phenomenon, with reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion achieved only in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes, including under identical ionic strength conditions, indicating the broad applicability of this electrolyte framework (Fig. 2c,d,f,g and Supplementary Figs. 15–18).

To isolate the role of PAs in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, SO42− was maintained as the KA, whereas structurally related CF3SO3−, CF3COO− or CH3COO− was introduced as the second anion. Density-functional-theory calculations reveal a polarity sequence of CH3COO− > CF3COO− > CF3SO3− (Supplementary Fig. 19), providing a basis for examining how anion polarity influences interfacial behaviours24,25. Molecular-dynamics simulations show similar water-enriched bulk environments across the three electrolytes (Supplementary Figs. 20–22), but distinct interfacial structures (Fig. 3d). CH3COO− reduces the interfacial water density while increasing anion enrichment, whereas CF3COO− and CF3SO3− retain high interfacial water intensity (Fig. 3e,f). In situ attenuated total reflection infrared (ATR-IR) spectroscopy further supports this interfacial redistribution. The δ-HOH vibration at 1,640 cm−1 remains pronounced with CF3SO3− or CF3COO− (Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Fig. 23), but is suppressed with CH3COO− alongside pronounced anion-associated signals26,27,28,29 (Fig. 3i). Notably, highly concentrated ZnCl2 retains a water-enriched interface despite its water-deficient bulk environment (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25). Differential capacitance measurements indicate stronger interfacial adsorption of CH3COO− than of CF3COO− and CF3SO3− (Supplementary Figs. 26 and 27), linking preferential adsorption of strongly PAs to the formation of a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment30.

a, Cyclic voltammetry profiles in electrolytes with different anions. b, GCD profiles in electrolytes with different anions. The rising and falling voltage curves correspond to charging and discharging processes, respectively. c, Cycling stability in electrolytes with different anions, with upper and lower curves representing Coulombic efficiency and specific capacity, respectively. Electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2. d, Schematic snapshot of the interfacial structure in the electrolyte with CH3COO−. e, Corresponding interfacial cumulated density profiles of H2O in electrolytes with different anions, with the grey shaded region highlighting interfacial variations. f, Corresponding interfacial cumulated density profiles of anions in electrolytes with different anions, with the pink shaded region highlighting interfacial variations. g–i, In situ ATR-IR spectra in the electrolytes with CF3SO3− (g), CF3COO− (h) and CH3COO− (i).

These polarity-dependent interfacial structures lead to distinct iodine conversion behaviour. CF3SO3− shows a negligible I0/I+ process, whereas CF3COO− enables I0/I+ oxidation but with limited reversibility. By contrast, CH3COO− supports reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion with improved stability and capacity (Fig. 3a–c and Supplementary Fig. 28). In situ ultraviolet–visible spectra and micro-computed-tomography analyses further link these differences to iodine species distribution, showing that CH3COO− confines iodine species within the electrode and suppresses their migration into the bulk electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 29 and 30). Together, these results establish a mechanistic relationship between anion polarity and the resulting water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment that governs the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Building on the understanding of PAs, the critical role of KAs in the KA–PA–Nuc framework was further explored. Nuc stabilize I+ through electron-rich nitrogen or oxygen centres, which also interact with water through hydrogen bonding and therefore compete with halogen-bond formation (Supplementary Fig. 31). Inspired by anion-specific effects on water–solute interactions, SO42−, CH3COO−, NO3−, CF3SO3− and ClO4− were compared in the same PA–Nuc baseline31,32,33,34 (Supplementary Fig. 32). Although these anions have little effect on the initial capacity, they produce different cycling stability (Supplementary Fig. 33). SO42− maintains nearly overlapping galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) profiles, whereas CH3COO− and CF3SO3− show intermediate cycling stability and ClO4− undergoes rapid deterioration (Fig. 4a–c and Supplementary Fig. 34), giving a stability sequence of SO42− > CH3COO− > CF3SO3− > ClO4−. NO3− deviates from this sequence owing to its limited electrochemical stability within the applied voltage range35 (Supplementary Fig. 35a,b).

a, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing SO42− at different cycles. b, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing CF3SO3− at different cycles. c, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing ClO4− at different cycles. Electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2. d, 2H NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. e, 1H NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. f, 13C NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. g, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing SO42−. h, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing CF3SO3−. i, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing ClO4−.

NMR spectroscopy and molecular-dynamics simulations reveal the molecular origin of these electrochemical differences. The 2H chemical shift follows SO42− > CH3COO− > NO3− > CF3SO3− > ClO4− (Fig. 4d), indicating progressively stronger anion-induced water polarization and restructuring of the aqueous hydrogen-bond network36,37. These differences in water–anion coordination translate into distinct water–Nuc interactions. The corresponding 15N chemical shifts, together with the inverse trends observed in 1H and 13C chemical shifts, indicate that KAs such as SO42− polarize hydration water and thereby weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding, whereas chaotropic anions such as ClO4− interact directly with the Nuc backbone and facilitate Nuc hydration32 (Fig. 4e,f, and Supplementary Figs. 32 and 36–38). Nuc solubility measurements, two-dimensional 1H–15N heteronuclear multiple bond correlation (HMBC) NMR spectra, and calculated Nuc–water distances and hydrogen-bond populations further support this interpretation (Fig. 4g–i, and Supplementary Figs. 35c, 39 and 40). By weakening Nuc–water interactions, SO42− increases the availability of Nuc for halogen-bond stabilization of I+, thereby promoting reversible iodine conversion. These results reveal how anionic chemistry regulates molecular water–Nuc interactions to govern the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Having established the complementary roles of PA and KA in interfacial and molecular regulation, we next examined how these effects manifest in the electrochemical processes governing iodine conversion. In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) combined with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis was used to decouple the complex impedance response and identify individual electrochemical processes38,39,40 (Supplementary Figs. 41–43). In the absence of either KA or PA, the DRT responses evolve distinctly with additional competing interfacial processes, whereas their combined presence maintains stable interfacial electrochemical behaviour throughout iodine conversion41,42 (Extended Data Fig. 1). Rate-dependent analysis identifies charge transfer, rather than ion transport, as the dominant kinetic contribution to iodine conversion in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 44–50). In situ Raman spectroscopy further links these electrochemical processes to iodine chemistry, revealing the reversible evolution of the Nuc–I+–Nuc species during cycling (Supplementary Figs. 51 and 52).

The KA–PA–Nuc framework supports four-electron iodine conversion across different operating conditions and cell configurations. Zn–I2 cells retain 96% of their capacity after 1,000 cycles at 1 A g−1 and 94% after 2,000 cycles at 2 A g−1, while sustaining four-electron conversion at iodine loadings up to 12.2 mg cm−2 (Supplementary Figs. 53–55, 58a and 59). This electrolyte framework is also compatible with different current collectors and pouch-cell configurations and extends to aqueous Al–I2 cells using Al–Zn alloy negative electrodes (Supplementary Figs. 56–58b,c, 60 and 61). A techno-economic analysis under standardized modelling assumptions further illustrates its theoretical cost-reduction potential by avoiding highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes and costly current collectors (Supplementary Fig. 58d–f and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Mechanistic and post-mortem analyses further reveal that the apparent low Coulombic efficiency and capacity fading involve coupled reversible and irreversible iodine inventory loss, with the latter becoming more pronounced at increased iodine loading (Supplementary Figs. 62–67 and Extended Data Figs. 2–4). Together, these results clarify the iodine conversion pathways while defining the applicability and remaining limitations of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, showing that sustained reversible four-electron iodine conversion requires not only stabilization of hypervalent iodine species but also broader management of the entire iodine inventory.

All chemicals were used as received without further purification unless otherwise stated. The manufacturer and purity of each material are specified at its first occurrence in Methods and are not repeated thereafter unless a different source or purity was used.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes were prepared by dissolving KA, PA and Nuc into deionized water at room temperature. For aqueous Zn–I2 batteries, KA and PA were 1.5 M ZnSO4 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M Zn (CH3COO)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich), respectively. To demonstrate the broad applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, various Nuc were used, including 2 M urea (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich), 2 M acetamide (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.2 M pyridine (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) or 0.4 M nicotinamide (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich). To explore the role of PAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 1.5 M ZnSO4 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. Zn(CH3COO)2, Zn(CF3COO)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) or Zn(CF3SO3)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 0.5 M to obtain electrolytes containing different PAs. To evaluate the role of KAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. ZnSO4, Zn(NO3)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), Zn(CF3SO3)2 or Zn(ClO4)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 1.5 M for comparative analysis. To compare electrolytes performance under a standardized ionic strength condition, the ionic strength of each electrolyte was calculated according to the equation:

where Ci and Zi represent the molar concentration and charge number of ion i, respectively. For aqueous Al–I2 batteries, the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte was prepared by dissolving 1.5 M Al2(SO4)3 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.5 Mg (CH3COO)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M nicotinamide into deionized water.

Iodine-activated carbon (I2–AC) composites were prepared using an evaporation–adsorption method. In brief, 0.5 g iodine (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) and 0.5 g activated carbon (AC; YP-80F, purity not specified, Kuraray) were manually ground in an agate mortar with a pestle for 10 min under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was sealed in a Teflon reactor and heated at 120 °C for 6 h. For the preparation of iodine positive electrodes using titanium (80 mesh, >99.5%, Hebei Conway Metal Products) or stainless steel mesh (80 mesh, 316L, Hebei Conway Metal Products) as the current collector, I2–AC, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, 60 wt% dispersion H2O, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P (purity not specified, Canrd) were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 40 mg I2–AC, 5 mg Super P and 5 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using a roller press (Etelux) and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The areal iodine loading was controlled by adjusting the thickness of the composite film. The dried film was then pressed onto the titanium or stainless steel mesh using the roller press. The resulting electrodes were punched into 12 mm disks using a manual disk punch (T07, ‌Hefei Kejing Material Technology).

For iodine positive electrodes using carbon paper (TGP-H-060, Toray) as the current collector, I2–AC, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, weight-average molecular weight, Mw ≈ 534,000 g mol−1 by gel permeation chromatography, powder, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg I2–AC, 20 mg PVDF and 20 mg Super P were manually mixed with N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) using an agate mortar and pestle in ambient conditions. The resulting slurry was manually and uniformly spread onto the carbon paper using a laboratory spatula. The coated electrodes were dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 8 h and subsequently cut into 12-mm disks using the manual disk punch. Commercial Zn foils (70 µm, >99.99%, ‌Qinghe Haoxuan Metal Materials) were used as negative electrodes as received.

To assess the potential of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, a Ag/AgCl electrode in saturated KCl (Beijing Jingke Instrument Science Instrument) was used as the reference, and AC electrodes were prepared as the counter electrode. The measured potentials are reported directly versus the Ag/AgCl reference electrode. For the preparation of AC electrodes, AC, PTFE and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg AC, 20 mg Super P and 20 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle at ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using the roller press and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The dried film was then pressed onto titanium mesh using the roller press. By adjusting the electrode thickness, the capacity of the AC electrode was controlled to be much higher than that of the iodine working electrode, ensuring its capability as the counter electrode for evaluating the electrochemical performance of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte. To further validate the applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, Al–Zn alloys were fabricated as negative electrodes following a previous study43. In brief, symmetric cells were assembled using Zn foils (70 µm, 16 mm in diameter) as electrodes and 2 M Al (CF3SO3)3 (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) as the electrolyte. During charging, Al3+ in the electrolyte deposited on and reacted with the metal Zn substrate, forming the Zn-supported Al–Zn alloys.

Halogen-bond complexes were synthesized via a cation-exchange reaction using corresponding silver analogues, following a previously reported procedure with some modifications44. All operations were carried out under a standard Schlenk line. In a typical synthesis, 0.94 mmol of the corresponding silver salt (Ag2SO4, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCH3COO, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3COO, >98%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3SO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgNO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; or AgClO4, >97%, Sigma-Aldrich) was added to a 20-ml vial equipped with a stir bar. The vial was sealed with a rubber septum and evacuated. Subsequently, 6.0 ml dry CH2Cl2 (purity not specified, VWR Chemicals) and 1.90 mmol pyridine (3.80 mmol for Ag2SO4) were added at room temperature under a nitrogen atmosphere. The mixture was stirred for 10 min to form the Ag(I)–pyridine bis-coordination complex. Next, 2.00 mmol of iodine (4.00 mmol for Ag2SO4) was added, and the reaction was allowed to proceed for an additional 20 min under continuous stirring. The supernatant was then carefully transferred to another vial via cannula filtration, followed by the addition of 15 ml dry n-hexane (>99%, Macron Fine Chemicals) to induce precipitation of the halogen-bond complex. The mixture was stored at −20 °C overnight to complete precipitation. Afterwards, the supernatant was removed using a syringe, and the resulting solid was washed with 20 ml dry n-hexane to remove any residual I2. Finally, the product was dried under vacuum on the Schlenk line.

In situ ATR-IR spectra were recorded by a Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS50 spectrometer equipped with a liquid nitrogen-cooled MCT-A detector. Gold-coated silicon plates were used as working electrodes, with Zn foils (70 µm, 10 mm in diameter) and glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter, Whatman) used as reference electrodes and separators, respectively. To assess the critical role of the PA in the interfacial environment, 1.5 M KA electrolyte was maintained as the baseline, and 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2, 0.5 M Zn(CF3COO)2 or 0.5 M Zn(CF3SO3)2 was separately added. An electrolyte volume of 500 μl was used for each measurement. During tests, the assembled batteries were connected to a Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat to run a cyclic voltammetry programme at a scan rate of 0.2 mV s−1 for a full charge and discharge cycle. All spectra were collected at a resolution of 4 cm−1, with 50 scans per measurement. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

Raman spectra were recorded using a Bruker Senterra II Raman spectrometer with a 532-nm excitation wavelength. The in situ Zn–I2 cell comprised an iodine positive electrode (12 mm in diameter, iodine mass loading 2.2 mg cm−2), a Zn negative electrode (70 µm, 12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter). An electrolyte volume of 200 μl was used. Raman spectra were collected during GCD cycling using an external Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

FTIR spectra of various electrolytes were obtained using an ATR-FTIR spectrometer (BRUKER, Platinum-ATR). Scanning electron microscopy characterization of electrodes was performed using a JEOL 7600 microscope. Ultraviolet–visible measurements were conducted on a Shimadzu UV-3600i Plus spectrophotometer. For in situ ultraviolet–visible measurements, a two-electrode Zn–I2 cuvette cell was connected to a Neware battery test system for GCD cycling. NMR analyses, including 1H, 13C and 1H–15N HMBC spectra, were carried out on a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 500). 15N spectra were collected using a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 700). Deuterium oxide (>99.9%, Fluorochem) was used as the solvent for electrolyte characterization, and dideuteromethylenechloride (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as the solvent for characterizing halogen-bond complexes. Micro-computed-tomography imaging was conducted using a Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa system with a ×4 objective, operating at a tube voltage of 80 kV and an exposure time of 8 s, achieving a voxel resolution of 0.8 μm. For each sample, a disk with a diameter of 2 mm was prepared to balance X-ray attenuation and representative sampling volume. The acquired computed-tomography datasets were subsequently processed and analysed using Avizo software.

Electrochemical studies of halogen-free electrolytes were performed using CR2025 coin cells, whereas those of halogen-containing electrolytes were performed using Swagelok cells. For CR2025 Zn–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode, Zn negative electrode (70 µm) and separator (GF/D) had diameters of 12 mm, 16 mm and 19 mm, respectively. For Swagelok Zn–I2 cells, corresponding electrodes and separators had the same diameter of 12 mm. For CR2025 Al–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode had a diameter of 12 mm, the Al–Zn alloy negative electrode had a diameter of 16 mm, and a GF/D separator with a diameter of 19 mm was used. An electrolyte volume of 100 μl was used for each cell. Coin cells were mechanically crimped at 50 kg cm−2 using a hydraulic crimping machine (MSK-110, Hefei Kejing Material Technology) during assembly. Swagelok cells were manually tightened during assembly.

For the 1.1-Ah pouch cell, 2 double-side coated iodine positive electrodes (10 × 15 cm), and 3 Zn negative electrodes (70 µm, 10 × 15 cm) were stacked alternately. The areal iodine loading of positive electrodes is controlled at 10 mg cm−2. Four glass fibre separators (GF/D, 10.1 × 15.1 cm) were utilized, and 1.5 ml electrolyte was added to each separator. The electrolyte consisted of 1.5 M ZnSO4, 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide. Titanium foils were connected to electrodes as tabs. After lamination, the assembled battery was encapsulated in an aluminium–plastic film and mechanically constrained using a customized model during electrochemical measurements. The applied pressure was not specifically quantified.

GCD tests were conducted using a Neware battery test system in a room maintained at an ambient temperature of approximately 25–28 °C. All other electrochemical measurements described below were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C. Cyclic voltammetry, linear sweep voltammetry and EIS measurements were performed using a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat. For the electrochemical stability window analysis, linear sweep voltammetry measurements were performed using a three-electrode configuration consisting of a titanium mesh working electrode (1 × 2 cm), an AC counter electrode (1 × 2 cm) and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode at a scan rate of 2 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to an exposed geometric area of 1 cm², and the potentials are reported directly versus Ag/AgCl. The polarization measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti CR2025 coin cells using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter), titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter) at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to the geometric area of the titanium electrode. For in situ EIS tests, a thin Zn wire was inserted into the coin cell as an additional reference electrode to establish a three-electrode configuration. This reference electrode was placed between the positive electrode and negative electrode, separated by two layers of separators (GF/A, Whatman). For measurements of the individual iodine positive electrode, the potential is reported versus the Zn reference electrode as potential (V versus Zn/Zn²+), whereas the full-cell and Zn negative electrode responses are reported as voltage (V) owing to the voltage was applied on full cell. For peak assignment, the assembled cells were connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat to perform staircase potentio EIS with a potential range of approximately 0.6–1.8 V. For rate-step identification, the assembled cells simultaneously connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat and a Neware battery test system to conduct potentio EIS and GCD cycling, respectively. All Nyquist plots were fitted using EC-Lab software based on the equivalent circuit (R1 + Q2/R2 + Q3/R3 + W4). DRT data were calculated from EIS data using MatlabR2019 with the DRT tool developed by Francesco Ciucci’s research group. The differential capacitance was calculated using the following equation:

where C is the differential capacitance, ω is the angular frequency and Zim is the imaginary component of the impedance. In this work, a specific frequency of 1,000 Hz was used. Measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti cells assembled in CR2025 coin-cell configuration, using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter) and titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) as the two electrodes and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter). The potential was varied from 1.0 V to 1.7 V versus Zn/Zn2+. No ohmic-drop (iR) correction was applied to the potentials or voltages reported in this work.

All molecular-dynamics simulations were performed using the LAMMPS package45 to investigate the bulk solvation structure of various aqueous electrolytes. The initial configurations were constructed using Packmol46, which randomly packed electrolyte components into a periodic cubic box according to the target molar ratios, ensuring no initial atomic overlaps. The simulation cell was then relaxed by energy minimization before subsequent equilibration. Force-field parameters for organic molecules were taken from the OPLS-AA family47,48, whereas others were adopted from validated aqueous zinc salt parameter sets in the literature. To partially account for polarization effects in concentrated electrolytes, the atomic charges were uniformly scaled (scaling factor 0.8)49. Interaction of water was represented by TIP3P50, and all X–H bonds were constrained using the SHAKE algorithm51. Each system was first energy-minimized and equilibrated in the isothermal–isobaric ensemble (300 K, 1 atm) using a Nosé–Hoover thermostat until both the density and potential energy were stable. Subsequently, production runs were performed in the canonical ensemble for 5 ns (5,000 ps) with a 1-fs integration step to ensure complete equilibration while avoiding structural drift.

Radial distribution functions gij(r) were computed to analyse ion pairing and solvation structure. Coordination numbers were obtained by integrating gij(r) up to their first minimum. Both radial distribution functions and hydrogen bonds were identified using the hydrogen-bond analysis tools implemented in VMD52. Average hydrogen-bond numbers and distributions were determined over the equilibrated trajectories to characterize the reorganization of the hydrogen-bond network by different anions.

To probe field-induced ion and molecular redistribution, an additional set of simulations was conducted in the canonical ensemble with a uniform static electric field applied along the z axis. The field strength corresponded to the experimentally estimated potential gradient.

Density-functional-theory calculations were performed using the Gaussian16 program package, using the M06-2X exchange-correlation functional53. Geometry optimizations were conducted using a mixed basis-set approach: the 6-311+G(d,p) basis set was applied to all elements excluding iodine54. Iodine was described using an effective core potential from the Stuttgart/Dresden group55. Solvent effects were accounted for using the polarizable continuum model, with water selected as the solvent56.

#1352. Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola said. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

The pace of the game was slow and Villarreal were in control until the later stages of the half. Koumas and Cody Gakpo created a chance and from the corner that resulted Mac Allister headed in Tsimikas’s cross. Liverpool were up and running. Ngumoha’s cross from the left was unwisely left by Cardona for Araújo to score and the game was level.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

Then came Ngumoha’s big second half, creating the third for Mac Allister. The teenager went past Cardona and the substitute Juan Foyth in a couple of strides. Wirtz dispatched the fourth from Gakpo’s ball.

Even so there was still time for Liverpool to show that they had sacrificed some defensive stability. The absence of a right-back cost them when substitute Tani Oluwaseyi ran into that area of the pitch to score Villarreal’s third late on. The third win of Liverpool’s Champions League season puts them second in the 36-team super-table, and behind defending champions Paris St-Germain only on goal difference.

Liverpool are also seeing a new star emerge. Ngumoha might be the most expensive academy signing in the game’s modern history but alongside the £100m men he looks like a risk that was worth taking.

We have said all night about momentum, and talking about how they Liverpool will play against Brighton at the weekend, I’ll be amazed if Rio [Ngumoha] doesn’t start because of the momentum that he has got from this game.

You see the fans, you see how everyone got a lift by him and that’s what they need at the weekend, they need someone to lift them.

They are flying. Their confidence is through the roof. A similar style to Villarreal. They are second in everything after Barcelona. It has been a good game to prepare and we will use it.

I am really happy with Rio. He is trying to improve everything and we are trying to correct things. He played a lot on the left and know he is playing a lot on the right and he has adapted really well. We encourage him always. Even defensively as well he is improving. He has become a more complete player – and we must not forget he is 18!

Rio Ngumoha was magnificent tonight. Such a threat, and he dedicated himself to his tasks. On the ball this kid has so much potential, and I say kid, but he’s a young man. He has so much quality and it’s stuff that you can’t teach to be honest.

What he does with the ball at his feet, that is God given ability, and his hard work on the training pitch, doing things day in and day out, and being ruthless, is what he said in his interview, and I like that. He wants to be decisive, and I love that about him.

I’m not tall but I love going in the box. I really like it. They know I like to attack the near post. I scored in the World Cup as well. It was a good header. The second goal, Rio, was amazing. I talk with him about cutting it back on the floor.

It’s not something I really practice. My dad is a bit smaller than me but he was quite good in the air so maybe it’s something I got from him.

Last year was a really difficult year for all of us. It was clear I was not at the level and I am the first one to say. Something wasn’t right in the group and this manager changed it. The way we play is different, I don’t like to compare. I’m feeling good.

A lot of things happened today. They were much better than us in the first half and we were much better in the second half. When we’ve been under pressure, we answered well. When we relaxed, we made mistakes. You cannot relax against very good opposition. I value the win.

We have to know that if we don’t go to the limit, it will be difficult. We are facing very good teams. It’s good to come back but we’ve started losing too many goals this season.

Florian Wirtz has scored or assisted in three consecutive games for the first time in his Liverpool career: 🅰️ vs LASK 🅰️ vs Brentford ⚽️ vs Villarreal https://t.co/woLWk2SGGL

It was a top performance from the boys. We were two goals down but the mentality was always there. We knew we were going to win.

It’s up there with one of the best I’ve played. I enjoyed myself and the team helped me a lot.

Whenever I get the ball and there’s an opportunity to go one v one or two v one, I believe in myself. I’ll just keep going and be ruthless.

Rio Ngumoha talking to Gabriel Clarke on Amazon Prime: “Definitely one of the best games I played. I enjoyed it.  Whenever I get the ball and go one v one, the more it makes the opposition worried.”

When he was reminded that he was the youngest Englishman to provide an assist in the Champions League, he said: “Records are amazing to break.”

And on playing on the right instead of the left wing: “It’s helped me a lot in training. Slowly I’m getting better on the right.”

And to hear the crowd chanting his name: “This stadium, we have the best fans. To hear my name being chanted is a dream.”

PSG’s 4-2 win over Barcelona tonight also puts them on nine points. Aston Villa, Arsenal, Real Madrid, Sporting and Real Betis are the teams playing tomorrow night with the opportunity to maintain a 100 per cent record.

Nine points from a possible nine for Liverpool in the Champions League, but they made hard work of it. Some dysfunction was probably to be expected after Iraola decided to start without Mac Allister, Isak, Wirtz and Barcola, but their defensive structure was unzipped far too easily at times.

On the other hand, they dragged themselves off the canvas and the night belonged to Rio Ngumoha. He looked dangerous every time he received the ball, set up the third goal, and received a standing ovation when he was substituted. Liverpool need to put that contract in front of him sharpish.

Still time for another hairy moment at the back for Liverpool, but Perez’ shot from the edge of the area is blocked and that will surely be that.

Pape Gueye floats a cross straight down the throat of Alisson. A wasted opportunity for Villarreal. But still a couple of minutes to play.

Just the three minutes of added time to play, and Liverpool are probably grateful for that.

Could Liverpool be in for a nervous finish? Their defence is caught square again after a run in behind from Ayoze Perez, and Oluwaseyi was totally unmarked at the back post to apply a simple finish at silence Anfield.

Cody Gakpo threatens to score Liverpool’s fifth with an overhead free-kick, teed up by McConnell’s chipped cross to the back post, but he could not keep the attempt down.

The game is meandering towards its conclusion now, though a Villarreal goal would make things interesting.

Another Liverpool youngster enjoys a taste of first-team actions: James McConnell is on for Nyoni.

2 - Rio Ngumoha (18y 52d) is the third-youngest player to provide multiple assists in a UEFA Champions League game behind Warren Zaïre-Emery v Milan (17y 231d) and Theo Walcott v Hamburger SV (17y 250d). Flying. https://t.co/CUbbleRhEJ

Perez hits the post for Villarreal with only Alisson to beat, but the flag is raised for offside. I think that would have stood had he found the net, Van Dijk may have been playing him just onside.

Ngumoha receives his standing ovation, lovely moment for him. He has strong claims to be in Liverpool’s best XI. Bradley Barcola replaces him, not the player Villarreal’s tired defenders needed to see.

That is surely game over now, Liverpool heading for three Champions League wins from three. Former Newcastle United forward Ayoze Perez is now on for Villarreal. Ngumoha will be replaced by Barcola shortly and I’m sure he will receive a standing ovation.

The game has been transformed, and Villarreal are falling to pieces. They were guilty of losing possession far too cheaply, but Wirtz deserves credit for finishing with an authority he has been accused of lacking. Well struck across the goalkeeper with his left foot, his first Liverpool goal since April.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Ngumoha has been Liverpool’s best player on the night, although Cardona sold himself all too easily near the touchline. Ngumoha makes the right decision to pick out Mac Allister with a low cross, and the midfielder converts with the simplest of finishes.

Isak then replaces Koumas immediately after the goal.

Alexis Mac Allister’s second goal but Anfield also singing about Rio Ngumoha. He went past two Villarreal defenders to create that one. He has been outstanding.

There will be time to talk more about Rio Ngumoha – this is his best performance in a Liverpool shirt, a coming-of-age night if you will – but it cannot be overlooked how Alexis Mac Allister has been transformed. He was unrecognisable last season but now he is every inch the man who was a major cog in the push for the title.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Tsimikas with a dangerous, driven cross from the left which is just beyond the reach of Koumas. Liverpool knocking on the door.

Nyoni’s standing foot was slipping, but he made a clean connection on his shot from range and it whistled just wide of the foot of the post. Ngumoha then has the crowd cooing again, with another drop of the shoulder to beat his man.

Gravenberch found himself sweeping up as Liverpool’s last man, there. The second half has had a more conventional feel, Liverpool making the running as they shoot towards the Kop and their opponents soaking up the pressure. A game of fewer chances since the break.

Always helps having knowledge in close vicinity: a quick discussion with Rafa Benitez about Liverpool’s set up for the second period. Ryan Gravenberch hasn’t been moved to play as a right-back, even though you might think that is the case. Liverpool, essentially, are playing man-against-man. It is going to ask players to be brave on the ball and composed when they are in possession, as the slightest slip will lead to problems. It is high risk and high reward.

Not enough power in Gakpo’s strike from the edge of the area and Gulasci saves. Ngumoha looking such a threat again, attracting the attention of three or four yellow shirts and winning Liverpool another corner. Former Spurs player Juan Foyth has just been introduced by Villarreal.

Liverpool more industrious when they lose possession early in the half. Nyoni then produces a silky turn away from pressure deep in his own half which elicits an “ooohh” from the home fans.

Gravenberch took the ball off Ngumoha’s toes in the box, and the Dutchman’s shot from a tight angle was saved by Gulasci at his near post. I think Ngumoha deserved to have the shot himself after more great skill to find a yard.

Wirtz replaces Araujo, which could mean Gravenberch at right-back.

Oluwaseyi, another of Villarreal’s Canadian cohort, is on too. He replaces Saliba.

Florian Wirtz has been readied for action and will soon enter the fray. You would think these will be the kind of conditions in which he will excel. He needs to. Liverpool are lucky to be level.

03:54 - Georges Mikautadze's opener for Villarreal (03:54) is the second-earliest goal Liverpool have conceded at home in major European competition behind only Elpídio Silva's strike in the 3rd minute for Boavista in the UEFA Champions League in September 2001. Cold. https://t.co/NvKmS5jLap

Dreadful first 30 minutes from Liverpool but they have woken up since, and now they are strong favourites to win the game from here. Iraola’s selection gamble backfired somewhat, but he may well get away with it.

From the second phase of a corner, Ngumoha did well to keep the ball alive and lift a cross to the back post. Cardona tried to usher the ball behind and made the fatal mistake of letting it bounce in his penalty area, and Araujo sneaked in to score from close range.

The goalscorer Cardona makes a mistake to let Ngumoha’s cross drift to the backpost. That’s Liverpool’s equaliser from Ronald Araujo. As soon as Liverpool have got their act together they have looked dangerous.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

The crowd were impatient with him early in the half, but Gakpo is looking more of a threat now, Cruyff-turning away and shooting in the box but Veiga was across to block. Just the one minute of added time to play.

Gakpo wins Liverpool a free-kick in a shooting position left of centre, tripped after Nyoni had carried the ball well through midfield. Too much air on the attempt from Mac Allister, who a couple of minutes earlier fired not too far wide from 25 yards.

Plenty for Andoni Iraola to be annoyed about, but as a spectacle this has been far more entertaining than initially assumed.

Really slick interplay from Villarreal again, and Moleiro’s shot from 25 yards is pushed over the bar by Alisson. You can pick holes in Liverpool, but Villarreal’s play deserves plaudits too.

Alexis Mac Allister grabs a goal back for Liverpool 🔴 Game 🔛 https://t.co/Ml9OYgbNq6

Liverpool have scarcely merited a goal but they have one via a set-piece. Alexis Mac Allister was up early at the near post and he produced a well-directed glancing header into the far corner. That changes the complexion of the game.

Great finish from Mac Allister. The opportunity for Gakpo to cross from the left - that won the corner - was made by Koumas’ hold-up play. First time he has really got hold of it and pinned the defender.

Another run from deep causes Liverpool’s defence problems, but Mikautadze took a touch when a first-time pass could have released the runner through on goal. More groans from the crowd when Tsimikas is caught on the ball.

Then Gakpo flashes a better ball across the face of goal, and Veiga glances it behind for a Liverpool corner.

Villarreal want a corner, and they should have one after a shot deflects off Araujo’s back. Goal kick given though.

Gakpo and Koumas are on the wrong wavelength, and there are groans from the crowd at another misplaced pass.

Liverpool need to dig themselves out of a hole now, Villarreal have cut them apart to score a simple second. Cardona, the left-back, with a run from deep, and Tsimikas was playing him onside. Cardona had all the time in the world to steady himself and roll the ball beyond Alisson.

Defensive calamity for Liverpool. Both Mikautadze and Cardona could have taken that through ball from Saliba and finished.

Straight through the heart of the defence 👀 Sergi Cardona doubles Villarreal's lead at Anfield 🤯 https://t.co/ZPHAkiLjN0

Liverpool far too easy to play through at the moment, Villarreal might not be an elite team but they have enough technique to pass and move well if given the time. Mikautadze lacks some pace up front, but has shown some silky touches. As Alan Shearer puts in on Amazon Prime: “Feels like a training match for Liverpool. So lazy. Where’s the urgency?”

Better from Liverpool with Nyoni driving forward and the ball almost running into the path of Gravenberch for a strike from the edge of the box. Villarreal diligent in their defensive work though, no clear sight of goal for the Liverpool players so far.

Anyone who is experiencing Anfield on a European night for the first time will be wondering what all the fuss is about. Aside from a couple of flurries following a Ronald Araujo tackle and a Rio Ngumoha dribble, it has been deathly quiet. Rafael Benitez, an architect of some of the wildest evenings here, is in the press box alongside Robbie Fowler and they are a reminder of how it used to be. Liverpool need to raise themselves to bring the crowd to life.

Ngumoha is the one ray of light for Liverpool so far, he has the beating of Villarreal left-back Cardona whenever he drops a shoulder. Gulasci palms his deflected cross over and Villarreal survive the corner.

The flag was eventually raised for offside, but Villarreal were in behind the Liverpool defence again after a misplaced Van Dijk pass. Liverpool have not got themselves out of the blocks at all. They have lost possession too cheaply and look vulnerable defensively.

Buchanan with a teasing low cross through the Liverpool penalty area, and the winger is justified when looking quizzically at his team-mates. If one of the yellow shirts had gambled they would have had a tap in.

Most of Liverpool’s attacks are being funnelled down their right so far, perhaps no surprise given that is where Ngumoha is stationed. Liverpool yet to test the goalkeeper, though.

Villarreal then throw a punch of their own down the other end, with Saliba turning and shooting at the edge of the box. Deflected, and Villarreal have a corner. Delivery is poor and Liverpool clear.

The Spanish team are moving the ball around with assurance, some nice touches from Saliba in their midfield (the Canada international is no relation to the Arsenal centre-back).

Hats off to Villarreal coach Inigo Perez, who is not wearing a hat or, indeed, a coat. Instead he is steadfastly ignoring the cold drizzle and treating this, from a touchline outfit point of view, like a warm summer’s evening on the Valencian coast. Polo shirt and slacks for the young Spanish coach.

No need for Liverpool to panic just yet, plenty of time to turn this around, and Rio Ngumoha is going the right way about it. Quick feet in the box to beat his man and fashion a yard for a strike, but his shot is blocked. Ngumoha is playing on Liverpool’s right tonight with Gakpo on the opposite flank.

What a remarkable start. Virgil van Dijk has looked a gear or two behind everyone in the opening stages. One bad touch required Jeremy Jacquet to make a swift recovery and that misplaced header has now handed Villarreal the lead. Social media will be abuzz with scrutiny about Van Dijk now, as is always the case when he errs, but it won’t be taken into consideration that he has been one of Liverpool’s best players in these opening 10 games. What price would you make him to atone with a header at the other end later in the game?

Van Dijk has made two dreadful mistakes in the first four minutes and this time he is punished. Liverpool’s captain was trying to guide a header back to Alisson, but the ball shanked off his forehead at the wrong angle and dropped for Mikautadze in the box. The striker was free, and he finished well across Alisson. That was not in the script.

The Georgian No 9 for Villarreal Georges Mikautadze had looked so lightweight in the early duels with Virgil Van Dijk and Jeremy Jacquet. They had muscled him off the ball more than once. That was a gift from Van Dijk and Mikautadze took it very well.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

Ryan Gravenberch has started the game in a more advanced midfield role with Nyoni and Mac Allister behind him. The home team are yet to string together a serious sequence of passes in the Villarreal half.

Liverpool trying to harry their opponents early on, but Van Dijk makes a hash of dealing with a simple long ball forward. Villarreal’s striker Mikautadze took too long to bring the ball down and the chance was gone with Jacquet closing him out.

It’s another young Liverpool team fielded in the Champions League, but they should have enough about them to see off this Villarreal side.

Out to get warm! ♨️ https://t.co/75qTJA6L42

We have two important wins for us but we cannot stop. A very good team in front of us and I hope we are at the level of the game.

Different circumstances. It’s out fourth game in 10 days, Florian [Wirtz] and Bradley [Barcola] have played almost every minute so we have to be sensible and the same with Alex [Isak].

I think he is doing very well [Leiws Koumas], or else we would not trust him to start these kinds of games.

Probably difficult to find someone who knows me better [than Inigo Perez], but we also know him!

Villarreal XI: Gulacsi, Mourino, Navarro, Veiga, Cardona, Saliba, Gueye, Buchanan, Comesana, Moleiro, Mikautadze

Subs: Junior, Costa, Freeman, Diatta, Gerard, Foyth, Akhomach, Macia, Oluwaseyi, Perez, El Jmili, Gaitan Diaz

Liverpool XI: Alisson; Araujo, Jacquet, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; Gravenberch, Nyoni, Mac Allister; Ngumoha, Koumas, Gakpo

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Kerkez, Wirtz, Isak, Barcola, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Laffey

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

#1350. Pat Cummins' remarkable 68-minute press conference took a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Usman Khawaja's integrity - Australia are in a civil war with no obvious resolution, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

Published: 05:20 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 05:21 EST, 13 November 2026

Pat Cummins is either the greatest actor in world sport – or the claim that the whole Australian team knew about the sandpaper plot in South Africa eight years ago is a figment of Usman Khawaja’s imagination.

After Cummins’s remarkable press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, in which he called Khawaja’s various assertions ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship, it was hard to discern any common ground, much less spot a middle way.

According to the blue corner, everyone was in on the scam, sandpaper was used not just at Cape Town but in the previous Test at Port Elizabeth, and there was a team meeting to discuss the question of collective responsibility.

According to the red, those who knew about the plan did not include the bowlers, nothing untoward happened at Port Elizabeth, and there was no meeting.

The only thing that can be said for certain after another tumultuous 24 hours for Australian cricket was that the two corners are now polar opposites, each eyeing the other with suspicion and incredulity. Barring an improbable climbdown, the twain can never meet.

Cummins, it must be said, eased into his work after an emotional start behind a lectern at the Cricket Central venue in Sydney’s Olympic Park. He began by stating his basic position, then invited questions, which for the next hour and a bit he handled with aplomb and a degree of statesmanship.

Pat Cummins held a remarkable press conference in Sydney to address the sandpaper claims

Speaking for more than an hour, Cummins dismissed Khawaja’s various assertions as ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship

This will not please those who still find it impossible to believe that Cummins and his fellow seamers on that trip, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, knew nothing of the scheme that led to bans for three batsmen – Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

After all, as any bowler will tell you, the idea that the condition of their most prized possession might be altered without their noticing is as absurd as trying to persuade a batsman to walk out without his favourite willow.

And yet. Cummins stuck to his guns, in contrast to Khawaja’s appearance on the ABC on Wednesday evening, when he repeatedly declined to name Cummins as one of the guilty party. And while Khawaja reacted to his TV grilling by cancelling media engagements, Cummins made it clear he would be answering every question that came his way.

Whichever side you believe, and whatever the doubts that remain, his press conference grabbed the momentum from Team Khawaja.

It also made the previous day’s appearance by Mitchell Marsh, Australia’s white-ball captain for the next three weeks against England, all the more bizarre. By refusing to engage with any of the questions raised by Khawaja’s autobiography, Marsh – himself a veteran of South Africa 2018 – did little to dispel the suspicion that Khawaja had a point.

And that in turn encouraged the view that Cummins, who called his own press conference without the knowledge of Cricket Australia, might be about to come clean.

Instead, he doubled down on the denial he and his bowling colleagues had issued in 2021, but now went further, taking a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Khawaja’s integrity.

‘Usman is a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,’ said Cummins. ‘He’s dealt with the way he’s presented his story in a very casual manner and it affects a lot of people. That’s what I’m grappling with at the moment, because I don’t think that’s OK. It’s not what friends do.’

Cummins plainly intended this to be his final word on the matter, but the problem facing Australian cricket is that the sore may never properly heal.

David Warner then hit back at Cummins and accused him of 'throwing Khawaja under the bus'

Only a couple of hours after Cummins finished, Warner – at Perth’s Optus Stadium as a TV pundit for the first ODI between Australia and England – was being asked for his view, and he didn’t hold back, repeating his belief that Khawaja’s version of events was ‘the truth’.

He added: ‘I really, really support him. I actually feel for him at the moment. I feel that the captain today threw Uzzy under the bus and I’m very, very disappointed about that.’

Disappointment. It’s mutual, and it’s everywhere. Cummins provided a brief distraction, but it doesn’t change the fact that this is a civil war with no obvious resolution.

Offered the chance to kick Australian cricket while it was down, England made humiliating contact with fresh air on the opening day of their eight-match white-ball trip.

Only hours after Pat Cummins had added a twist to the sandpaper saga by dismissing Usman Khawaja’s claims that the whole squad knew about the ball-tampering plans in South Africa eight years ago as ‘complete and utter nonsense’, Harry Brook’s side were blown away for 131 in the first ODI – having at one stage been 65 for eight.

Australia then romped home by seven wickets with more than 26 overs in hand to take a 1–0 lead into the second game of this three-match series in Adelaide on Sunday. For England, anyway, complete and utter nonsense felt about right.

It is not quite a year since they began their Ashes campaign here at the Optus Stadium by being bowled out in 32.5 overs in their first innings and 34.4 in their second – before stumbling to a 4–1 defeat.

Now, they obligingly split the difference, dismissed in 33.4 as Mahli Beardman, a 21-year-old fast bowler from Dunsborough, a couple of hours drive down the coast from Perth, picked up six for 34 – the best figures for Australia by an ODI debutant.

His first victim was Joe Root, caught behind for a painful 17 off 36 balls, and his second Brook, who had made only a single when he fidgeted fatally outside off stump.

That might have been enough to satisfy most newcomers, but Beardman had barely started. Jordan Cox made two before edging a poke, and Sam Curran top-edged a pull to fine leg for a duck.

When Liam Dawson, yet to score, squeezed a drive to backward point, Beardman had five wickets in 28 balls – not bad for a player whose only previous taste of international cricket had come in a T20 in Pakistan in January.

He then ended a lively last-wicket stand of 29 by removing Jofra Archer, who had just driven him down the ground for four. It was the only authentic boundary England managed off his bowling: the other, a streaky inside edge from Root, summed up the problems posed by his pace, bounce and accuracy. As bids for a place on next summer’s Ashes tour go, this was hard to ignore.

‘Laying in bed last night, that’s not what I had planned,’ said Beardman, who was taken under his wing by Australian fast-bowling legend Dennis Lillee after a mutual friend spotted him as a young teenager bowling at a bin down the side of a house. ‘It was an incredible game and it all happened so fast.’

If England had learned lessons from their collapses in the last year’s Test here, they showed little sign of being able to implement them. Players drove on the up, as they had so heedlessly a year earlier, and failed to cope with the Perth bounce.

England head coach Brendon McCullum was critical of his side's failure to adapt to the pitch, and called on them to learn from their mistakes going forward.

'It’s a bit like batting on a trampoline,' said McCullum. 'There are certain shots that are very difficult to execute. We talked about trying to put those away. We probably knew we were in for a low-scoring contest, but we expected to get a few more runs than 130.

'We're disappointed but there are some good lessons for us. If you look towards the World Cup in South Africa there’s going to be some pitches there that will test us from a bounce point of view.'

And all this after they had played a warm-up game at the WACA – a grievous omission before the Ashes – and trained with such intensity that white-ball mentor Kevin Pietersen had declared it the best practice session he had seen from an England team.

In the event, their top-scorer was Gus Atkinson, who hit an unbeaten 29 from No 10, including England’s only six.

Mitchell Marsh, stroke-less in the previous day’s press conference, put that into perspective by clearing the ropes four times during a 29-ball half-century, while Cooper Connolly – dropped by Tom Banton at midwicket on five – hit two sixes himself.

England’s only consolation had come at the start of Australia’s reply, when Atkinson bowled Travis Head first ball off the inside edge. Head it was who had taken care of Australia’s fourth-innings chase here a year ago, thrashing a 69-ball century that knocked the stuffing out of Ben Stokes’s attack.

Instead, it was Marsh who went for his shots, stopped only when he flicked Jamie Overton to Ben Duckett at deep midwicket, by which time Australia were already halfway there. For a few hours, at least, no one was talking about sandpaper.
